questions.title: Authorization boundary
questions.prompt: Where must access control apply?

choices.text: Only in a prompt asking the model not to reveal secrets
choices.why: The model has already received unauthorized content.

choices.text: In retrieval and content delivery before unauthorized text reaches the model
choices.why: Eligibility is enforced outside generation.

choices.text: Only after the answer is displayed
choices.why: Disclosure has already happened.

choices.text: Only when documents are initially embedded
choices.why: Permissions can change afterward.

questions.explanation: The generator must not become the permission enforcement mechanism. Scope candidates and fetched content to the caller, and define how changed permissions invalidate index metadata or cached answers. Test authorization on both initial retrieval and later cache reuse, because an answer containing protected evidence can leak even when the current query fetches no new documents.
questions.tradeoff: Fresh eligibility checks add query cost and dependency concerns.
questions.followup: How would you handle group revocation during an existing conversation?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An assistant retrieves company documents before generating answers. Users belong to different groups; document permissions can change. Embeddings are stored in a shared index.

questions.title: Permission-aware cache
questions.prompt: What belongs in an answer-cache eligibility decision? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The caller's authorized scope or a safe equivalent partition
choices.why: Identical questions can have different permitted evidence.
That can reuse a privileged answer for another user.

choices.text: Relevant document and policy versions or freshness checks
choices.why: Old answers can contain newly restricted material.
Vector shape does not establish permission.

questions.explanation: Answer reuse must preserve the evidence boundary of the original generation. A semantically similar question is not enough to make an answer shareable across users. Track the evidence versions used to produce an answer, so a policy or document change can invalidate precisely the cached results whose authorization assumptions no longer hold.
questions.tradeoff: More scoped keys reduce hit rate.
questions.followup: Could some public answers be shared safely across all tenants?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An assistant retrieves company documents before generating answers. Users belong to different groups; document permissions can change. Embeddings are stored in a shared index.

questions.title: Index update lag
questions.prompt: A document permission revocation must prevent any new disclosure after the revocation is acknowledged; semantic indexing lags five minutes. Which design meets that contract?

choices.text: Ask users not to query during updates
choices.why: That is not an enforcement control.

choices.text: Trust the old embedding metadata indefinitely
choices.why: The stale policy still authorizes access.

choices.text: Enforce current fail-closed authorization, or complete a serving-version/invalidation barrier before acknowledging revocation
choices.why: The acknowledgment boundary must establish that stale authorization cannot cause a new disclosure; an unspecified finite delay is not immediate revocation.

choices.text: Delete every index on every ACL change
choices.why: It is disproportionate and harms availability.

questions.explanation: Embedding freshness and access authority are different concerns. The stated revocation contract needs an enforceable boundary: current authorization checks must fail closed, or a revocation barrier must cover serving paths and in-flight disclosures before acknowledgment. Merely limiting stale permissions to five seconds still permits a post-acknowledgment disclosure and does not satisfy this requirement.
questions.tradeoff: Extra filtering can reduce retrieval recall or add latency.
questions.followup: How would you handle an unavailable authorization service?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An assistant retrieves company documents before generating answers. Users belong to different groups; document permissions can change. Embeddings are stored in a shared index.

questions.title: Security evaluation
questions.prompt: Which test most directly targets cross-tenant leakage?

choices.text: Ask identical queries as users with disjoint permissions and inspect evidence plus answer
choices.why: It exercises retrieval and cached-generation boundaries.
A helpful answer can leak secrets.
Authenticated horizontal escalation remains untested.

choices.text: Check only that embeddings are numerical
choices.why: Representation type is unrelated to access.

questions.explanation: Inspect the documents supplied to the model as well as final text. A model declining to repeat a secret does not excuse retrieving that secret for an unauthorized user. Include users whose permissions change mid-session, because conversation state can retain privileged material after a later retrieval request correctly filters the same document out.
questions.tradeoff: Audit traces themselves contain sensitive context and need controls.
questions.followup: How would shared conversation memory enter the same test?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An assistant retrieves company documents before generating answers. Users belong to different groups; document permissions can change. Embeddings are stored in a shared index.

questions.title: Same dimensions trap
questions.prompt: Can a B query vector be safely compared against A document vectors merely because dimensions match?

choices.why: Equal shape does not align learned coordinates.

choices.text: Yes, if all vector values are positive
choices.why: Sign does not establish semantic alignment.

choices.text: No; model identity and compatible embedding space matter
choices.why: Distance only has meaning within the intended representation.

choices.text: No vector models can ever be migrated
choices.why: Versioned migration is possible.

questions.explanation: A vector's dimension is a storage shape, not a semantic schema. Query and document representations must come from compatible encoders and preprocessing. Version the normalization and preprocessing alongside the encoder, since even the same model artifact can produce incompatible comparisons if one path changes how inputs are prepared.
questions.tradeoff: Parallel indexes increase temporary storage.
questions.followup: How would you detect accidental cross-version queries?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A search system stores vectors from embedding model A. Model B uses the same vector length but a different learned coordinate space. Existing documents remain searchable during migration.

questions.title: Safe dual operation
questions.prompt: Which rollout supports online comparison?

choices.text: Maintain versioned A and B indexes with matching query encoders
choices.why: Each query evaluates a coherent representation.

choices.text: Overwrite half the vectors without version labels
choices.why: One index mixes incompatible meanings.

choices.text: Route B queries randomly into A or B storage
choices.why: Results become uninterpretable.

choices.text: Delete A before B covers all required documents
choices.why: Search coverage is lost.

questions.explanation: Version both the query path and indexed data. Shadow comparisons can measure relevance before switching authority, while A remains a recovery path. Keep new document ingestion and deletions synchronized into both supported versions during the overlap, so a rollback preserves current coverage rather than restoring only historical searchability.
questions.tradeoff: Dual encoding and indexing cost compute.
questions.followup: Which documents should be prioritized in the backfill?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A search system stores vectors from embedding model A. Model B uses the same vector length but a different learned coordinate space. Existing documents remain searchable during migration.

questions.title: Cutover evidence
questions.prompt: What matters beyond successful vector writes?

choices.why: It proves shape, not usefulness.

choices.text: Coverage, relevance by query segment, latency and permission preservation
choices.why: The migration changes both data and retrieval behavior.
Compression can reduce recall.

choices.text: Only a better average similarity score
choices.why: Scores across models may not be comparable.

questions.explanation: Evaluate user-relevant retrieval outcomes on a stable corpus and representative queries. Raw scores can shift calibration, so do not compare them as if they were the same unit. Review rare entities, languages and permission-filtered searches separately, because an average relevance improvement can hide a serious regression in a small but important population.
questions.tradeoff: Relevance labels and segment coverage require curation.
questions.followup: How would multilingual or rare-entity queries be represented?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A search system stores vectors from embedding model A. Model B uses the same vector length but a different learned coordinate space. Existing documents remain searchable during migration.

questions.title: Rollback after new writes
questions.prompt: New documents exist only in B. What makes rollback to A incomplete?

choices.why: Age alone is not the issue.

choices.text: The UI has a new search icon
choices.why: Presentation is unrelated.

choices.text: Both indexes have the same dimensions
choices.why: That does not establish coverage.

choices.text: A lacks newly accepted documents unless dual ingestion or catch-up is maintained
choices.why: Rollback requires current data, not just an old binary.

questions.explanation: A usable rollback path must keep up with authoritative changes. Otherwise reverting the query encoder silently removes recent content from results. Define a retirement checkpoint for A only after the rollback obligation ends, and record any interval in which reverting would knowingly sacrifice recently accepted document coverage.
questions.tradeoff: Maintaining both ingestion paths prolongs migration cost.
questions.followup: When can A's catch-up stream be safely retired?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A search system stores vectors from embedding model A. Model B uses the same vector length but a different learned coordinate space. Existing documents remain searchable during migration.

questions.title: Future information
questions.prompt: What is wrong with the training join?

choices.text: It can expose facts unavailable at prediction time
choices.why: Offline evaluation becomes unrealistically favorable.

choices.text: Latest values are always less accurate
choices.why: They may be accurate now but temporally invalid then.
They can if defined at the correct time.

choices.text: The join is wrong only if types differ
choices.why: Temporal correctness is separate from type correctness.

questions.explanation: The feature must represent what could have been known for that prediction. A later balance can encode consequences of the very event the model is trying to predict. Retain event and availability timestamps where needed to distinguish a feature that existed historically from one the online decision system could actually have observed at that moment.
questions.tradeoff: Historical storage and event-time reconstruction increase cost.
questions.followup: How would delayed source ingestion affect what was actually knowable?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A fraud model predicts at transaction time. Training currently joins each historical transaction to the customer's latest account balance, which may include events occurring afterward.

questions.title: Point-in-time retrieval
questions.prompt: Training must reproduce what the production model could actually know at each historical decision. Which feature lookup fits that requirement?

choices.text: Always use the newest feature row
choices.why: That leaks future state.
It does not represent the decision context.

choices.text: Use recorded serving features, or state that was both event-time eligible and actually available by the decision time
choices.why: A retrospectively corrected value can be valid for an earlier event time without having been available to the production model then.

choices.text: Use the label as a feature
choices.why: That directly reveals the target.

questions.explanation: Reproducing production decisions requires both event-time eligibility and actual availability by the prediction timestamp, or the features recorded during serving. A late-arriving correction must not become knowledge the model supposedly had earlier. An ideal event-time reconstruction can support a separate retrospective experiment, but it must not be presented as faithful historical serving behavior.
questions.tradeoff: Reproducing actual availability needs more lineage metadata.
questions.followup: Which timestamps must the feature pipeline retain?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A fraud model predicts at transaction time. Training currently joins each historical transaction to the customer's latest account balance, which may include events occurring afterward.

questions.title: Offline-online mismatch
questions.prompt: A corrected temporal join reduces offline accuracy. What is the right interpretation?

choices.text: The corrected pipeline must be worse for production
choices.why: The old score may have been inflated by leakage.

choices.text: The estimate may now be more realistic; validate serving behavior and labels
choices.why: Lower offline scores can reflect removal of impossible information.

choices.text: Restore future values to recover the metric
choices.why: That recreates leakage.
Evidence remains necessary.

questions.explanation: A metric drop can be an improvement in measurement validity. Reassess thresholds and business costs using data available under the real decision process. Explain which impossible information was removed and compare business decisions under realistic inputs, so stakeholders do not mistake a more honest estimate for a broken evaluation pipeline.
questions.tradeoff: More honest evaluation may delay launch or require better features.
questions.followup: How would you explain this change to non-ML stakeholders?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A fraud model predicts at transaction time. Training currently joins each historical transaction to the customer's latest account balance, which may include events occurring afterward.

questions.title: Reproduce the training decision
questions.prompt: Match each uncertainty to the versioned artifact needed to resolve it. Use each choice once.

items.text: Which input records and historical facts were eligible?
How were raw values normalized and missing fields interpreted?
Which learned parameters produced this score?
How did a score become approve, review or reject?

choices.text: Data snapshot, lineage and point-in-time policy
choices.why: These identify the observations available to the experiment or decision.
Names and shapes do not establish normalization, units or missing-value behavior.
The exact learned parameters must be identified independently of a mutable display name.
The business action can change even when the model score is identical.

questions.explanation: A model file is only one component of a reproducible decision. The data eligibility boundary, feature transformations and action policy also influence the outcome. Version and retain appropriate evidence for each layer, while respecting deletion and privacy obligations rather than assuming reproducibility permits unlimited raw-data retention. Link the final action to all four artifact identities where feasible, because identical model parameters can produce different decisions after a transformation or policy change.
questions.tradeoff: Lineage and historical artifacts increase storage and governance work.
questions.followup: Which evidence can be retained when the original personal data must be deleted?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A fraud model predicts at transaction time. Training currently joins each historical transaction to the customer's latest account balance, which may include events occurring afterward.

questions.title: Schema is not enough
questions.prompt: Why can identical feature names still produce bad predictions?

choices.why: They do not define units or normalization.

choices.text: Transformations, defaults or freshness can differ despite matching names
choices.why: The model receives a different distribution.
Values drive inference.
Data semantics matter.

questions.explanation: Feature compatibility includes meaning, units, missing-value behavior and time. A valid tensor shape can still contain systematically different values from training. Define a semantic feature contract including units, defaults and freshness, and treat changes to that contract as releases that can affect an otherwise unchanged model artifact.
questions.tradeoff: Shared code reduces drift but needs versioning.
questions.followup: How would you detect a changed unit from cents to whole currency?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A recommendation model trains with one normalization function but serves with a separately implemented function. Both functions accept the same feature names.

questions.title: Parity test
questions.prompt: Which test directly checks a fixed example across paths?

choices.text: Compare feature values and predictions from training and serving transformations
choices.why: It isolates representation drift for the same input.
Both paths can succeed with different values.
Text size is not semantic equivalence.
The skew is in feature processing.

questions.explanation: Use a fixed model and stable input so differences point to infrastructure rather than learning randomness. Include missing and boundary-value cases, not just typical examples. Include missing, zero, extreme and malformed values in the parity corpus, since normal examples often fail to expose different default handling or scaling between implementations.
questions.tradeoff: Exact numerical equality may need a documented floating-point tolerance.
questions.followup: How would online freshness differences be separated from transformation bugs?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A recommendation model trains with one normalization function but serves with a separately implemented function. Both functions accept the same feature names.

questions.title: Feature rollout
questions.prompt: A new feature arrives in training before online serving can supply it. Best policy?

choices.text: Deploy and let missing values mean whatever the library chooses
choices.why: The behavior is accidental.

choices.text: Fill every user with a random feature value
choices.why: That does not match training semantics.

choices.text: Gate rollout on serving availability or train/evaluate the defined missing-value path
choices.why: The deployed input contract is tested.

choices.text: Use the true future outcome as a temporary substitute
choices.why: That leaks target information.

questions.explanation: The model and serving pipeline form one release unit semantically, even if owned by different teams. A fallback is valid only if it was evaluated under the expected missingness pattern. Make the missing-feature rate visible during rollout and compare it with the evaluated fallback distribution, rather than assuming a nominal default is safe for every customer.
questions.tradeoff: Coordination can slow model iteration.
questions.followup: Who owns the feature's freshness SLO and incident response?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A recommendation model trains with one normalization function but serves with a separately implemented function. Both functions accept the same feature names.

questions.title: Monitoring choice
questions.prompt: What should monitoring include beyond prediction latency?

choices.why: It does not reveal feature drift.
Loading does not establish useful inputs.

choices.text: Only training accuracy from last month
choices.why: Serving distributions can change.

choices.text: Feature distributions, missingness, freshness and segmented outcomes
choices.why: The pipeline's semantic health becomes observable.

questions.explanation: A fast model can make consistently wrong decisions when inputs drift. Monitor leading input signals and delayed outcome evidence separately because labels may arrive much later. Separate data-pipeline incidents from model-quality drift so operators can repair missing or stale features without retraining a model that was functioning correctly on its intended inputs.
questions.tradeoff: High-dimensional monitoring needs selected signals and alert ownership.
questions.followup: How would you avoid alerting on harmless seasonal shifts?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A recommendation model trains with one normalization function but serves with a separately implemented function. Both functions accept the same feature names.

questions.title: Queue separation
questions.prompt: Which scheduling design best protects the interactive contract?

choices.text: One unbounded FIFO for all jobs
choices.why: Large offline work can delay interactive requests.

choices.text: Interactive requests wait until the largest possible batch fills
choices.why: Batch accumulation can consume the deadline.

choices.text: Separate bounded classes with deadline-aware batching and controlled sharing
choices.why: Utilization does not erase latency priorities.

choices.text: Dedicated maximum hardware for every request
choices.why: That ignores the stated efficiency goal.

questions.explanation: Batch waiting belongs to end-to-end latency. Separate demand classes so throughput-oriented offline work cannot consume the entire interactive budget. Include queue accumulation in the latency budget and bound borrowing, so an offline burst cannot occupy all execution slots just before interactive demand increases.
questions.tradeoff: Reserved interactive capacity may be underused at quiet times.
questions.followup: How can offline work borrow spare capacity safely?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. One inference service handles interactive requests with a 150 ms deadline and offline jobs with no immediate response requirement. Dynamic batching improves accelerator utilization.

questions.title: Variable input cost
questions.prompt: Why is request count alone a weak admission metric?

choices.text: Input lengths and output work can vary substantially
choices.why: Equal request counts can require unequal compute and memory.

choices.text: Every inference takes exactly one clock cycle
choices.why: No such model was specified.
Architecture and input shapes differ.

choices.text: Counting is impossible in distributed systems
choices.why: Counts are possible but incomplete.

questions.explanation: Admission should approximate the constrained resource, such as tokens, tensor shape or estimated compute. Validate estimates against observed cost and enforce hard safety bounds. Reserve capacity for plausible output growth or stop generation at a controlled bound, then compare estimates with actual usage to detect systematic undercharging of expensive requests.
questions.tradeoff: Cost estimation itself can be imperfect.
questions.followup: What happens when a request produces far more output than predicted?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. One inference service handles interactive requests with a 150 ms deadline and offline jobs with no immediate response requirement. Dynamic batching improves accelerator utilization.

questions.title: Autoscaling signal
questions.prompt: What should drive scaling beyond average GPU utilization?

choices.text: Scale only from total registered users
choices.why: Registered population can differ greatly from current inference demand and request cost.

choices.text: Queue age, deadline risk, workload shape and warmup time
choices.why: Scaling targets the user-visible backlog.

choices.text: Scale only when model-loading operations are slow
choices.why: Loading time affects reaction delay but does not measure queued demand or deadline risk.

choices.text: Scale only from host CPU utilization
choices.why: GPU, accelerator memory or batching queues may be limiting while the CPU remains relatively idle.

questions.explanation: High utilization can be healthy throughput or harmful deadline pressure. New replicas also need model loading and cache warmup, so reactive scaling has a delay. Account for model loading and warmup before expecting a newly scheduled replica to drain urgent queues, and use admission control when scaling cannot react within the deadline.
questions.tradeoff: Extra warm capacity costs money.
questions.followup: Which burst should be absorbed by admission rather than scale-out?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. One inference service handles interactive requests with a 150 ms deadline and offline jobs with no immediate response requirement. Dynamic batching improves accelerator utilization.

questions.title: Batch policy evaluation
questions.prompt: What is a convincing comparison of two batching policies?

choices.why: It is a configuration value.

choices.text: Only throughput on equal-size synthetic inputs
choices.why: Mixed production shapes can behave differently.
Latency and errors remain unknown.

choices.text: Useful throughput, tail/deadline misses, fairness and cost on representative traces
choices.why: It measures efficiency within service constraints.

questions.explanation: An efficient batcher can still starve a class or violate latency promises. Compare the whole allocation contract, not only aggregate hardware occupancy. Evaluate long and short requests in the same test trace, because a policy that performs well on uniform input can hide starvation or memory pressure from mixed shapes.
questions.tradeoff: Trace replay must protect sensitive inputs.
questions.followup: How would you evaluate a policy under an input-length attack?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. One inference service handles interactive requests with a 150 ms deadline and offline jobs with no immediate response requirement. Dynamic batching improves accelerator utilization.

questions.title: Trust boundary
questions.prompt: How should those document instructions be treated?

choices.text: As equivalent to the user's authorized request
choices.why: The document is untrusted task data.

choices.text: As untrusted content, not authority to invoke tools
choices.why: Retrieval does not grant permission.

choices.text: As mandatory because they are formatted prominently
choices.why: Formatting does not change trust.

choices.text: As safe if the document ranks first
choices.why: Relevance score is not authorization.

questions.explanation: Separate data being analyzed from instructions controlling the system. A useful retrieval result can still contain adversarial text, so tool permissions must not depend only on model interpretation. Treat documents, retrieved snippets and stored memory as separate untrusted inputs, since the same attempted authority escalation can arrive indirectly rather than through the immediate user prompt.
questions.tradeoff: Content filtering alone cannot guarantee resistance.
questions.followup: What should the assistant say about suspicious instructions in the source?

questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An assistant summarizes external documents and can request internal actions through tools. A retrieved document includes instructions to export private records to a remote URL.

questions.title: Tool enforcement
questions.prompt: Which controls help independently of prompt wording? Select all that apply.

choices.why: The tool checks actual caller authority.

choices.text: Grant every tool broad admin credentials
choices.why: A mistaken call has excessive impact.

choices.text: Let retrieved text set the tool's destination allowlist
choices.why: The attacker controls the policy.

choices.text: Require confirmation for sensitive external effects and restrict destinations
choices.why: Authority and exfiltration boundaries remain explicit.

questions.explanation: Enforce permissions where effects occur. Model instructions can guide behavior, but deterministic tool boundaries reduce harm when interpretation fails. Validate tool arguments against caller-specific scope at execution time, because a model can produce syntactically valid parameters that still request unauthorized resources or destinations.
questions.tradeoff: Extra approvals and narrow tools reduce automation convenience.
questions.followup: Which read-only tools can still leak sensitive data?

questions.title: Detection metric
questions.prompt: Why is a prompt-only jailbreak success rate insufficient?

choices.why: They do, but the system boundary is broader.
Architecture and permissions also matter.

choices.text: Real risk includes retrieval, memory, tool permissions and effect execution
choices.why: A blocked phrase does not prove end-to-end safety.

choices.text: Any refused prompt proves every tool is safe
choices.why: Refusal behavior is only one layer.

questions.explanation: Evaluate complete workflows with controlled canary data and bounded effects. Measure whether unauthorized information or actions cross the actual boundary, not merely whether the model repeats a phrase. Use canary secrets and harmless effect simulators in evaluation, so the test can detect boundary crossing without exposing real confidential data or executing damaging actions.
questions.tradeoff: End-to-end adversarial tests need safe sandboxes.
questions.followup: How would a delayed attack through stored conversation memory be tested?

questions.title: Least-authority redesign
questions.prompt: Which tool interface reduces risk most directly?

choices.text: A narrowly scoped operation with validated arguments and explicit authorization
choices.why: The tool exposes only the intended capability.

choices.text: A general shell with an administrator token
choices.why: It greatly expands possible effects.

choices.text: A URL fetcher allowed to call any internal endpoint
choices.why: It can become an exfiltration or SSRF path.

choices.text: A tool whose policy is supplied by the document
choices.why: The untrusted source defines its own authority.

questions.explanation: Tool design can make dangerous outcomes structurally harder to express. Keep authorization and destination validation outside generated text and treat model arguments as untrusted inputs. Prefer a bounded business operation over a general-purpose executor when the task permits it, reducing how much authority a mistaken or manipulated argument can exercise.
questions.tradeoff: Narrow tools require more engineering for varied workflows.
questions.followup: How would you preserve useful flexibility without exposing arbitrary execution?

questions.title: Approximation meaning
questions.prompt: What can approximation change?

choices.text: The nearest candidates returned relative to exact search
choices.why: Speed and memory can trade against recall.
Authorization is a separate constraint.
Index search does not retrain the model.

choices.text: Every query result must be wrong
choices.why: Approximate methods can return exact neighbors on many queries.

questions.explanation: Approximate retrieval is an algorithmic tradeoff with measurable misses. Evaluate it against exact neighbors and task quality rather than assuming the word approximate means unusable. Measure misses across representative filters and query segments, not only an average on easy queries, because approximation quality can degrade sharply for selective or unusual searches.
questions.tradeoff: Exact evaluation can be expensive on a large corpus.
questions.followup: How would you sample difficult queries without bias?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A retrieval service uses an approximate nearest-neighbor index to meet latency targets. A small exact-search reference set is available for evaluation.

questions.title: Measure recall
questions.prompt: Which comparison is informative?

choices.why: It does not measure neighbor retrieval.

choices.text: Only the number of index files
choices.why: Storage layout is not recall.

choices.text: Overlap with exact top-k under the same embeddings and eligibility rules
choices.why: The comparison isolates index approximation.

choices.text: Compare different models and corpora simultaneously
choices.why: Too many factors change to attribute recall differences.

questions.explanation: Hold representation and filtering constant when measuring the index. Otherwise a relevance difference may come from model changes or permissions rather than search approximation. Keep the exact reference's distance metric and eligibility rules identical, otherwise observed differences combine approximation with changes in the problem being solved.
questions.tradeoff: Filtered search can have different recall and latency behavior.
questions.followup: How would a very selective tenant filter affect candidate retrieval?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A retrieval service uses an approximate nearest-neighbor index to meet latency targets. A small exact-search reference set is available for evaluation.

questions.title: Index selection
questions.prompt: What should guide choosing compression versus a higher-recall index?

choices.why: Quality and latency can become unacceptable.

choices.text: Measured recall, task outcomes, latency, memory and update behavior
choices.why: The full workload contract determines the tradeoff.

choices.text: Only a benchmark from another corpus
choices.why: Vector distributions and filters differ.
It does not determine every operational property.

questions.explanation: Index choice is workload-dependent. Include insertion, deletion and rebuild costs because a read benchmark alone can hide poor fit for a frequently changing corpus. Include index maintenance under concurrent reads in the experiment, since frequent inserts, deletes or rebuilds can dominate the cost of a nominally fast query configuration.
questions.tradeoff: Higher recall often consumes more compute or memory.
questions.followup: Which failure would make a slower exact fallback worthwhile?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A retrieval service uses an approximate nearest-neighbor index to meet latency targets. A small exact-search reference set is available for evaluation.

questions.title: Relevance versus recall
questions.prompt: Exact nearest neighbors still produce poor answers. What next?

choices.text: Increase index recall beyond exact search
choices.why: Exact search already defines that reference.
Poor semantics can occur with correct distances.
Replication does not improve relevance.

choices.text: Evaluate embeddings, chunking, retrieval filters and downstream grounding
choices.why: The index may be correct while the representation is unhelpful.

questions.explanation: Nearest-vector correctness is not the same as useful evidence retrieval. Trace failures through candidate generation and answer generation before changing infrastructure. Inspect whether relevant source passages were present among candidates before blaming generation, and whether correct candidates actually supported the answer before tuning the vector index again.
questions.tradeoff: Semantic evaluation requires labeled or reviewed cases.
questions.followup: How would you distinguish missing evidence from poor answer synthesis?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A retrieval service uses an approximate nearest-neighbor index to meet latency targets. A small exact-search reference set is available for evaluation.

questions.title: Aggregate blind spot
questions.prompt: What is the main issue with the single average?

choices.text: Averages cannot be computed for models
choices.why: They can but can hide distributional harm.

choices.text: Every segment must have identical accuracy
choices.why: Different base rates can produce different metrics.

choices.text: It can hide a material regression in a consequential segment
choices.why: The product impact is not uniform.

choices.text: The model must have no useful improvement
choices.why: Some segments may improve genuinely.

questions.explanation: Evaluate outcomes at the granularity relevant to harm and business goals. Aggregate gains do not automatically justify a concentrated unacceptable loss. Predefine consequential segments and report uncertainty, avoiding both post-hoc cherry-picking and the assumption that every small segment has enough evidence for a precise metric.
questions.tradeoff: Segment evaluation needs enough data and careful uncertainty reporting.
questions.followup: Which segments should be defined before seeing results?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A fraud model's true outcomes arrive weeks later. Traffic shifts during a holiday. A new model improves an offline aggregate metric but harms one important customer segment.

questions.title: Delayed feedback
questions.prompt: What can be monitored before final labels arrive?

choices.text: Input drift, decision rates and proxy guardrails with explicit limits
choices.why: They provide early signals without pretending to be final accuracy.

choices.text: Final fraud loss with zero delay
choices.why: The labels are not yet known.
It says little about changed serving traffic.

choices.text: No metrics until all labels arrive
choices.why: Leading operational signals are still useful.

questions.explanation: Distinguish leading signals from confirmed outcomes. A proxy can detect unusual behavior but may not estimate the final business loss reliably. Revisit proxy usefulness once delayed labels arrive, because a convenient leading indicator can drift away from the business outcome it was originally intended to approximate.
questions.tradeoff: Proxy alerts can be noisy or misleading.
questions.followup: How would you backtest a proxy's relationship to eventual loss?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A fraud model's true outcomes arrive weeks later. Traffic shifts during a holiday. A new model improves an offline aggregate metric but harms one important customer segment.

questions.title: Canary decision
questions.prompt: What is a responsible rollout with uncertain seasonal effects?

choices.text: Ship globally from the aggregate offline score alone
choices.why: Seasonal and segment risk remains untested.

choices.text: Use bounded exposure, segment guardrails and delayed-outcome review
choices.why: The rollout gathers evidence while limiting harm.
No finite experiment removes all uncertainty.

choices.text: Select only easy customers for the canary and generalize globally
choices.why: The sample is unrepresentative.

questions.explanation: Match rollout exposure to the consequences of a wrong decision. Preserve a stable comparison cohort and avoid declaring success before important delayed labels mature. Keep treatment assignment and comparison populations stable enough to interpret the holiday effect, and retain a recovery path while high-consequence labels remain unresolved.
questions.tradeoff: Long evaluation windows slow iteration.
questions.followup: Which reversible actions can be tested faster than irreversible decisions?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A fraud model's true outcomes arrive weeks later. Traffic shifts during a holiday. A new model improves an offline aggregate metric but harms one important customer segment.

questions.title: Objective mismatch
questions.prompt: The model reduces chargebacks by rejecting many legitimate users. What should staff engineers revisit?

choices.text: Increase parameter count before revisiting the decision objective
choices.why: A more expressive model can optimize the same incomplete objective and preserve the rejection harm.

choices.text: Optimize inference latency while retaining the same threshold policy
choices.why: Faster harmful decisions do not address the false-positive tradeoff.

choices.text: Report only the chargeback metric because it improved
choices.why: That hides the legitimate-user cost rather than evaluating the whole product outcome.

choices.text: The objective, thresholds and costs of false positives and false negatives
choices.why: The optimized metric omitted part of the product tradeoff.

questions.explanation: Model accuracy is not a complete product objective. Decision thresholds translate scores into actions with different costs, so review both model and policy. Model false-positive and false-negative costs explicitly and review threshold changes separately from model changes, since a different action policy can produce the observed harm without new parameters.
questions.tradeoff: Cost estimates can be uncertain and vary by segment.
questions.followup: How would an appeal or human-review path change the optimal threshold?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A fraud model's true outcomes arrive weeks later. Traffic shifts during a holiday. A new model improves an offline aggregate metric but harms one important customer segment.

questions.title: Admission unit
questions.prompt: Which budget is more informative than request count alone?

choices.why: Connection count does not account for large variation in prompt and generation cost.

choices.text: Estimated input/output work with hard per-request and tenant bounds
choices.why: The policy approximates actual resource consumption.

choices.text: A fixed per-request charge independent of token or work estimates
choices.why: Equal request counts can consume very different amounts of compute and memory.

choices.text: Only yesterday's completed-request rate per tenant
choices.why: Historical rate does not bound the cost of today's request shape or burst.

questions.explanation: A single long generation may cost more than many short requests. Combine estimates with enforced ceilings and reconcile actual use so underestimation does not become unlimited authority. Combine aggregate tenant budgets with individual request bounds, because a tenant can exhaust capacity through either a few enormous requests or many individually acceptable ones.
questions.tradeoff: Overestimation can reject legitimate work.
questions.followup: How would streamed output update the remaining budget?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An assistant service pays per token and has bounded inference capacity. Requests vary in input length and requested output. One tenant can submit many long prompts.

questions.title: Cancellation accounting
questions.prompt: A user disconnects after receiving half the output. What should the service do?

choices.text: Propagate cancellation where supported and account for work already consumed
choices.why: Disconnect does not make prior compute free.

choices.text: Assume the model stopped automatically everywhere
choices.why: Backends may continue work.

choices.text: Refund all compute metrics to zero
choices.why: Resources were already used.

choices.text: Always finish maximum output regardless of policy
choices.why: That can waste scarce capacity.

questions.explanation: Transport lifecycle and inference lifecycle are separate. Measure whether cancellation actually stops backend work and retain honest usage accounting for completed computation. Trace cancellation across the client, gateway and inference worker to verify where compute actually stops, and treat any already committed external tool action separately from text generation.
questions.tradeoff: Cancellation races can leave some unavoidable excess work.
questions.followup: What should a retry reuse from a partially completed generation?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An assistant service pays per token and has bounded inference capacity. Requests vary in input length and requested output. One tenant can submit many long prompts.

questions.title: Fairness policy
questions.prompt: Which policy protects smaller tenants under load?

choices.why: A large tenant can monopolize queue space.

choices.text: Per-request limits only with unlimited request count
choices.why: A tenant can still flood many bounded requests.

choices.text: Per-tenant work quotas, concurrency shares and bounded queues
choices.why: Both individual and aggregate pressure are controlled.

choices.text: Equal request counts despite radically different lengths
choices.why: Resource allocation can remain unequal.

questions.explanation: Fairness needs a cost model and an admission boundary. Count requests for abuse signals, but allocate scarce compute using a measure closer to consumed work. Observe per-tenant queue age and completed useful work under overload, so a policy that looks fair by request count does not systematically disadvantage short or low-volume workloads.
questions.tradeoff: Precise accounting can add overhead.
questions.followup: How would unused quota be borrowed without permanent starvation?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An assistant service pays per token and has bounded inference capacity. Requests vary in input length and requested output. One tenant can submit many long prompts.

questions.title: Cost-quality routing
questions.prompt: A cheaper model is proposed for simple queries. What must be evaluated?

choices.why: Longer outputs or more retries can erase savings.
Names do not establish task capability.
Coverage is inadequate.

choices.text: Task-segment quality, latency, refusal/safety behavior and total completed-task cost
choices.why: Routing should preserve the service contract.

questions.explanation: Compare cost per successful task, not only cost per token. A fallback loop can increase both latency and expense if the initial model often fails. Measure retries, escalation and abandoned tasks in total cost, since a cheaper first attempt can become more expensive when it frequently requires a second model or human repair.
questions.tradeoff: A classifier/router becomes another component to evaluate.
questions.followup: What uncertainty threshold should send a task directly to the stronger model?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An assistant service pays per token and has bounded inference capacity. Requests vary in input length and requested output. One tenant can submit many long prompts.

questions.title: Lineage key
questions.prompt: What should connect derived artifacts to their source?

choices.text: Stable source identity and version lineage
choices.why: Affected chunks, vectors and caches can be located.

choices.text: Only a checksum of each chunk without source or version links
choices.why: A checksum identifies bytes but does not by itself locate all artifacts derived from one source across rechunking.

choices.text: Only the embedding-model version attached to each vector
choices.why: That identifies the representation, not which document and source version produced it.
Dates help scan ranges but are too coarse to reliably connect a source to every derived artifact.

questions.explanation: Deletion and correction need an inventory of derivation, not just a primary-file path. Version lineage also prevents an old update from recreating removed content. Keep source identity independent of chunk boundaries, because a later rechunking pass should not make old derived copies impossible to find or remove.
questions.tradeoff: Lineage metadata adds storage and maintenance.
questions.followup: How would one chunk derived from several sources be represented?

questions.title: Embedding removal limit
questions.prompt: Deleting a vector proves what?

choices.text: All textual copies and logs are erased
choices.why: Other stores have independent lifecycles.

choices.text: Any model trained on the document has forgotten it
choices.why: Training effects are a separate problem.

choices.text: That vector is removed from the addressed index under its deletion contract
choices.why: Broader deletion needs additional evidence.
Backups were not part of the operation.

questions.explanation: Be precise about the artifact and serving boundary changed. Removing retrieval state is not equivalent to removing source text, caches or learned model effects. Report deletion by artifact class and serving boundary, avoiding a single global claim that incorrectly equates removal from an index with erasure from every derived system.
questions.tradeoff: Broader guarantees may require redesign or constrained data use.
questions.followup: How would the product communicate distinct retention and training policies?

questions.title: Replay prevention
questions.prompt: A delayed indexing job contains an old source version after deletion. What should happen?

choices.text: Index it because the job was queued first
choices.why: Queue age does not override current eligibility.

choices.text: Reject it using deletion/version evidence at publication
choices.why: Derived state cannot resurrect obsolete content.

choices.text: Delete the current user's entire account
choices.why: That exceeds the affected source.

choices.text: Rely on eventual vector similarity to hide it
choices.why: Search relevance is not deletion enforcement.

questions.explanation: Publication should recheck whether the source version remains eligible. A durable tombstone or equivalent fence must outlive the replay window it protects. Make deletion evidence durable across worker restart and backup replay, and recheck it when publishing results rather than trusting the eligibility of an old queued job.
questions.tradeoff: Long replay windows increase metadata retention.
questions.followup: How would backup restoration preserve later deletion intent?

questions.title: Completion report
questions.prompt: Which report is defensible?

choices.text: One green check after the first file deletion
choices.why: Derived stores may remain active.

choices.text: A count of deletion jobs submitted
choices.why: Submission is not completion.

choices.text: A statement that AI deletion is impossible in every case
choices.why: Different artifacts have different controllable boundaries.

choices.text: Per-artifact serving completion, unresolved copies and explicit training/backup limits
choices.why: The report separates proven removal from remaining obligations.

questions.explanation: Avoid one overloaded deleted state across systems with different semantics. Report where serving access is removed and where retention or model effects require separate handling. Track unresolved or unreachable stores as pending or unknown, so a fast response from one subsystem does not become false evidence that the whole deletion workflow completed.
questions.tradeoff: Fine-grained reports need durable workflow state.
questions.followup: Which unresolved artifact should block the user-facing completion acknowledgement?

questions.title: Choose the key lifetime
questions.prompt: A client times out and retries the same intended payment. Which key should it send?

choices.text: A fresh key for every attempt
choices.why: That represents separate operations to the service.

choices.text: The original key with the original parameters
choices.why: This preserves the business operation identity.

choices.text: A deterministic hash of amount and destination, reused for every matching payment
choices.why: Two intentionally separate payments can have identical parameters; payload equality does not establish one intent.

choices.text: A new server-issued key obtained only from the first success response
choices.why: If that response is lost, the client lacks the identity needed to retry the original intent safely.

questions.explanation: The key identifies one intended payment, whereas a timeout only identifies an unsuccessful attempt to observe its result. Reusing the original key lets the service return or reconcile the first outcome without creating a second intent. The request parameters must remain consistent.
questions.tradeoff: Clients must persist the key through retries and restarts.
questions.followup: When should a user intentionally generate a new key?

questions.title: Reject conflicting intent
questions.prompt: The same merchant reuses a key with a different amount. What is appropriate?

choices.why: The key's intent becomes ambiguous.

choices.text: Ignore the key for changed parameters
choices.why: That can create an unintended second charge.

choices.text: Reject the mismatch with a documented conflict response
choices.why: One key must not describe two different intents.
The key is merchant-scoped.

questions.explanation: A reused key with a changed amount cannot safely mean both 'retry the first payment' and 'create this different payment.' Rejecting the mismatch preserves an unambiguous intent. Canonicalization must account for defaults and equivalent representations, not merely compare raw JSON formatting.
questions.tradeoff: Canonicalization must handle defaults and equivalent representations consistently.
questions.followup: Which fields belong in the intent fingerprint?

questions.title: Atomic first execution
questions.prompt: Two identical requests arrive concurrently. What prevents two payment rows?

choices.text: Atomically claim a unique merchant-key and create the payment within the transaction
choices.why: Only one transaction can establish the intent's first result.

choices.text: Check a process-local map before writing
choices.why: Other processes can pass the same check.

choices.text: Use Serializable isolation for payment inserts but write the replay claim in a later transaction
choices.why: Serializable execution does not connect two separately committed intents when the unique operation claim is outside the payment transaction.

choices.text: Write the idempotency key only after sending success
choices.why: A crash leaves committed work without deduplication evidence.

questions.explanation: Two processes can both pass a separate absence check before either writes. A unique merchant-key claim enforced inside the same transaction as payment creation gives one atomic winner. A process-local mutex would protect only one instance and would disappear on restart.
questions.tradeoff: A shared transactional boundary can limit independent scaling.
questions.followup: How would the design change with an external payment provider?

questions.title: Expiry changes the guarantee
questions.prompt: An identical request arrives after the seven-day retention window. What must clients know?

choices.text: It is guaranteed to replay forever
choices.why: That exceeds the stated retention contract.

choices.text: Search only for a prior payment with the same amount and destination
choices.why: Identical payment parameters can describe two legitimate business operations, so this is not reliable intent identity.

choices.text: Deleting the replay record cancels the payment
choices.why: Replay-state retention does not undo business history.

choices.text: The old key may no longer prevent re-execution; reconciliation needs durable business identity
choices.why: Clients must not assume an expired cache is permanent deduplication.

questions.explanation: The service's deduplication promise ends when its retained replay evidence expires; the original payment does not disappear with that evidence. A late retry therefore needs a durable business identifier or an explicit reconciliation path. Clients must not assume that an old key remains protective forever.
questions.tradeoff: Permanent business identifiers can require longer-lived indexes.

questions.title: Identify necessary tests
questions.prompt: Which tests exercise the replay contract? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Concurrent requests with the same merchant and key
choices.why: This tests the first-execution race.

choices.text: Crash after commit but before response
choices.why: This tests recovery of ambiguous success.
Those do not exercise deduplication.

choices.text: Same key under different authenticated merchants
choices.why: This tests the stated scoping boundary.

questions.explanation: Concurrent duplicates test whether first execution is atomic; a post-commit crash tests whether an uncertain caller can recover the original result. Cross-merchant reuse tests namespace isolation. These are different failure boundaries, so a sequential happy-path replay test cannot replace the full set.
questions.tradeoff: Tests need deterministic fault injection around commit.

questions.title: Migration across versions
questions.prompt: A new API version changes defaults. How should a staff engineer preserve old retries?

choices.text: Reinterpret stored keys under the new defaults

choices.text: Version or preserve canonicalization and stored replay semantics
choices.why: Retries must retain their original meaning.

choices.text: Purge all replay records at deploy time
choices.why: That breaks the seven-day promise.

choices.text: Accept any parameters under an existing key to avoid version conflicts
choices.why: This hides genuinely changed intent and can return a result for a different requested payment.

questions.explanation: An old request must keep its original interpretation after deployment. If a new default changes the canonical amount, currency or destination associated with a stored key, a legitimate retry can become a conflict or a different payment. Preserve versioned interpretation until the promised replay window closes.

questions.title: Idempotence is not identical response text
questions.prompt: Why can an idempotent DELETE return success first and not-found later?

choices.why: It concerns intended server effects.

choices.text: DELETE can only be called once
choices.why: It can be repeated.

choices.text: The intended resource-removal effect remains the same
choices.why: The response can reflect that the resource is already absent.

choices.text: Every DELETE is automatically free of all application bugs
choices.why: Implementations must still honor their contracts.

questions.explanation: HTTP idempotence concerns the intended state change: the resource is absent after either one deletion or repeated deletions. It does not require identical response bodies or status codes. Applications may offer stronger replay-result guarantees, but those are additional contracts beyond the basic method property.
questions.tradeoff: Stable replay results may be useful beyond basic HTTP idempotence.

questions.title: Offset drift
questions.prompt: Why can offset pagination repeat an item after new items are inserted at the front?

choices.why: They are positional counts.
The same offset now identifies a different boundary.

choices.text: Immutable IDs prevent every pagination anomaly
choices.why: IDs alone do not stabilize offsets.
HTTP can carry any documented pagination contract.

questions.explanation: Offset 20 refers to the twenty-first current position, not a stable item boundary. New entries inserted ahead of it shift positions, so a later page can repeat previously seen rows. Deletions can cause the converse skip; a deterministic keyset boundary avoids this positional drift.
questions.tradeoff: Offsets remain useful for small stable datasets and random page jumps.
questions.followup: What anomaly can deletion cause before an offset?

questions.title: Tie-breaking cursor
questions.prompt: Which cursor boundary avoids losing items with equal timestamps?

choices.why: It cannot distinguish same-time items.
It remains position-based.
The pair defines a total order for continuation.
That is not necessarily the last returned item's boundary.

questions.explanation: Timestamp alone does not distinguish several activities created at the same instant. Continuing strictly before that timestamp can skip the remaining ties, while including it can repeat rows. The timestamp-and-ID pair supplies a unique total-order boundary that the query and index must both honor.
questions.tradeoff: Composite comparisons and matching indexes are required.
questions.followup: What changes if the sort key becomes mutable?

questions.title: Do not overpromise snapshots
questions.prompt: Does keyset pagination alone guarantee a frozen view of every item existing at page one?

choices.text: No; snapshot semantics require an additional version or snapshot mechanism
choices.why: A stable boundary is not a complete historical snapshot.

choices.text: Yes; every opaque token is a database snapshot
choices.why: Opacity does not imply storage semantics.

choices.text: Yes; immutable creation times prevent deletion
choices.why: Rows can still be deleted.

choices.text: No; pagination can never use snapshots
choices.why: Snapshot-based exports are possible with explicit support.

questions.explanation: Keyset pagination stabilizes continuation relative to a sort boundary, but rows can still be deleted or changed while the client pages. A frozen historical view requires an explicit snapshot or versioned export contract. Token opacity describes representation, not any particular consistency guarantee.
questions.tradeoff: Snapshots consume resources and need expiry policies.

questions.title: Bind the token
questions.prompt: Why reject a cursor reused with a different tenant or filter?

choices.text: Tokens must always be readable JSON
choices.why: Opacity is allowed and often useful.
Filters define the result set.
Authorization is still required.

choices.text: The continuation boundary was issued for a different query context
choices.why: Reusing it can skip data or cross an intended isolation boundary.

questions.explanation: The token was issued for one tenant, filter and ordering context. Reusing it with a different query can apply a boundary to the wrong result set, producing omissions or violating isolation assumptions. Bind and validate that context while still performing ordinary authorization on every request.

questions.title: Defend list endpoints
questions.prompt: Which limits should the API apply? Select all that apply.

choices.why: It bounds per-request response and work.
A token alone must not bypass current access checks.

choices.text: Unlimited query complexity because results are paginated
choices.why: Pagination need not bound scan or join cost.
Clients need to handle invalidated continuation state.

questions.explanation: Page size limits output, but a selective-looking endpoint may still scan or join enormous intermediate data. Authorization, query-cost limits and token expiry therefore remain independent controls. A small returned page is not evidence that the request was cheap or that the continuation token grants access.
questions.tradeoff: Stricter limits can require exports for large clients.

questions.title: Evolve cursor internals
questions.prompt: The storage layout changes. What is a robust token strategy?

choices.text: Promise clients they can parse internal row offsets
choices.why: That couples the API to physical storage.

choices.text: Version opaque tokens and maintain or explicitly expire old interpretations
choices.why: This supports controlled evolution.
Old requests may continue from the wrong position.

choices.text: Change every resource ID during deploy
choices.why: That causes unrelated compatibility problems.

questions.explanation: Clients should treat a cursor as a service-issued continuation capability with a documented lifetime, not a physical row offset they can manufacture. Versioned interpretation permits storage migrations without silently changing old boundaries. If compatibility cannot be maintained, expiration must be explicit and recoverable.
questions.tradeoff: Supporting old tokens can delay removal of old lookup paths.
questions.followup: How long should compatibility last for interactive versus batch clients?

questions.title: Empty does not always mean done
questions.prompt: A service returns no items but a nonempty continuation token after scanning a sparse filtered range. What should a compliant client do?

choices.why: The continuation token indicates more scanning may remain.
That can loop or duplicate work.

choices.text: Continue according to the documented token contract
choices.why: Output count and scan completion are separate.

choices.text: Stop whenever the returned count is below the requested page size
choices.why: A sparse filtered scan can return a short page before its continuation is exhausted.

questions.explanation: A filtered scan can consume its work budget without finding a matching row and still have more candidate data to inspect. The nonempty continuation token communicates that unfinished scan. Clients should follow the documented completion signal rather than infer completion from an empty or short page.
questions.tradeoff: Sparse pages may make poor interactive experiences.
questions.followup: When should the server scan further before returning?

questions.title: Use an index aligned with access
questions.prompt: Which index most naturally supports this tenant-scoped continuation query?

choices.text: Tenant, created_at, id in compatible order
choices.why: It aligns scope and ordered range traversal.

choices.text: Tenant alone, with the time ordering performed over all matching tenant rows
choices.why: This scopes the tenant but lacks the ordered continuation path, potentially requiring a large scan and sort.

choices.text: Created_at alone without tenant or ID tie-breaking
choices.why: It omits tenant scoping and the unique ordering boundary required by this query.

choices.text: Tenant and ID, without created_at in the ordering key
choices.why: It does not directly support the API's primary creation-time order.

questions.explanation: The query first narrows by tenant, then traverses a creation-time range with a unique ID tie-breaker. An index arranged around that access pattern can avoid repeatedly sorting or scanning unrelated tenants. Other sort modes may need different indexes, each with additional write and storage cost.
questions.tradeoff: Additional indexes increase write and storage cost.

questions.title: Prevent a lost update
questions.prompt: Which request contract prevents an editor from silently overwriting a newer revision?

choices.why: A stale replacement can overwrite newer content.

choices.text: PUT with If-Match for the revision read
choices.why: The replacement is conditional on the expected current representation.

choices.text: GET immediately before an unconditional PUT
choices.why: Another writer can still intervene.
Timing does not enforce the revision invariant.

questions.explanation: The editor's replacement was constructed from one specific representation. If-Match turns that dependency into a server-enforced condition, so a newer committed edit causes rejection instead of silent overwrite. The comparison and write must be atomic; a preliminary GET followed by unconditional PUT is insufficient.
questions.tradeoff: Users may need to resolve conflicts manually.
questions.followup: What changes if edits are mergeable operations instead of replacements?
questions.context: Hypothetical document API returns a strong entity tag with each representation. Editors read revision 17 and submit replacements. The server can atomically compare the current revision and write a replacement. No automatic merge policy is defined.

questions.title: A failed precondition
questions.prompt: Another editor has committed revision 18. This client still supplies revision 17. What should this API do?

choices.why: Idempotence does not authorize a stale overwrite.
No partial merge semantics are defined.

choices.text: Reject the unmet precondition without applying the replacement
choices.why: This preserves the newer revision.

choices.text: Retry with revision 18 automatically and unchanged content
choices.why: That bypasses the user's conflict decision.

questions.explanation: Revision 17 is no longer current, so applying the replacement would discard work the editor did not observe. A failed precondition preserves revision 18 and asks the client to reread or resolve the conflict. Automatically substituting the new tag would bypass the protection rather than handle the conflict.
questions.tradeoff: Conflict handling shifts some complexity to clients.
questions.followup: How should the UI present the latest content and the user's unsaved edits?
questions.context: Hypothetical document API returns a strong entity tag with each representation. Editors read revision 17 and submit replacements. The server can atomically compare the current revision and write a replacement. No automatic merge policy is defined.

questions.title: Close the check-write race
questions.prompt: Where must the revision comparison happen?

choices.text: Within the same atomic update as the content replacement
choices.why: No competing write can slip between the check and effect.
Other writers are not controlled by this browser.

choices.text: In a separate unlocked database query
choices.why: The current revision can change after the query.

choices.text: Only in a periodically refreshed cache
choices.why: The cache may lag the authoritative revision.

questions.explanation: A separate check leaves a window in which another editor can commit before the replacement. Enforcing revision equality inside the same atomic database update closes that window. Browser checks or stale-cache comparisons can improve user feedback, but they cannot establish the authoritative concurrency invariant.
questions.tradeoff: Hot documents may generate many conflicts.
questions.followup: When would serialized editing outperform repeated optimistic conflicts?

questions.title: Select the validator
questions.prompt: Why require a strong rather than weak entity tag for this comparison?

choices.why: Tag length is not the semantic distinction.

choices.text: Strong tags eliminate the need for authorization
choices.why: Concurrency validation is not access control.

choices.text: A weak tag implies a checksum failure
choices.why: Weak validators can intentionally identify semantically equivalent representations.

choices.text: The replacement should depend on representation identity, not merely weak equivalence
choices.why: If-Match uses strong comparison for this purpose.

questions.explanation: A weak validator can group representations considered equivalent for some purposes without asserting byte-level identity. Replacement protection needs the stronger comparison defined for If-Match. Validator generation must still account for representation variants; a strong tag is not an authorization token or a universal content checksum.
questions.tradeoff: Representation variants require careful validator generation.
questions.followup: How would content encoding or projection affect entity tags?

questions.title: Keep independent safeguards
questions.prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Authorization remains necessary with a matching tag
choices.why: A correct revision does not grant edit rights.

choices.text: An idempotency key can identify retries but does not replace the expected revision
choices.why: Replay identity and stale-write prevention address different races.

choices.text: If-Match proves the user saw the latest revision at commit time
choices.why: It only checks that the supplied revision matches then.

choices.text: A successful conditional write can return the new entity tag
choices.why: That gives the client the next concurrency token.

questions.explanation: Authorization answers whether this caller may edit; an idempotency key identifies repeated intent; the entity tag identifies the representation on which the edit depends. None substitutes for the others. Returning a new tag after success gives the client a valid basis for its next conditional edit.
questions.tradeoff: More explicit contracts make client implementations more demanding.
questions.followup: Which error should a client resolve first when authorization and preconditions both fail?

questions.title: A phased requirement change
questions.prompt: Existing clients use unconditional PUT. Product now requires lost-update protection. What rollout is safest?

choices.text: Reject every old client without measuring adoption
choices.why: That may break supported clients abruptly.

choices.text: Introduce and measure conditional writes, migrate clients, then enforce a documented cutoff
choices.why: This makes the compatibility transition explicit.

choices.text: Silently invent an If-Match from the current server state
choices.why: That preserves overwriting rather than protecting the user's read.

choices.text: Keep accepting unconditional updates while claiming universal protection
choices.why: The stated guarantee would remain false.

questions.explanation: Requiring preconditions changes the contract for clients that previously sent unconditional replacements. Measure adoption and migrate those writers before enforcing a documented cutoff. During overlap, do not claim universal lost-update protection: a legacy unconditional writer can still overwrite a conditional writer's work.
questions.tradeoff: The transition period retains weaker behavior for legacy clients.
questions.followup: How would you isolate legacy behavior without weakening new clients?

questions.title: Test more than happy-path revisioning
questions.prompt: Which test most directly exercises atomic enforcement when two authorized writers both read current revision 17 before racing to replace it?

choices.why: They avoid the competing-writer race.

choices.text: Send concurrent replacements with different current documents and inspect only successful HTTP responses
choices.why: Different documents do not contend on the same revision; HTTP success alone also omits durable-state verification.

choices.text: Release both revision-17 conditional writes together; verify one commit, one precondition failure and the final durable revision and content
choices.why: Both requests begin with the current revision, so one must win the same atomic comparison and the other must observe a failed precondition.
That tests access control, not the revision race.

questions.explanation: Both authorized writers first read the current revision, then race without another writer or injected failure. Atomic conditional replacement should commit exactly one change and reject the other precondition. Two already-stale requests could both reject without testing this race. Inspect the durable revision and content as well as responses; one passing schedule is evidence, not a general proof.
questions.tradeoff: Deterministic concurrency tests need synchronization hooks.
questions.followup: What if both edits produce byte-identical content?

questions.title: Choose an explicit conflict model
questions.prompt: Writers conflict continuously on one popular document. What should staff evaluation compare?

choices.text: Serialized ownership, operation-based merging and optimistic retries against editing needs
choices.why: The right model depends on collaboration semantics and contention.
This may amplify contention without resolving semantics.
That abandons the protection precisely when contention is high.

choices.text: Store independent drafts but publish whichever full replacement arrives last
choices.why: Draft preservation can aid recovery, but last-writer-wins publication still violates the promised overwrite protection.

questions.explanation: Frequent conflicts may indicate that whole-document replacement is the wrong collaboration model. Compare serialized ownership, domain-specific mergeable operations and bounded optimistic retries against actual editing semantics. Removing the precondition improves apparent success rate only by discarding the very protection the API promised.
questions.tradeoff: Mergeable operations need domain rules and more complex history.
questions.followup: Which edits commute, and which require a human decision?

questions.title: Return a useful acceptance response
questions.prompt: What should the caller receive after durable acceptance?

choices.text: A success body claiming all records were imported
choices.why: Acceptance is not completion.

choices.text: An operation identifier and a way to inspect status
choices.why: The caller can observe the long-running lifecycle.

choices.text: No identifier because the connection stays open
choices.why: A long-lived connection is not a durable lookup handle.

choices.text: A random worker hostname as the permanent identifier
choices.why: Workers can fail or move.

questions.explanation: The durable operation resource lets a client reconnect and inspect work without depending on the original HTTP connection or worker process. choices.why: That removes useful visibility.

choices.text: Provide a recommended polling interval and enforce appropriate limits

choices.text: Create a new import on every status request
choices.why: A read should not duplicate the operation.

questions.title: Backward-compatible status evolution
questions.prompt: A new state PAUSED is introduced. Which client contract reduces breakage?

choices.text: Require clients to crash on every unknown state
choices.why: That makes additive evolution brittle.

choices.text: Document unknown-state handling and stable terminal-state semantics
choices.why: Clients can remain safe when a new nonterminal state appears.

choices.text: Reuse FAILED to mean temporarily paused
choices.why: That changes established semantics.

choices.text: Remove the operation resource for paused jobs
choices.why: That destroys continuity and observability.

questions.title: Recover workers safely
questions.prompt: The worker crashes after committing some records. Which recovery design fits the partial-import contract?

choices.text: Restart from the first row without any deduplication
choices.why: That may repeat committed effects.

choices.text: Declare the operation successful because it started
choices.why: Starting proves nothing about completion.

choices.text: Persist progress and use stable per-record replay identity
choices.why: Recovery can resume without multiplying effects.

choices.text: Change the operation ID after every crash
choices.why: That separates retries from their original intent.

questions.explanation: A worker can commit a record and crash before its progress checkpoint advances. Recovery must therefore tolerate replay at that boundary, using stable record identity or an idempotent update. questions.tradeoff: Fine-grained checkpoints add writes and state management.

questions.title: Scan pollution
questions.prompt: Why can the daily scan harm interactive hit rate?
questions.explanation: Caching every observed value is not always beneficial when scans have little reuse. An admission policy decides whether an observed object deserves scarce cache space; eviction decides which resident object leaves. A scan of one-use entries can hurt even a correct LRU implementation, so bypassing or isolating that traffic can outperform merely increasing the cache.

questions.title: Choose a rollout criterion
questions.prompt: Which comparison supports replacing the eviction policy?
questions.explanation: Evaluate outcomes under the relevant distribution and failure conditions, not an abstract popularity ranking.
