choices.why: They can be transferred and caught up.

choices.text: Old writes and new reads may have no shared durable history without a transition protocol
choices.why: Quorum intersection inside each set does not bridge the two sets.

choices.text: Keep the old and new sets' quorum sizes equal
choices.why: Equal thresholds do not establish shared history or overlapping authority between disjoint memberships.

choices.text: A larger N automatically transfers state
choices.why: Replica count does not copy data.

questions.explanation: Each configuration can satisfy its own quorum rule while the old and new replica sets share no member or transferred history. A read on D, E and F therefore need not know what A, B and C acknowledged. Reconfiguration must coordinate catch-up and authority changes across the membership boundary.
questions.tradeoff: Joint or staged transitions add operational complexity and temporary resource cost.
questions.followup: What evidence should gate removal of the old replicas?
questions.caseTitle: Quorum arithmetic is not the whole protocol
questions.context: Hypothetical replicated register has three fixed replicas A, B and C. Writes normally wait for two durable acknowledgments; reads query two and select the highest valid version returned. Unless a question changes it, one writer issues nonoverlapping writes with monotonically increasing versions. No replica substitution is allowed.

questions.title: One replica unavailable
questions.prompt: With N=3, R=2 and W=2, one replica is unreachable. What follows under the fixed-set protocol?

choices.why: Two reachable replicas can satisfy both thresholds.
The reachable replicas still perform work.

choices.text: Reads and writes can still satisfy their thresholds if the other two respond
choices.why: The unavailable member does not by itself eliminate quorum.

choices.text: The unreachable replica is guaranteed to be up to date
choices.why: It may miss writes during the outage.

questions.explanation: Two reachable replicas can satisfy both the two-response read threshold and the two-acknowledgment write threshold. That preserves the possibility of progress, not an immediate-response guarantee. The missing replica may become stale, and the remaining pair has no margin for another unavailable participant until recovery restores redundancy.
questions.tradeoff: Two remaining replicas leave no additional failure margin.
questions.followup: What repair is required before the recovered replica serves weak reads?

questions.title: Check a consistency claim
questions.prompt: What evidence best tests a claimed linearizable register implementation?

choices.text: Record operation invocation/response intervals and values, then check legal real-time-respecting histories under faults
choices.why: Linearizability constrains externally observed histories.

choices.text: Only compare final values after all replicas converge
choices.why: Convergence can hide earlier stale reads.
That omits protocol behavior.
Performance does not prove a consistency model.

questions.explanation: Linearizability constrains the values returned during execution and their relation to invocation and response times. Replicas can converge to the same final state after having served an illegal intermediate history. Record and check histories under faults, treating uncertain timeouts appropriately; passing tests remain evidence rather than a complete formal proof.

questions.title: Choose the narrow guarantee
questions.prompt: Which guarantee directly matches the product requirement?

choices.why: That is stronger than the stated session-specific need.
The user's later reads must include their completed updates.

choices.text: Only eventual convergence without a session bound
choices.why: That can show the writer an old profile immediately afterward.

choices.text: A globally sorted list of all profile edits
choices.why: The requirement concerns one user's subsequent observations.

questions.explanation: The requirement is session-specific: after this user completes an update, their later protected reads must not move behind it. Read-your-writes expresses that without requiring unrelated users to see the update immediately. The design must define what constitutes one session across devices, application servers and reconnects.
questions.tradeoff: Session state must survive relevant routing and client transitions.
questions.followup: Should signing in on a second device inherit the first device's freshness requirement?
questions.caseTitle: A user reads their own update
questions.context: Hypothetical profile service writes to a primary and asynchronously replicates to read replicas. The update response includes a monotonically increasing account version. The product requires a user's later session reads to include their completed updates; unrelated users may briefly see older profiles.

questions.title: Use the version token
questions.prompt: A replica is at version 40 and the session token requires at least 42. What should routing do?

choices.text: Return version 40 and label it current
choices.why: That violates the session requirement.

choices.text: Discard the session token because replicas are healthy
choices.why: Health is not catch-up.

choices.text: Wait within a bound or route to a source at least at version 42
choices.why: The read must meet its causal lower bound.

choices.text: Invent version 42 metadata around version 40 content
choices.why: Relabeling does not update the state.

questions.explanation: The session token says this read requires at least version 42. Replica health at version 40 is insufficient, so the service must wait within a bound, choose a qualifying source or report that the requested guarantee is unavailable. Relabeling old content or dropping the token would conceal a contract violation.
questions.tradeoff: Waiting or rerouting increases latency and primary load.
questions.followup: What should the API return if no qualifying source is reachable?

questions.title: Sticky routing is conditional
questions.prompt: Why is sticking a user to one replica insufficient by itself?

choices.text: That replica may not have applied the user's write
choices.why: Affinity does not establish replication progress.
It need not.

choices.text: A single replica cannot store profiles
choices.why: It can store them.

choices.text: All replicas always advance at the same rate
choices.why: Asynchronous replication allows different lag.

questions.explanation: Affinity says where a request goes, not how far that destination has replicated. A sticky replica can remain behind the user's completed write, and failover can choose an even older replica. Combine routing with explicit progress evidence if the product promises read-your-writes or monotonic session observations.
questions.tradeoff: Version-aware routing needs metadata and failure handling.
questions.followup: How would a sticky session failover preserve the same guarantee?

questions.title: Failover after a completed update
questions.prompt: The primary fails before an acknowledged update reaches any read replica. What is the core conflict?

choices.text: The token can reconstruct the full profile
choices.why: A version number is not the missing payload.

choices.text: Any healthy replica automatically has acknowledged data
choices.why: Acknowledgment policy determines that.

choices.text: The client must have made a syntax error
choices.why: The scenario is a durability gap.

choices.text: Serving old state violates the session promise; preserving it may require waiting or failing until recovery
choices.why: Availability and freshness cannot both be fabricated from absent data.

questions.explanation: The required update was acknowledged under a policy that did not preserve it on any surviving read replica. A session token identifies the missing frontier but cannot reconstruct its payload. Preserving the freshness promise can therefore require waiting or failing until recovery; stronger replication at acknowledgment changes that risk.
questions.tradeoff: Synchronous replication can reduce the risk at added write latency.

questions.title: Session-state design
questions.prompt: Which details need explicit definition? Select all that apply.

choices.why: A session may move between stateless servers.

choices.text: Whether tokens are scoped per account or partition
choices.why: Version comparisons must be meaningful in their namespace.

choices.text: Treating a token as authorization to read any account
choices.why: Freshness metadata is not permission.

choices.text: How token requirements combine after several writes
choices.why: Later reads must not accidentally forget a required frontier.

questions.explanation: The token is meaningful only within a defined account or partition namespace and only if every relevant hop preserves it. Multiple writes may require combining frontiers rather than replacing one arbitrarily. Treat the token as freshness metadata, validate its scope and continue to enforce independent access authorization.
questions.tradeoff: Large multi-partition sessions may require more complex frontiers.

questions.title: Measure the guarantee
questions.prompt: Which metric most directly detects regressions?

choices.why: A live replica can be stale.

choices.text: Reads returning a version below the session's required frontier
choices.why: This observes a concrete contract violation.
Fast stale responses can look healthy.
Byte volume does not establish per-session ordering.

questions.explanation: A read returning a version below the session's required frontier is a concrete violation, even if it is very fast and every replica is healthy. Measure that invariant together with wait, fallback and failure rates. Otherwise a routing optimization may appear successful only because it silently serves older state.
questions.tradeoff: Version instrumentation adds response and telemetry metadata.
questions.followup: What privacy-safe aggregation would reveal affected clients?

questions.title: Do not confuse guarantees
questions.prompt: A user reads version 50, then version 49 after switching replicas, without making a write. What is violated?

choices.why: No user write is involved in this example.
Distinct ordered versions can still be served in the wrong observation order.
The user's observations moved backward.
The replicas may still converge eventually.

questions.explanation: Monotonic reads prohibit a session from observing version 50 and later falling back to 49, even when the user made no write. Read-your-writes alone addresses a different history involving the user's own completed updates. A system promising both may need to advance the session frontier after reads as well as writes.
questions.tradeoff: Maintaining both can require tracking reads as well as writes.
questions.followup: How would the session frontier advance after reading another user's newer update?

questions.title: Relax a noncritical path deliberately
questions.prompt: A public avatar thumbnail can lag even for its uploader. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Document that endpoint's weaker freshness separately from protected profile reads
choices.why: Different resources can have different contracts.

choices.text: Silently ignore tokens on every endpoint
choices.why: That weakens unrelated guarantees.

choices.text: Claim session consistency while serving arbitrary old thumbnails
choices.why: The claim would be misleading.

choices.text: Force all profile writes to wait for every CDN edge
choices.why: That may be unnecessary for the accepted thumbnail semantics.

questions.explanation: A public thumbnail can have a weaker visibility contract than security-sensitive or user-edited profile fields, if the product explicitly accepts that behavior. Keep the endpoint distinction visible to clients and monitoring. Silently ignoring session requirements everywhere would turn a narrow optimization into an undocumented system-wide consistency regression.
questions.tradeoff: Multiple contracts require clear client expectations.
questions.followup: Which profile fields cannot tolerate the same relaxation?

questions.title: Find the race
questions.prompt: Reader R fetches version 4, writer commits version 5 and deletes the cache, then R stores version 4. What happened?

choices.why: Only the cache was overwritten.

choices.text: A delayed cache fill reintroduced an older value after invalidation
choices.why: The delete did not cancel the in-flight reader.

choices.text: The writer's database commit must have failed
choices.why: The commit is stated to succeed.

choices.text: Cache-aside guarantees this schedule cannot happen
choices.why: The simple pattern alone does not prevent it.

questions.explanation: The writer's invalidation removes the cache value present at that instant but does not cancel the reader already holding version 4. When the reader later fills the empty cache, it recreates stale state after version 5 committed. Preventing this requires a protocol that accounts for in-flight fills, not merely successful deletion.
questions.tradeoff: A stronger cache protocol needs versions, ordering or additional coordination.
questions.followup: How would you reproduce this race deterministically?
questions.caseTitle: A stale reader refills an invalidated cache
questions.context: Hypothetical cache-aside service stores authoritative records in a database and caches whole records. On a cache miss, a reader fetches the database then populates the cache. A writer commits a new value and deletes the cache key. Database records carry monotonically increasing versions.

questions.title: What TTL can and cannot do
questions.prompt: What does a finite TTL provide in this race?

choices.why: The stale entry can still be served before expiry.

choices.text: Permanent prevention of old cache fills
choices.why: TTL does not control fill ordering.

choices.text: A bound on that entry's residence after its insertion, subject to refresh semantics
choices.why: Expiry can limit one stale entry but is not a full consistency proof.

choices.text: Atomicity between the cache and database
choices.why: They remain separate systems.

questions.explanation: A TTL limits how long one inserted entry remains eligible under its expiration policy. It does not synchronize that entry with database commits or stop a delayed stale fill. Refresh-on-access and repeated stale fills can extend effective staleness, so any claimed maximum data age needs stronger, explicitly stated assumptions.
questions.tradeoff: Short TTLs increase misses and database demand.
questions.followup: Which exact assumptions are needed to claim a maximum data-age bound?

questions.title: Version-aware fill needs a floor
questions.prompt: Why is 'replace only if the incoming version is newer than the cached value' insufficient when deletion removes all version metadata?

choices.text: An empty cache has no remembered version 5 to reject delayed version 4
choices.why: The comparison loses its reference point.

choices.text: Numeric comparison cannot be used for any cache version
choices.why: The scenario explicitly provides monotonic versions; the issue is forgetting the comparison floor after deletion.

choices.text: Conditional cache writes always block readers forever
choices.why: That is not inherent.
It can, but the cache comparison may not consult it.

questions.explanation: If deletion erases all version evidence, the subsequent empty cache has nothing against which to reject delayed version 4. A compare-with-current-value rule therefore loses the knowledge that version 5 was already authoritative. Retained invalidation versions, tombstones or an authoritative check can preserve that lower bound until stale fills are excluded.
questions.tradeoff: Version floors require retention and careful garbage collection.
questions.followup: When is it safe to forget an invalidation version?

questions.title: An authoritative correctness path
questions.prompt: A permission revocation must take effect before later protected reads succeed. What is the safer requirement?

choices.text: Use the same eventual cache as public profile text without changes
choices.why: Revocation has a stricter correctness boundary.

choices.text: Make the cache TTL slightly shorter and claim immediate revocation
choices.why: A nonzero stale window remains.

choices.text: Rely only on a cache-hit-rate target
choices.why: Hit rate does not establish authorization freshness.

choices.text: Use a serving protocol that validates the required revocation version or consults authoritative state
choices.why: The protected decision must obey the stronger contract.

questions.explanation: A permission decision has a stronger visibility requirement than ordinary cached display text. Serving an old authorization value after completed revocation can violate the protected-read invariant. Validate the required revocation frontier or consult authoritative state, and define truthful behavior when that stronger path is unavailable rather than silently weakening it.
questions.tradeoff: Stronger validation adds latency and can reduce availability.
questions.followup: Could bounded revocation delay be an acceptable explicit product contract?

questions.title: Test cache consistency separately
questions.prompt: Which tests target the described race? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Pause a reader after its database read, then complete a write and invalidation
choices.why: This creates the delayed-fill window.

choices.text: Resume the reader and inspect the cached version
choices.why: This checks whether stale data is reintroduced.

choices.text: Only verify that delete returned success
choices.why: Delete success does not account for a later fill.

choices.text: Test retries and reordered invalidation messages
choices.why: Delivery behavior can create additional stale states.

questions.explanation: Pause the miss reader after it obtains old database state, then let the writer commit and invalidate before resuming the fill. That deterministic schedule targets the actual race instead of hoping load reproduces it. Inspect cache and database versions, and separately test reordered or retried invalidation delivery.
questions.tradeoff: Fault hooks add test-only complexity.
questions.followup: Which invariant can a property-based test check across randomized schedules?

questions.title: A read-through fallback
questions.prompt: If a cache entry is below a caller's required version, what should the service do?

choices.text: Return it because it is a hit
choices.why: A hit can violate the caller's freshness requirement.

choices.text: Bypass or wait for a source meeting that version requirement
choices.why: The cache is an optimization, not permission to return stale data.

choices.text: Increase the cached version without changing its payload
choices.why: That falsifies evidence.
That weakens the contract.

questions.explanation: A cache hit is useful only when the entry satisfies the requesting session's lower bound. If it does not, route to a sufficiently current source, wait within the budget or fail explicitly. This keeps the cache an optimization rather than allowing hit-rate goals to rewrite the caller's consistency contract.
questions.tradeoff: Fallback traffic can surge when replicas or invalidations lag.
questions.followup: How would you reserve database capacity for freshness-sensitive reads?

questions.title: Deletion is also a versioned fact
questions.prompt: Why might a deleted record need a tombstone rather than mere absence?

choices.text: Absence always distinguishes never-created from deleted
choices.why: Those states can look identical.

choices.text: Tombstones remove every need for retention policy
choices.why: They themselves need lifecycle rules.

choices.text: An older replica or in-flight fill could otherwise resurrect the record
choices.why: The deletion needs ordering evidence relative to old values.
They can be represented and replicated.

questions.explanation: Absence does not necessarily distinguish a record that never existed from a newer deletion of an older value. A tombstone carries the deletion's ordering evidence so stale replicas or in-flight fills cannot resurrect the record. Reclaim it only when the protocol can exclude those older copies or replays.
questions.tradeoff: Tombstones consume storage until older copies can no longer reappear.
questions.followup: How do offline clients affect safe tombstone cleanup?

questions.title: A useful measurement pair
questions.prompt: What should accompany cache hit rate when evaluating this design?

choices.text: Returned-version freshness and database fallback load
choices.why: These reveal correctness and cost, not just reuse.

choices.text: Only the total number of cache keys
choices.why: Key count does not show whether values are current.
A live cache can serve stale content.
Size does not reveal visibility ordering.

questions.explanation: Hit rate measures reuse, not whether the reused data satisfies the product's freshness promise. Returning old values for longer can improve hit rate while harming correctness. Pair it with returned-version freshness and fallback load so the team sees both the consistency cost and the database pressure of its caching policy.
questions.tradeoff: Freshness measurements need version propagation or trusted timestamps.
questions.followup: Which endpoints warrant stricter monitoring than the rest?

questions.title: Merge a counter state
questions.prompt: Replica A has components (3,1); B has (2,4). What merged value follows from the stated rule?

choices.why: That double-counts shared component history.
Take each component's maximum, then sum.

choices.text: 4, by taking the largest total component only
choices.why: The counter's value sums all components.
Averaging is not the defined merge.

questions.explanation: The component for A is the largest known cumulative contribution from A, and similarly for B. Taking maxima yields (3,4), whose sum is 7; summing the two complete states would count overlapping history twice. The result relies on components being monotonic and tied to stable replica identities.
questions.tradeoff: Metadata grows with the set of replica identities.
questions.followup: How would you retire a replica identity safely?
questions.caseTitle: Offline edits need explicit merge semantics
questions.context: Hypothetical offline application replicates two toy data types. A grow-only counter stores one nondecreasing component per replica and merges by component-wise maximum; its value is the sum. An observed-remove set tags every add uniquely; a remove deletes only tags it has observed. All updates are eventually delivered.

questions.title: Duplicate state delivery
questions.prompt: Why does merging the same counter state twice not increment the value twice?

choices.text: The network guarantees every message arrives once
choices.why: The scenario only promises eventual delivery.

choices.text: A receiver must remember every network packet ID forever
choices.why: This state-based merge does not require packet deduplication.
Applying the same maximum again does not change the result.

choices.text: The second message is always empty
choices.why: The payload can be identical and nonempty.

questions.explanation: Component-wise maximum is idempotent: merging the same state again cannot increase any component beyond the value already known. Duplicate transport delivery is therefore harmless to this state-based counter without tracking every packet. Replacing components arbitrarily or storing only an unqualified scalar total would remove the provenance this argument needs.
questions.tradeoff: A naive scalar total would not retain enough provenance.
questions.followup: What property is also needed to tolerate different merge orders?

questions.title: Concurrent add and remove
questions.prompt: Replica A removes all observed tags for item X while offline B creates a new tag for X. After merge, is X present?

choices.text: Yes; the new unobserved add tag survives
choices.why: The remove only covers tags it observed.

choices.text: No; every remove wins over every concurrent add
choices.why: That is not the defined observed-remove rule.

choices.text: Only if A's wall clock is larger
choices.why: The toy rule does not use wall-clock order.

choices.text: The merge is undefined because operations overlap
choices.why: The rule explicitly defines the concurrent outcome.

questions.explanation: The remove operation names only add tags that A had observed. B's concurrent new tag is not among them, so it survives and X is present after merge. This is the specified add-wins outcome, not a universal definition of deletion; product semantics must decide whether that behavior is desirable.
questions.tradeoff: A different remove-wins design would encode different semantics.
questions.followup: Which behavior would users expect for a blocked-contact list?

questions.title: Convergence is not a business invariant
questions.prompt: Why is this grow-only counter unsuitable by itself for preventing inventory below zero?

choices.text: Merging more frequently makes uncoordinated decrements safe for every stock level
choices.why: Faster convergence does not allocate exclusive rights to consume the same scarce units.

choices.text: Eventual delivery prevents all concurrent actions
choices.why: Replicas can update independently.

choices.text: The counter has no read operation
choices.why: Its value is defined as the sum.

choices.text: Convergence does not authorize bounded decrements or allocate scarce rights
choices.why: Inventory safety requires additional rules beyond this increment-only data type.

questions.explanation: This data type guarantees convergence for nondecreasing per-replica increments under its merge rule. It does not define safe decrements, reserve inventory rights or prevent independent replicas from collectively overselling. A scarce-resource invariant needs additional coordination or an explicitly proven allocation model, even if all replicas would eventually agree on the invalid result.
questions.tradeoff: Adding rights allocation reduces the freedom of independent writers.
questions.followup: How would you distribute and reclaim inventory rights during partitions?

questions.title: Match the merge law
questions.prompt: Match each merge example to the property it illustrates. Use each choice once.

choices.why: Swapping operands leaves the merge result unchanged.
Regrouping several merges leaves the result unchanged.
Merging the same state with itself has no additional effect.
An allowed local update advances the component in the defined partial order rather than erasing prior contribution.

questions.explanation: The first three examples concern the merge operation: operand order, grouping and repeated state respectively. The fourth concerns allowed local evolution before merging. questions.title: A product-semantic migration
questions.prompt: Product wants removes to win over concurrent adds instead. What is necessary?

choices.text: Only rename the type in documentation
choices.why: The current merge still preserves unobserved adds.

choices.text: Design and migrate to compatible remove-wins metadata and rules
choices.why: Conflict semantics are encoded in stored state and operations.

choices.text: Delete random tags until tests pass
choices.why: That has no defined correctness property.

choices.text: Increase synchronization frequency and claim the rule changed
choices.why: Fewer conflicts do not redefine their outcome.

questions.explanation: Remove-wins behavior requires different causal metadata or rules from the specified observed-remove add-wins set. Renaming the type or synchronizing more frequently does not change the concurrent outcome. Treat the change as a compatibility migration, particularly for offline replicas that may later return with old-format state and operations.

questions.title: Lease expiry does not stop code
questions.prompt: Worker A pauses, its lease expires, and B acquires the next lease. Why can A still be dangerous?

choices.text: Expired leases automatically erase A's queued requests
choices.why: The lease service does not control every delayed request.

choices.text: A may resume and send a write based on its old ownership belief
choices.why: Process execution can outlive lease validity.

choices.text: B cannot obtain a lease until A exits
choices.why: The service uses expiry, not process exit.

choices.text: Only synchronized clocks could allow this schedule
choices.why: Long pauses alone are enough.

questions.explanation: The lease service has stopped recognizing A as owner, but it cannot force A's process or already queued network requests to disappear. choices.why: Past ownership does not supersede newer accepted ownership.

choices.text: Ask A whether it thinks its lease is valid

choices.why: The resource has already observed a higher generation.

choices.text: Fencing tokens automatically travel to every resource
choices.why: They must be propagated.

choices.why: The resource must reject paths that do not participate.

questions.title: Close the snapshot-watch gap
questions.prompt: Why start the watch at r+1 after reading the snapshot at r?

choices.text: Starting only from the current time is always equivalent
choices.why: Updates between snapshot and watch creation could be missed.

choices.text: It requests the history immediately after the snapshot's frontier

choices.text: It replays only revisions before the snapshot
choices.why: r+1 follows r.

choices.text: It guarantees the controller will never disconnect
choices.why: The protocol handles history, not permanent connectivity.

questions.explanation: The snapshot represents a complete view at revision r, so changes beginning at r+1 form its logical continuation. Starting only from the time the watch happens to connect can omit updates in between. questions.title: Recover after compaction
questions.prompt: The requested start revision is compacted. What should the controller do?

choices.text: Retry the same compacted revision indefinitely
choices.why: The missing retained history will not reappear.

choices.text: Skip to now while keeping old local state
choices.why: That can permanently miss intervening changes.

choices.text: Read a fresh consistent snapshot and rebuild the mirror before resuming
choices.why: A new snapshot replaces the unavailable history prefix.
The controller's lag does not justify deleting source state.

questions.explanation: When etcd has compacted the requested history, the controller can no longer prove incremental coverage from its old checkpoint. A fresh consistent snapshot supplies a new complete state and revision frontier. questions.title: Checkpoint atomicity
questions.prompt: Why persist local state and its last-applied revision together?

choices.text: A crash must not claim a revision whose state changes were not durably applied
choices.why: Otherwise restart can skip necessary events.

choices.text: The checkpoint revision alone is enough to reconstruct any lost local value after source compaction
choices.why: Compacted history may no longer contain the events needed to repair local state falsely claimed by the checkpoint.

choices.text: Every watch response must create a new etcd transaction
choices.why: Local persistence does not require that.

choices.text: Atomic persistence eliminates all duplicate deliveries
choices.why: Replayed events can still occur around recovery boundaries.

questions.explanation: The checkpoint claims that every relevant change through its revision is reflected in durable local state. Advancing it first can make restart skip an update that was never applied. Keeping state and revision atomic preserves that claim; a lagging checkpoint instead requires replay-safe local application to tolerate repeated events.

choices.why: That prevents useful failure recovery.

Using that cached identity as permission to mutate another resource therefore exposes a stale-owner window. Lease timing is an execution attempt property.

choices.text: A fresh UUID on every timer firing without a business uniqueness constraint
choices.why: Overlapping timers would create duplicate logical work.

questions.title: Create the run atomically

choices.text: Both check absence, then insert without a constraint
choices.why: The check and insert can race.

choices.text: Let the later timer create a second bill
choices.why: Timer order does not define a new business obligation.

choices.text: Use a unique durable run key and atomic insert-or-observe behavior
choices.why: Only one logical run record should be established.

choices.text: Rely only on synchronized scheduler clocks
choices.why: Clock agreement does not prevent concurrent execution.

questions.explanation: Two schedulers can both observe absence before either creates the run. A unique durable business key makes creation an atomic race with one logical result, while the loser observes that existing run. questions.tradeoff: The shared run store becomes part of the scheduling dependency chain.

choices.text: Reconcile using the stable operation identity; retry with the same key only within the provider's guaranteed replay contract
choices.why: The original external effect may already exist.

choices.why: That can falsely report a charge that failed.

choices.text: A crash can leave unperformed work recorded as finished

questions.title: Backfill missed periods
questions.prompt: After a three-day scheduler outage, what is a controlled recovery policy?

choices.why: That can overload billing and payment dependencies.

choices.text: Enumerate missing logical periods, create deduplicated runs, and drain under capacity limits
choices.why: Recovery preserves coverage without an uncontrolled burst.

choices.text: Bill every tenant once with no period identity
choices.why: That prevents precise reconciliation.

questions.title: Compatibility bridge
questions.prompt: What is the safest initial schema change?

choices.why: Old readers stop finding their field.

choices.text: Add the new field while preserving old reads and writes
choices.why: Both binary generations can operate.
Rollback loses its required schema.
New changes may be missed.

questions.explanation: An additive phase allows mixed versions; migration must synchronize ongoing writes. Keep both representations usable while binaries overlap, and define one authoritative interpretation of each value. A backfill alone misses writes occurring during the scan, so compatible writes or captured changes must bridge the migration interval.
questions.tradeoff: Temporary duplicate state needs reconciliation.
questions.followup: How would a failed dual write be detected?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Old and new application binaries overlap during deployment. Old binaries read customer_name. The new design uses display_name. Writes continue throughout migration.

questions.title: Required migration dependencies
questions.prompt: Order these stages under the stated rule: old binaries must remain deployable until new reads are verified.

items.text: Expand schema and deploy compatible writes.
Backfill and reconcile historical values.
Switch reads and verify new-field correctness.
Retire old binaries, then remove the old field.

questions.explanation: Destructive contraction follows verified new reads and retirement of old consumers. Each stage establishes a prerequisite for the next: schema support, complete values, verified new reads and finally retirement of old dependencies. Removing old state before old consumers leave turns a routine rollback into a data-repair problem.
questions.tradeoff: The bridge increases temporary complexity and storage.
questions.followup: What if a rarely run batch job still reads the old column?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Old and new application binaries overlap during deployment. Old binaries read customer_name. The new design uses display_name. Writes continue throughout migration.

questions.title: Rollback boundary
questions.prompt: When does rollback to the old binary become unsafe?

choices.text: As soon as the new field exists
choices.why: Additive fields need not break old code.
CPU does not establish schema compatibility.

choices.text: When old-required state is removed or no longer maintained
choices.why: The old binary cannot interpret the remaining state.

choices.text: Only after every user logs out
choices.why: Sessions do not define database compatibility.

questions.explanation: Rollback is a data-and-code property, not merely an image-selection operation. An old image can restart successfully yet fail on rows written under a new incompatible schema. Review the rollback window as a supported combination of binary, schema and data semantics rather than as an image retained in a registry.
questions.tradeoff: Long rollback windows delay cleanup.
questions.followup: How would you test a rollback against recently written rows?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Old and new application binaries overlap during deployment. Old binaries read customer_name. The new design uses display_name. Writes continue throughout migration.

questions.title: Migration completion
questions.prompt: Which evidence justifies contraction?

choices.text: Consumer inventory, no old accesses, reconciliation and rollback decision
choices.why: It covers readers, data and recovery intent.
Rare consumers may remain.
Historical and concurrent data remain unchecked.
Elapsed time alone proves no dependency.

questions.explanation: Define completion around actual dependencies rather than calendar confidence. Check interactive services, batch jobs, exports and rollback binaries that may still use the old field. Reconciliation should establish value correctness and ongoing synchronization; elapsed time and a green deployment indicator do not close those obligations.
questions.tradeoff: Observability for rarely executed jobs costs effort.
questions.followup: How would unknown external consumers change the retirement policy?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Old and new application binaries overlap during deployment. Old binaries read customer_name. The new design uses display_name. Writes continue throughout migration.

questions.title: Confounded comparison
questions.prompt: Why is aggregate canary versus control latency insufficient?

choices.text: Traffic mix and shared provider changes can confound attribution
choices.why: The populations are not comparable.

choices.text: Five percent is mathematically too small for any analysis
choices.why: Sample adequacy depends on rates and effect sizes.
Comparable user-impact metrics can help.

choices.text: A green deployment means metrics are irrelevant
choices.why: Deployment success does not prove application health.

questions.explanation: Compare like-for-like cohorts and inspect shared dependency behavior. Mobile-heavy traffic can have a different latency baseline from desktop traffic, and the provider slowdown affects both versions. Compare matched cohorts and dependency timings before attributing the aggregate difference to the new release.
questions.tradeoff: Stratification reduces samples in each segment.
questions.followup: Which segments matter to checkout conversion?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A checkout release goes to five percent of requests. Mobile users mostly hit the canary; desktop users mostly hit the control. A payment provider is simultaneously slowing down.

questions.title: Guardrail metrics
questions.prompt: Which measures are useful together? Select all that apply.

choices.why: A live process can reject all payments.

choices.text: User-visible success and latency by cohort
choices.why: These expose outcome regressions.
It does not measure checkout behavior.
They help explain whether the change or environment is stressed.

questions.explanation: Pair outcome guardrails with diagnostic signals, avoiding attribution from one aggregate. Measure whether users successfully complete checkout within the relevant latency objective, then use dependency and saturation signals to explain changes. A healthy process or fast deployment step does not show that payments are correct and usable.
questions.tradeoff: More signals require clear abort rules.
questions.followup: How would low-frequency duplicate charges be monitored?

questions.title: Expansion decision
questions.prompt: Canary traffic has too few expensive payment types to evaluate them. What is best?

choices.text: Expand globally because aggregate p50 improved
choices.why: The risky segment is untested.

choices.text: Treat no observed failures as proof of safety
choices.why: Rare-event coverage is absent.

choices.text: Extend or target representative exposure before expanding
choices.why: The decision gains evidence for the missing segment.

choices.text: Suppress segment metrics to simplify the gate
choices.why: That hides uncertainty.

questions.explanation: Absence of failures in absent traffic is not reassuring evidence. Rare payment paths may carry disproportionate risk even when they contribute little to aggregate traffic. Deliberately obtain representative evidence or document the remaining uncertainty before expanding; zero observed failures among zero examples proves nothing about that segment.
questions.tradeoff: Targeted exposure can lengthen release time.
questions.followup: What risk would justify shipping before full statistical certainty?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A checkout release goes to five percent of requests. Mobile users mostly hit the canary; desktop users mostly hit the control. A payment provider is simultaneously slowing down.

questions.title: Rollback trigger ownership
questions.prompt: Who should define release abort criteria?

choices.why: Business harm is application-specific.

choices.text: Only the author after seeing results
choices.why: Post-hoc thresholds invite bias.

choices.text: No one; any metric movement triggers rollback
choices.why: Normal noise causes instability.

choices.text: Service owners before rollout, tied to user harm and recovery
choices.why: Thresholds become actionable and accountable.

questions.explanation: A canary needs a decision policy as well as traffic splitting. Agree on user-harm thresholds, observation windows and who can stop the rollout before results arrive. This avoids choosing convenient criteria after seeing a favorable metric and makes a noisy canary operationally actionable.
questions.tradeoff: Conservative gates slow releases but reduce harmful exposure.
questions.followup: How would an incident in a shared provider suspend the experiment?

questions.title: Surge deadlock
questions.prompt: New pods remain pending while old pods stay healthy. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Only application logs in pending pods
choices.why: Unscheduled pods may not run application code.

choices.text: Scheduler capacity against surge and resource requests
choices.why: The rollout may lack room for replacement capacity.

choices.text: Increase the rollout progress deadline without inspecting resource requests
choices.why: More time does not resolve an unschedulable surge when the cluster has no available capacity.

choices.text: Relax readiness thresholds on the old pods
choices.why: Healthy old pods are not the scheduling bottleneck for pending replacements.

questions.explanation: A zero-unavailable policy needs sufficient temporary capacity or an explicit capacity tradeoff. A zero-unavailable rollout can require old and replacement capacity to coexist. If the scheduler cannot place the surge pods, the deployment can stall without any application failure; inspect requested resources and actual cluster headroom.
questions.tradeoff: Headroom costs money outside deployments.
questions.followup: How would peak and rollout capacity be budgeted together?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Ten instances barely handle peak traffic. A rollout can create new instances before removing old ones, but cluster resource headroom is limited.

questions.title: Readiness purpose
questions.prompt: What should readiness establish for a new API replica?

choices.why: Image presence does not mean it can serve.
Startup can precede readiness.

choices.text: That it can safely accept the relevant traffic
choices.why: Routing should wait for usable service state.

choices.text: That every remote service is perfectly healthy
choices.why: Overbroad checks can remove all replicas during shared failures.

questions.explanation: Readiness is a routing eligibility decision, not a universal dependency health certificate. Readiness should say whether this replica can accept the traffic routed to it. A probe that requires every optional dependency to be healthy can remove all replicas during a shared downstream incident and amplify the original failure.
questions.tradeoff: Overly strict readiness can amplify outages.
questions.followup: Which dependencies are mandatory for every request versus optional?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Ten instances barely handle peak traffic. A rollout can create new instances before removing old ones, but cluster resource headroom is limited.

questions.title: Capacity versus speed
questions.prompt: The cluster cannot surge and cannot tolerate one fewer replica at peak. Best decision?

choices.text: Add temporary capacity or move the rollout to a safe demand window
choices.why: One of the conflicting resource constraints must change.

choices.text: Set unavailable replicas to zero and wait for magic capacity
choices.why: The scheduling constraint remains.
Peak capacity is knowingly violated.
Traffic can reach unusable instances.

questions.explanation: Configuration cannot satisfy incompatible capacity constraints without changing resources, demand or risk. No rollout setting creates missing compute resources. If all existing capacity is required at peak and no replacement can be scheduled, add capacity, reduce demand, choose another window or explicitly accept reduced service capacity.
questions.tradeoff: Temporary capacity and off-peak windows have cost and scheduling tradeoffs.
questions.followup: How would an urgent security release change the risk decision?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Ten instances barely handle peak traffic. A rollout can create new instances before removing old ones, but cluster resource headroom is limited.

questions.title: Rollout health
questions.prompt: Which completion criterion is strongest?

choices.why: Counts can include unhealthy application behavior.
The control-plane operation may succeed despite user regressions.
Removal does not prove replacements serve correctly.

choices.text: Ready capacity plus version-specific user outcomes and saturation
choices.why: It combines orchestration state with service behavior.

questions.explanation: Orchestrator success and business success are different layers. Replica readiness is necessary but not sufficient for correct application behavior. Track version-specific success, latency and saturation after routing traffic, because all desired pods can be running while the new code returns incorrect results.
questions.tradeoff: Outcome gates need metrics and ownership.
questions.followup: How should partial rollout state appear in incident dashboards?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Ten instances barely handle peak traffic. A rollout can create new instances before removing old ones, but cluster resource headroom is limited.

questions.title: Drain boundary
questions.prompt: What should termination do?

choices.text: Remove routing eligibility, stop new work and drain accepted requests
choices.why: This preserves in-flight work within the grace budget.
Accepted operations may be interrupted.

choices.text: Keep accepting requests until the final second
choices.why: New work cannot finish in the remaining time.

choices.text: Return success for all active requests without completing them
choices.why: That violates the response contract.

questions.explanation: Shutdown is a controlled transition from accepting work to finishing it. First stop new admission at the routing and application boundaries, then let accepted work finish inside the remaining grace budget. Account for propagation delay so requests arriving during endpoint removal do not start work that cannot complete.
questions.tradeoff: Routing propagation and application drain both consume time.
questions.followup: How would you reserve margin for slow endpoint removal?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. API requests can last 40 seconds. A terminating instance should stop accepting new work and finish accepted work within a 60-second grace period. Clients may retry timed-out operations.

questions.title: Ambiguous client retry
questions.prompt: A request commits just before the connection closes. What protects a retry?

choices.text: Assume closed connections imply no commit
choices.why: Commit and response delivery are different events.

choices.text: A durable operation identity and idempotent result handling
choices.why: The retry can recover the same effect.
It reduces but cannot eliminate response loss.

choices.text: Retry with a new business ID
choices.why: That may create a second effect.

questions.explanation: Graceful shutdown reduces interruptions but does not remove distributed outcome ambiguity. The server's durable effect and the client's receipt of its response are separate events. A retry should recover the result for the same logical operation rather than create another effect simply because shutdown interrupted the connection.
questions.tradeoff: Idempotency records need retention and payload checks.
questions.followup: How long should an operation identity remain valid?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. API requests can last 40 seconds. A terminating instance should stop accepting new work and finish accepted work within a 60-second grace period. Clients may retry timed-out operations.

questions.title: Grace timeout
questions.prompt: Some requests legitimately take five minutes. What should change?

choices.text: Increase the grace period to 90 seconds and keep the five-minute synchronous contract
choices.why: That still leaves a gap between operation duration and the process lifecycle bound.

choices.text: Allow indefinite graceful termination for every deployment
choices.why: It can preserve individual requests but removes a bounded deployment and failure-recovery policy.

choices.text: Automatically retry every long request on the replacement replica
choices.why: Retry is safe only with durable progress and idempotent effects; otherwise it can duplicate work.

choices.text: Make long work resumable or asynchronous, or revise the bound explicitly
choices.why: The operation lifecycle fits deployment reality.

questions.explanation: Long-lived business work should not depend accidentally on one process lifetime. A five-minute operation cannot reliably finish inside a one-minute process termination allowance. Either revise the lifecycle bound or move the business operation into durable resumable work, with the API exposing progress rather than tying success to one process.
questions.tradeoff: Asynchronous workflows require status and retry semantics.
questions.followup: How would an export job resume after replacement?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. API requests can last 40 seconds. A terminating instance should stop accepting new work and finish accepted work within a 60-second grace period. Clients may retry timed-out operations.

questions.title: Deployment test
questions.prompt: Which test provides useful drain evidence?

choices.why: No in-flight behavior is exercised.
A clean exit can still lose requests.

choices.text: Terminate under representative traffic and reconcile accepted operations
choices.why: It exposes routing, drain and retry interactions.
Startup does not test shutdown.

questions.explanation: Measure accepted work through terminal outcomes across forced lifecycle changes. Run termination while representative operations are active, then reconcile every accepted request to a final state. Include retries and response loss so the test distinguishes successful draining from merely moving duplicate or lost work to another replica.
questions.tradeoff: Representative tests need careful isolation from production side effects.
questions.followup: Which assertions distinguish duplicated, lost and merely delayed work?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. API requests can last 40 seconds. A terminating instance should stop accepting new work and finish accepted work within a 60-second grace period. Clients may retry timed-out operations.

questions.title: Removed field reuse
questions.prompt: What should happen when account_id is removed?

choices.text: Reuse field 7 for a string called campaign_id
choices.why: Old bytes can be misinterpreted as new meaning.
Existing encoded messages rely on field numbers.

choices.text: Reserve the removed number and name
choices.why: Future schema authors cannot accidentally repurpose them.

choices.text: Assume new code never sees old messages
choices.why: Replay and old consumers are explicit requirements.

questions.explanation: Wire identity survives source-code renaming and deployment timing. Persisted bytes identify fields by their numbers, not by the latest source-code name. Reserving removed identifiers prevents future code from assigning a new meaning to old replay data or messages from still-supported producers.
questions.tradeoff: Reserved identifiers remain unavailable for future reuse.
questions.followup: How would persisted events be tested against future decoders?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A proto3 event has field 7 named account_id. Messages are persisted for replay, and old consumers remain active for months.

questions.title: Presence semantics
questions.prompt: A new scalar limit must distinguish unset from explicitly zero. Which proto3 design fits?

choices.text: An implicit scalar with zero default only
choices.why: Unset and explicit zero are not distinguishable by that field alone.

choices.text: Use explicit presence such as optional
choices.why: The receiver can tell absence from a set zero.
Encoding details are not a business presence contract.
Names do not carry presence on the binary wire.

questions.explanation: Presence is part of API semantics, not just serialization size. Explicit zero may mean a deliberately disabled limit while absence may mean inherit a default. Preserve that distinction in the schema and document how consumers interpret it instead of inferring presence from payload size or encoding accidents.
questions.tradeoff: Consumers must define default behavior when absent.
questions.followup: What should a patch request mean when limit is omitted?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A proto3 event has field 7 named account_id. Messages are persisted for replay, and old consumers remain active for months.

questions.title: Wire-safe versus semantic-safe
questions.prompt: A new optional field parses everywhere. Is the rollout necessarily safe?

choices.text: No; defaults, authorization and business interpretation still need review
choices.why: Parsing compatibility does not prove semantic compatibility.

choices.text: Yes; a decoder accepting bytes proves behavior
choices.why: Accepted bytes can change decisions incorrectly.

choices.text: Only if the serialized payload remains within the old size limit
choices.why: Size compatibility does not prove that defaults or business interpretation remain correct.

choices.text: Only if the new field uses an unused number
choices.why: Unused numbering is necessary for many changes, but does not establish semantic compatibility.

questions.explanation: A transport can carry data safely while services disagree about meaning. An added field may parse correctly while introducing an unsafe default or a business rule old consumers do not enforce. Review behavior under absence, unknown values and mixed versions, not only whether decoders accept the byte stream.
questions.tradeoff: Contract tests add coordination across teams.
questions.followup: How would an old consumer handle a new mandatory business rule?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A proto3 event has field 7 named account_id. Messages are persisted for replay, and old consumers remain active for months.

questions.title: Replay compatibility gate
questions.prompt: Which release gate covers the months-long compatibility window?

choices.text: Compile only the newest producer and consumer together
choices.why: Mixed versions and historical bytes are untested.

choices.text: Discard old events before each release
choices.why: That violates replay requirements.
Formatting is not wire behavior.

choices.text: Test supported old/new pairs plus historical event fixtures
choices.why: This exercises the actual compatibility matrix.

questions.explanation: Retention and client support windows define which combinations matter. Test the combinations that can actually coexist during the stated support and retention windows. Historical fixtures are especially important because replay can introduce an old producer's bytes long after that producer has been decommissioned.
questions.tradeoff: A larger matrix increases maintenance cost.
questions.followup: When can an old decoder safely leave the support matrix?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A proto3 event has field 7 named account_id. Messages are persisted for replay, and old consumers remain active for months.

questions.title: Deployment versus release
questions.prompt: What does deploying with the flag off achieve?

choices.text: It proves the new algorithm is correct
choices.why: Unused code may still be wrong.

choices.text: It separates binary rollout from user exposure
choices.why: Enablement can be controlled after deployment.
Startup and shared code can still regress.

choices.text: It removes the need for monitoring
choices.why: Flagged paths still need outcome evidence.

questions.explanation: A flag controls exposure, not all effects of a binary change. The new path can be activated gradually without repeating the binary deployment, which reduces exposure coupling. However, shared initialization, libraries and background work can still change while the feature is off, so dark deployment still needs verification.
questions.tradeoff: Two paths increase test surface.
questions.followup: What shared initialization could fail even while the flag is off?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new recommendation algorithm is deployed dark. A flag enables it per tenant. The fallback remains the old algorithm, and changing the flag does not alter stored data.

questions.title: Sticky assignment
questions.prompt: Why keep a tenant's assignment stable during an experiment?

choices.why: Outcomes can be associated with a consistent treatment.
Sample size and noise still matter.
Stable assignment does not ensure fairness.

choices.text: It makes the old algorithm unnecessary immediately
choices.why: Fallback still provides recovery.

questions.explanation: Stable units make experimentation and incident attribution easier. Assign the experiment at the unit whose behavior should remain consistent, such as tenant or user. Switching treatment between successive requests can mix state and obscure attribution, although stable assignment alone does not ensure representative or balanced cohorts.
questions.tradeoff: Large tenants can create imbalanced cohorts.
questions.followup: Would user-level or tenant-level assignment better avoid interference?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new recommendation algorithm is deployed dark. A flag enables it per tenant. The fallback remains the old algorithm, and changing the flag does not alter stored data.

questions.title: Kill switch limit
questions.prompt: The new code writes incompatible persistent state. What changes?

choices.text: Turning off the flag automatically rewrites all state
choices.why: Flags do not undo durable mutations.
Persistent effects survive exposure changes.

choices.text: Rollback must account for data compatibility and repair
choices.why: Disabling future writes is not recovery of past writes.
That is disproportionate and violates durability.

questions.explanation: Reversibility must be designed across state, not assumed from a switch. A switch can stop future execution but cannot automatically undo values already persisted by the new path. Design compatible data formats or a repair workflow before calling a state-changing feature reversible; test rollback on newly written records.
questions.tradeoff: Compatible storage formats may delay feature simplification.
questions.followup: How would you make the write path forward- and backward-readable?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new recommendation algorithm is deployed dark. A flag enables it per tenant. The fallback remains the old algorithm, and changing the flag does not alter stored data.

questions.title: Flag retirement
questions.prompt: What is the strongest retirement criterion?

choices.text: The author is tired of maintaining it
choices.why: Preference does not prove safety.

choices.text: One successful request used the new path
choices.why: Coverage is insufficient.

choices.text: The flag has existed a month
choices.why: Elapsed time is not evidence.

choices.text: Stable outcomes, complete adoption and an explicit recovery plan
choices.why: Removal is tied to operational confidence.

questions.explanation: A permanent accidental flag accumulates hidden configuration states. Retire the branch only after its support and recovery purpose is deliberately closed. Check outcome stability and consumer adoption, then remove dead configuration and tests together so a forgotten flag does not become an undocumented operational state.
questions.tradeoff: Removing a fallback reduces complexity but removes a recovery option.
questions.followup: Which flags should remain as deliberate load-shedding controls?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new recommendation algorithm is deployed dark. A flag enables it per tenant. The fallback remains the old algorithm, and changing the flag does not alter stored data.

questions.title: Protect foreground work
questions.prompt: Which control is most appropriate?

choices.text: Run all rows in one giant transaction
choices.why: Long locks and resource use can harm foreground traffic.
The harm remains hidden.

choices.text: Use bounded batches with checkpointing and adaptive throttling
choices.why: Work is resumable and pressure can be controlled.
Connection contention can worsen.

questions.explanation: A backfill is competing production load and needs explicit resource boundaries. Treat the backfill as a competing workload with checkpoints and a resource budget. Batches should be small enough to pause and retry safely, and throttling should respond to foreground service health rather than only the backfill's own completion speed.
questions.tradeoff: Throttling extends completion time.
questions.followup: Which signal should reduce backfill concurrency first?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A 400-million-row migration derives a new index from existing rows. Live writes continue. Database latency rises when the backfill runs without limits.

questions.title: Concurrent write correctness
questions.prompt: A row changes after the scan reads it but before the derived write. What prevents stale overwrite?

choices.text: Version-aware conditional writes or equivalent ordered reconciliation
choices.why: The old snapshot cannot replace newer derived state.
The race remains possible.
That can widen stale windows.
Equal counts do not prove correct values.

questions.explanation: Backfill ordering must coexist with live updates. A stale scan result must not overwrite a newer live update in the target. Compare source versions or replay ordered changes through a design that preserves the latest state, including deletion markers and retries.
questions.tradeoff: Version checks and replay require additional metadata.
questions.followup: How would deletions interact with the backfill?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A 400-million-row migration derives a new index from existing rows. Live writes continue. Database latency rises when the backfill runs without limits.

questions.title: Completion proof
questions.prompt: Which evidence is needed before switching reads?

choices.text: The scan reached the last primary key
choices.why: Concurrent updates may still be missing.

choices.text: Coverage, value reconciliation and caught-up change processing
choices.why: These cover both historical and live state.
That does not establish correctness.
Size is not semantic agreement.

questions.explanation: A cursor position is progress, not certified completeness. Reaching the final scan key proves traversal, not that every derived value matches current source state. Combine historical coverage with change-stream catch-up and semantic reconciliation at a defined boundary before routing authoritative reads.
questions.tradeoff: Reconciliation consumes capacity and may require sampling plus targeted full checks.
questions.followup: Which invariants demand full rather than sampled verification?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A 400-million-row migration derives a new index from existing rows. Live writes continue. Database latency rises when the backfill runs without limits.

questions.title: Pause and resume
questions.prompt: How should an interrupted backfill restart?

choices.why: That increases load and can repeat side effects.
Coverage is lost.

choices.text: Trust in-memory offsets after a crash
choices.why: They may not reflect durable work.

choices.text: Use durable checkpoints and idempotent range processing
choices.why: Repeated ranges remain safe while progress survives.

questions.explanation: Checkpoint advancement must correspond to durable completion, not dispatch. Advance a durable checkpoint only after the corresponding effects are safely recoverable. Reprocessing a range after a crash must be idempotent, so repeating completed work is preferable to silently skipping a range whose completion is uncertain.
questions.tradeoff: Coarse checkpoints repeat more work; fine ones add overhead.
questions.followup: What if a checkpoint commits but a derived write did not?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A 400-million-row migration derives a new index from existing rows. Live writes continue. Database latency rises when the backfill runs without limits.

questions.title: Configuration compatibility
questions.prompt: What should older binaries do when the new optional field appears?

choices.text: Crash on any unknown field by assumption
choices.why: That makes staged overlap impossible.

choices.text: Handle the additive field according to an explicit compatibility contract
choices.why: Mixed-version behavior is designed rather than accidental.
Other services lose required state.

choices.text: Read whatever default happens to deserialize
choices.why: An accidental default may change policy.

questions.explanation: Configuration is an API consumed by deployed binaries. The configuration format is an interface shared by several binary generations. Define defaults, validation and supported additions explicitly, and test both current and rollback consumers so a global change does not break regions not yet upgraded.
questions.tradeoff: Compatibility code persists through the support window.
questions.followup: How would validation reject typos without rejecting approved additions?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Three regions serve independently but share a global configuration service. A release changes request parsing and needs a new configuration field.

questions.title: Regional canary limit
questions.prompt: Why can a regional rollout still have global impact?

choices.text: The changed region may mutate shared global configuration
choices.why: Isolation follows dependencies, not geographic labels.
Independent serving was specified.

choices.text: A canary cannot reduce any risk
choices.why: It can bound region-local effects.

choices.text: Global DNS always sends all users to one region
choices.why: That was not specified.

questions.explanation: Map shared state before claiming a release has regional blast-radius limits. Regional API fleets can still write the same global state, so geographic staging does not automatically bound impact. Identify shared mutable dependencies and version or scope their updates before claiming a release affects only one region.
questions.tradeoff: Independent config versions add management complexity.
questions.followup: Which writes must be blocked or scoped during a regional canary?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Three regions serve independently but share a global configuration service. A release changes request parsing and needs a new configuration field.

questions.title: Rollback preparation
questions.prompt: What must be checked before enabling the new global field?

choices.why: Other binary versions consume the same field.
Artifact availability does not prove config compatibility.

choices.text: Compatibility of active and rollback binaries with the new configuration
choices.why: Rollback paths are consumers too.
Traffic does not define parsing semantics.

questions.explanation: Recovery binaries must understand the state that will exist after rollout. The environment after a rollback includes configuration already published by the new release. Verify that old code handles that state before enabling it globally, or retain an explicit compatible configuration rollback path alongside the binary.
questions.tradeoff: Retaining compatibility can delay cleanup.
questions.followup: When is it safe to stop supporting the old config format?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Three regions serve independently but share a global configuration service. A release changes request parsing and needs a new configuration field.

questions.title: Expansion evidence
questions.prompt: What supports moving from one region to the next?

choices.text: No aggregate alerts during a short quiet interval
choices.why: Sparse traffic may not exercise rare or expensive request paths.

choices.text: Choose the region with the fewest users and expand once its pods are healthy
choices.why: Smallness reduces exposure but does not prove that the cohort represents later regions' workloads.

choices.text: The regional deployment controller reports all desired replicas ready
choices.why: Readiness establishes orchestration progress, not the user and shared-dependency outcomes needed for expansion.

choices.text: Representative workload outcomes and shared-dependency guardrails
choices.why: Both local behavior and possible global effects are evaluated.

questions.explanation: A canary needs representative evidence at the relevant failure boundaries. Use the region to learn about representative request paths and observe effects on shared dependencies. A small canary can be unrepresentative, and a deploy command's success says nothing about user outcomes or global configuration side effects.
questions.tradeoff: Waiting for rare traffic extends rollout duration.
questions.followup: How would you safely generate representative synthetic traffic?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Three regions serve independently but share a global configuration service. A release changes request parsing and needs a new configuration field.

questions.title: Rebuild mismatch
questions.prompt: What weakens the staging evidence?

choices.text: Production may contain different resolved dependencies or build inputs
choices.why: The tested and deployed artifacts need not match.

choices.text: Source revisions can never be tested
choices.why: They can, but source identity is not full artifact identity.
The issue is artifact equivalence, not log honesty.
Scale matters but does not explain binary mismatch.

questions.explanation: A source revision alone does not identify all build inputs. Unpinned dependency resolution, compiler versions or build inputs can produce different executable content from the same source commit. Staging evidence applies most directly to the tested artifact, so identify and control the actual promoted payload.
questions.tradeoff: Reproducible builds still need environment compatibility checks.
questions.followup: Which metadata identifies the exact deployed artifact?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A release is tested in staging, then rebuilt separately for production from the same source revision. Dependency resolution is not pinned.

questions.title: Promotion policy
questions.prompt: Which practice best preserves tested artifact identity?

choices.text: Rebuild at every environment using latest dependencies
choices.why: Outputs may drift.
Runtime dependencies may still differ.

choices.text: Promote the same immutable artifact by digest
choices.why: The payload tested is the payload deployed.
Mutable labels obscure identity.

questions.explanation: Artifact promotion narrows the gap between test evidence and deployment. An immutable digest names the exact executable content that passed tests. Keep environment-specific settings separately versioned and reviewed, since promoting identical bytes does not guarantee that a different configuration has identical behavior.
questions.tradeoff: Environment-specific configuration must remain separately controlled.
questions.followup: How would you track configuration alongside artifact identity?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A release is tested in staging, then rebuilt separately for production from the same source revision. Dependency resolution is not pinned.

questions.title: Supply-chain response
questions.prompt: A promoted artifact's dependency is compromised. What is a sound response?

choices.text: Keep the artifact because it passed staging before the compromise was discovered
choices.why: Earlier tests do not remove a newly identified vulnerable or compromised dependency.

choices.text: Identify affected digests, contain exposure and rebuild from reviewed inputs
choices.why: Traceability enables targeted remediation.

choices.text: Rebuild the same source immediately with unconstrained latest dependencies
choices.why: That may remove one issue but introduces unreviewed inputs and weakens provenance.

choices.text: Roll back every service regardless of whether it contains the affected component
choices.why: A global rollback can create unnecessary risk and may still select an affected artifact.

questions.explanation: Immutability supports provenance and rollback; it does not certify security. Use provenance to find the affected artifact digests and their deployments, then contain or replace them with reviewed inputs. Immutability is valuable for scope and reproducibility, but it can faithfully preserve a vulnerable dependency too.
questions.tradeoff: Emergency replacement still needs focused validation.
questions.followup: How would you find all services using the affected component?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A release is tested in staging, then rebuilt separately for production from the same source revision. Dependency resolution is not pinned.

questions.title: Release evidence bundle
questions.prompt: Which bundle best supports later investigation?

choices.why: It does not identify executable content.
The branch may move.
Build inputs and configuration remain unknown.

choices.text: Artifact digest, source revision, build provenance, config version and rollout outcomes
choices.why: It connects construction to observed deployment.

questions.explanation: Release traceability is a chain, not one identifier. The evidence chain should connect source and dependency inputs to the built digest and then to deployment configuration and observed outcomes. A branch name or timestamp alone cannot reconstruct what code and policy were actually serving.
questions.tradeoff: Collecting and retaining evidence has operational cost.
questions.followup: What evidence should be independent of the compromised build runner?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A release is tested in staging, then rebuilt separately for production from the same source revision. Dependency resolution is not pinned.

questions.title: Semantic incompatibility
questions.prompt: Why is changing the number's meaning unsafe even if parsing succeeds?

choices.why: They can with explicit precision and units.

choices.text: Old consumers will interpret the new value using the old unit
choices.why: Wire validity does not preserve meaning.
That is not the correctness issue.
No such behavior was specified.

questions.explanation: Units are part of the contract and must be explicit during coexistence. A numeric field can remain syntactically valid while changing every downstream calculation by a scale factor. Unit meaning must remain explicit across producers, consumers and historical replay; the decoder cannot infer it safely from a plausible value.
questions.tradeoff: A new field or event version adds transitional complexity.
questions.followup: How would you handle currencies with different minor-unit exponents?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A producer wants to replace an event's amount unit from cents to whole currency units without changing the field name. Consumers update on independent schedules.

questions.title: Compatible introduction
questions.prompt: Which rollout fits independent consumers?

choices.text: Add an explicitly named/versioned representation and migrate consumers
choices.why: Both meanings remain distinguishable.
Old readers calculate incorrect amounts.

choices.text: Require every team to deploy in the same millisecond
choices.why: That coordination assumption is unrealistic.

choices.text: Infer units from whether values are large
choices.why: Legitimate values overlap.

questions.explanation: Do not encode version negotiation in guessed business-value ranges. Introduce a representation whose name or version makes the new unit unambiguous, then migrate consumers while maintaining the old contract as needed. Range-based guessing fails because legitimate small and large amounts overlap between units.
questions.tradeoff: Dual representation needs consistency checks.
questions.followup: Which representation remains authoritative during migration?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A producer wants to replace an event's amount unit from cents to whole currency units without changing the field name. Consumers update on independent schedules.

questions.title: External consumer retirement
questions.prompt: A partner is offline for weeks and may replay old events. What governs retirement?

choices.text: Retire the old representation at the producer's next quarterly release
choices.why: The producer cadence does not define a disconnected partner's support or replay obligations.

choices.text: Retire it when a compatible SDK becomes available
choices.why: Availability of an upgrade is not evidence that supported consumers have adopted it.

choices.text: The agreed support and replay window plus consumer evidence
choices.why: The contract includes disconnected consumers.

choices.text: Retire it after a day with no old-version live traffic
