choices.why: Offline partners and historical replay can reintroduce the old representation later.

questions.explanation: Consumer absence is not proof of abandonment. An offline partner can return with a supported binary and replay retained events. Retirement therefore follows the agreed compatibility horizon and evidence about consumers, not only current traffic or the release date of a replacement SDK.
questions.tradeoff: Long support windows increase maintenance.
questions.followup: How would a deprecation deadline be communicated and enforced?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A producer wants to replace an event's amount unit from cents to whole currency units without changing the field name. Consumers update on independent schedules.

questions.title: Error containment
questions.prompt: Some new events used the wrong unit. What is the safest recovery direction?

choices.text: Overwrite history without tracking affected IDs
choices.why: Consumers cannot reconcile corrections.

choices.text: Replay every event as if new
choices.why: That can duplicate business effects.
Money invariants remain violated.

choices.text: Identify affected versions and issue idempotent auditable corrections
choices.why: Recovery preserves traceability and avoids duplicate effects.

questions.explanation: Repair should distinguish original events, corrected interpretations and already-applied effects. Identify which event versions and business effects used the wrong interpretation before repairing them. Corrections should have stable identities and audit links so replaying a repair does not duplicate charges, credits or other downstream effects.
questions.tradeoff: Correction workflows can be operationally expensive.
questions.followup: How would you prove all downstream balances were reconciled?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A producer wants to replace an event's amount unit from cents to whole currency units without changing the field name. Consumers update on independent schedules.

questions.title: Timeout interpretation
questions.prompt: What state should checkout record immediately?

choices.why: The charge may have committed.
No success evidence was received.
The observed boundary is ambiguous.
Network failure does not reverse a commit.

questions.explanation: Response loss is not business rollback. The provider may have committed before the response disappeared, so neither success nor failure is established by the timeout. Persist the unresolved operation and reconcile using its stable identity rather than inviting a second independent charge.
questions.tradeoff: Unknown states require user communication and recovery workers.
questions.followup: How should the interface discourage accidental duplicate checkout?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A checkout sends a charge request to an external provider with a stable merchant operation ID. The request times out after the provider may have committed.

questions.title: Safe retry identity
questions.prompt: What should a retry reuse under the provider's supported idempotency contract?

choices.text: The same logical operation key and equivalent payload
choices.why: It refers to the same charge intent.
The provider sees separate operations.

choices.text: Use the customer ID as the key for every checkout
choices.why: One customer can make several legitimate purchases, which would incorrectly collide.

choices.text: Reuse the key while silently substituting the newly selected amount
choices.why: The key should not identify two different charge intents; payload conflicts need explicit handling.

questions.explanation: Identity must be stable per intent, not per network attempt or customer lifetime. The key identifies the business intent across attempts, while payload equivalence prevents one identity from being reused for a different amount or recipient. Respect the provider's retention and conflict behavior rather than assuming deduplication lasts forever.
questions.tradeoff: Provider deduplication retention must cover retry behavior.
questions.followup: What should happen when retries exceed the provider's retention window?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A checkout sends a charge request to an external provider with a stable merchant operation ID. The request times out after the provider may have committed.

questions.title: Provider switch
questions.prompt: The first provider's result remains unknown. What is dangerous about charging a second provider immediately?

choices.why: They can, which creates the risk.

choices.text: Both providers may charge because their idempotency domains differ
choices.why: One provider's key does not coordinate the other.

choices.text: A second provider always refunds the first
choices.why: No cross-provider transaction exists.
Protocol differences do not provide coordination.

questions.explanation: Provider failover crosses an external correctness boundary. Each provider can correctly deduplicate within its own domain and still charge once, producing two charges for one order. A failover policy must resolve or explicitly accept the first provider's uncertainty before creating authority in another payment system.
questions.tradeoff: Urgency may require explicit risk handling and later compensation.
questions.followup: How would reconciliation distinguish duplicate charges from legitimate repeated purchases?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A checkout sends a charge request to an external provider with a stable merchant operation ID. The request times out after the provider may have committed.

questions.title: Closure evidence
questions.prompt: What establishes the final order state?

choices.why: Attempts do not prove effect.
Time is not provider outcome evidence.
It may be incomplete or stale.

choices.text: Authoritative provider state correlated to the merchant operation and local ledger
choices.why: Evidence joins external and internal effects.

questions.explanation: Close uncertainty with verified business state, not transport guesses. Correlate provider status, local order state and ledger effects by the merchant operation identity. Retry counts or elapsed time cannot establish whether money moved; unresolved mismatches need an exception path rather than a fabricated terminal state.
questions.tradeoff: Reconciliation needs ownership and an exception queue.
questions.followup: What discrepancies should block automatic closure?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A checkout sends a charge request to an external provider with a stable merchant operation ID. The request times out after the provider may have committed.

questions.title: Atomic postings
questions.prompt: What must the transaction include?

choices.text: Debit now and credit in an unrelated future write
choices.why: A crash can leave an unbalanced transfer.

choices.text: Both postings and required balance/invariant checks
choices.why: The commit boundary covers the transfer invariant.
It does not atomically move value.
The authoritative ledger remains unchanged.

questions.explanation: The business invariant determines the transaction boundary. Debit, credit and relevant balance checks must commit as one invariant-preserving operation in the stated single database. Persisting the audit separately or delaying one posting permits a crash to expose an unbalanced transfer even if each write is individually durable.
questions.tradeoff: Cross-database transfers require a different protocol.
questions.followup: Which invariant would a double-entry consistency check verify?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A wallet transfers one currency between two accounts in one transactional database. A committed transfer must contain balanced postings and must not allow unauthorized overdraft.

questions.title: Concurrent spending
questions.prompt: Two debits each see sufficient balance before either commits. What prevents overspending?

choices.text: Serialize or atomically condition the authoritative balance transition
choices.why: Both debits cannot spend the same available amount.
Freshness is not atomic arbitration.
Uniqueness does not protect balance.

choices.text: Subtract in two application threads without database coordination
choices.why: The race remains.

questions.explanation: Correct balance reads alone do not prevent a check-then-act race. The available amount is a contested resource that both callers can observe before either acts. Lock or condition the authoritative state transition, or use suitable serializable behavior with retries, so the same spendable funds cannot authorize both debits.
questions.tradeoff: Contention may limit throughput for hot accounts.
questions.followup: How would reserved and settled balances differ?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A wallet transfers one currency between two accounts in one transactional database. A committed transfer must contain balanced postings and must not allow unauthorized overdraft.

questions.title: Correction model
questions.prompt: A posted transfer is later found incorrect. Which repair preserves auditability?

choices.why: The explanation for prior balances disappears.

choices.text: Edit arbitrary postings without a linked reason
choices.why: Historical reconciliation becomes ambiguous.

choices.text: Append linked reversing or adjusting entries under a defined policy
choices.why: The correction remains traceable.

choices.text: Ignore it if the total is small
choices.why: Magnitude does not remove the invariant.

questions.explanation: Financial state benefits from explicit correction history rather than invisible mutation. Keep the original effect visible and add a linked correction describing why and how the balance changed. Silent mutation makes prior reports and reconciliation difficult to explain, while explicit adjustments can be replayed and audited under stable identities.
questions.tradeoff: Append-only history requires richer reporting.
questions.followup: How would the correction avoid exceeding available funds incorrectly?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A wallet transfers one currency between two accounts in one transactional database. A committed transfer must contain balanced postings and must not allow unauthorized overdraft.

questions.title: Materialized balance
questions.prompt: A fast balance table is derived from postings. What proves it remains trustworthy?

choices.text: Its row count equals account count
choices.why: Counts do not verify amounts.

choices.text: Its cache hit rate is high
choices.why: Performance is not correctness.
Staleness can look stable.

choices.text: Reconciliation against authoritative postings and tracked projection progress
choices.why: Both arithmetic and completeness are checked.

questions.explanation: A derived balance is only as complete and correct as its update pipeline. A projection can have every account row yet contain incorrect or incomplete sums. Reconcile arithmetic against authoritative postings and track which history has been applied, treating lag or unexplained differences as evidence gaps rather than valid current balances.
questions.tradeoff: Reconciliation consumes resources and needs discrepancy handling.
questions.followup: Which discrepancies require pausing withdrawals?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A wallet transfers one currency between two accounts in one transactional database. A committed transfer must contain balanced postings and must not allow unauthorized overdraft.

questions.title: Exclusive hold
questions.prompt: Which operation enforces one current holder?

choices.text: Read available and later write held without a condition
choices.why: Competing buyers can both act on the read.
The interface is not a shared authority.

choices.text: Atomically transition available to held with a unique hold identity
choices.why: Competing requests arbitrate at one boundary.

choices.text: Use separate locks only in each API process
choices.why: Different processes do not share those locks.

questions.explanation: Hold acquisition must be conditional and authoritative. The availability read is advisory until one atomic transition gives the seat to a specific hold identity. Another buyer racing on the same row must observe a conflict or later state, not independently convert the same prior availability into ownership.
questions.tradeoff: A hot seat creates deliberate contention.
questions.followup: How would availability replicas avoid promising a guaranteed purchase?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A concert seat has one authoritative availability row. Users may hold it for two minutes before confirming purchase. Holds can expire while payment is still processing.

questions.title: Late confirmation
questions.prompt: Payment returns after hold expiry and reassignment. What must confirmation check?

choices.why: Payment does not prove the seat is still owned.

choices.text: The current hold identity/version and valid transition
choices.why: A stale holder cannot claim a reassigned seat.

choices.text: Only the buyer's original browser timestamp
choices.why: The browser does not own the seat state.

choices.text: Only whether the seat number exists
choices.why: Existence is not entitlement.

questions.explanation: A hold identifier fences late work after expiry. The payment outcome does not preserve a hold that has expired and been reassigned. Confirmation must prove it still owns the current hold generation, and successful payment for an invalidated hold needs an explicit refund or recovery policy.
questions.tradeoff: A successful payment may require refund or manual recovery.
questions.followup: How would payment authorization rather than capture reduce this risk?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A concert seat has one authoritative availability row. Users may hold it for two minutes before confirming purchase. Holds can expire while payment is still processing.

questions.title: Expiration semantics
questions.prompt: Why is deleting a cache key insufficient as the only expiration mechanism?

choices.text: Authoritative ownership and late requests still need a coherent transition
choices.why: Cache disappearance does not arbitrate confirmation.
They can, but that is not the whole invariant.

choices.text: Every expiry must require a human
choices.why: Automation can enforce defined rules.
External payment work is independent.

questions.explanation: Time-based availability must connect to the same state machine as confirmation. A cache TTL can remove a convenient representation but does not coordinate late confirmation with reassignment. Tie expiration checks and sweepers to the authoritative reservation state machine so all contenders obey the same ownership and deadline rules.
questions.tradeoff: Lazy expiry checks can complement sweepers.
questions.followup: Which clock and deadline authority would you choose?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A concert seat has one authoritative availability row. Users may hold it for two minutes before confirming purchase. Holds can expire while payment is still processing.

questions.title: Partition behavior
questions.prompt: A region cannot reach the seat authority. The system promises no double-booking. What should it do?

choices.why: Two regions may sell the same seat.

choices.text: Accept an independent local reservation and label it guaranteed
choices.why: The isolated region cannot establish that another region has not already committed the same seat.

choices.text: Confirm locally and refund whichever buyer loses reconciliation
choices.why: That may be a business compromise, but it violates the stated no-double-booking promise.

choices.text: Decline or defer authoritative confirmation until coordination is restored
choices.why: The invariant takes precedence over write availability.

questions.explanation: Strict exclusivity limits independent operation during partitions. Two disconnected regions selling from stale copies cannot both guarantee exclusive ownership of one physical seat. Under the strict no-double-booking promise, the region without authoritative coordination must defer commitment or return an honest unavailable result.
questions.tradeoff: Users may face reduced availability.
questions.followup: Which weaker product promise would permit offline reservations?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A concert seat has one authoritative availability row. Users may hold it for two minutes before confirming purchase. Holds can expire while payment is still processing.

questions.title: Stock accounting
questions.prompt: Which invariant fits reservations?

choices.text: Available plus reserved plus sold accounts for the controlled stock under defined adjustments
choices.why: States explain where each unit resides.
That enables overselling.
Duplicate transport becomes duplicate demand.
Pending claims still consume capacity.

questions.explanation: Reservation state separates temporary claims from completed sale. Model stock as controlled quantities in explicit states so a unit cannot simultaneously be available and reserved. Restocking, damage, returns and sale finalization need defined transitions, rather than treating a cache count as an independently editable truth.
questions.tradeoff: Returns and replenishment need explicit additional transitions.
questions.followup: How would damaged stock be represented?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An item has 100 units. Orders reserve stock before payment. Reservations can be released, finalized or expire; duplicate workflow messages are possible.

questions.title: Duplicate release
questions.prompt: A release message is delivered twice. What is safe?

choices.why: The second delivery invents stock.
Different reservations would collide.

choices.text: Condition release on the reservation's current state and identity
choices.why: Only the first valid transition returns units.
Inventory remains stuck reserved.

questions.explanation: Idempotency belongs to the reservation transition, not just the queue. The first valid release changes reserved to released and returns its quantity; a repeated release should observe the terminal state and do nothing. The same arbitration must handle races with confirmation so one reservation cannot both sell and return its units.
questions.tradeoff: State retention must cover delayed messages.
questions.followup: How would release race with finalization?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An item has 100 units. Orders reserve stock before payment. Reservations can be released, finalized or expire; duplicate workflow messages are possible.

questions.title: Multi-warehouse promise
questions.prompt: Stock is spread across independent warehouses. What must the API distinguish?

choices.text: All warehouse counts are one atomic total by default
choices.why: Independent authorities do not imply global atomicity.
Availability display can be stale while commitment is controlled.
Allocation needs location identity.
Economics does not enforce exclusivity.

questions.explanation: Discovery and commitment can offer different guarantees if explicit. A fast aggregate availability view can help customers discover options without guaranteeing every displayed unit. Commit through warehouse authorities under a defined allocation workflow, and decide explicitly whether a multi-warehouse order uses coordinated reservation or compensating release.
questions.tradeoff: Cross-warehouse splitting adds workflow complexity.
questions.followup: When should an order reserve all warehouses atomically versus compensate?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An item has 100 units. Orders reserve stock before payment. Reservations can be released, finalized or expire; duplicate workflow messages are possible.

questions.title: Demand spike policy
questions.prompt: A flash sale overwhelms reservation capacity. What protects useful work?

choices.why: Users wait for stale demand indefinitely.
Contention intensifies.

choices.text: Advertise unlimited stock to reduce checks
choices.why: The product becomes incorrect.

choices.text: Bound admission, expire stale demand and preserve authoritative stock transitions
choices.why: Capacity policy does not weaken inventory correctness.

questions.explanation: Overload handling should not create stock or promise unowned units. Bound the amount of outstanding demand and reject or expire requests that can no longer serve the user. Keep stock arbitration correct under overload; faster admission or aggressive retries cannot create additional inventory and may increase contention.
questions.tradeoff: Fair queuing may trade throughput for perceived fairness.
questions.followup: How would bots and legitimate retries receive different treatment?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An item has 100 units. Orders reserve stock before payment. Reservations can be released, finalized or expire; duplicate workflow messages are possible.

questions.title: Two invariants
questions.prompt: Which constraints are required together? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Unique redemption per promotion and user
choices.why: It protects the per-user limit.
Different requests from one user can still redeem twice.

choices.text: Atomic budget consumption bounded by the campaign limit
choices.why: It protects the global cap.

choices.text: A cached count refreshed each minute only
choices.why: It can overshoot under concurrency.

questions.explanation: Per-user uniqueness and total budget are independent invariants. A uniqueness rule for promotion and user prevents repeat redemption by one customer, but does not limit different users collectively. Couple that rule with atomic campaign-budget consumption or safely allocated sub-budgets to preserve both constraints under concurrent replicas.
questions.tradeoff: Central budget contention may need allocated sub-budgets.
questions.followup: How would safe regional quotas avoid oversubscription?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A promotion allows 1,000 total redemptions and one redemption per user. Multiple API replicas handle claims concurrently.

questions.title: Check then insert
questions.prompt: Why can separate count and insert operations fail?

choices.text: Counts cannot be stored in databases
choices.why: Databases can store and query counts; the issue is concurrent claim arbitration.

choices.text: Concurrent callers can observe the same remaining slot
choices.why: The check and claim are not one atomic decision.
That is not the primary race.
Appropriate isolation and constraints can arbitrate.

questions.explanation: The last coupon is a contested resource, not a display number. If one slot remains, two callers can each read a count of 999 before either inserts, then both claim success. A transaction with appropriate isolation, a conditional budget update and uniqueness constraints must turn the check and claim into one authoritative decision.
questions.tradeoff: Strong arbitration adds latency under a hot campaign.
questions.followup: Which database exception should be a business conflict rather than a server error?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A promotion allows 1,000 total redemptions and one redemption per user. Multiple API replicas handle claims concurrently.

questions.title: Budget sharding
questions.prompt: How can independent regional budgets preserve a hard global maximum?

choices.text: Allocate disjoint quotas whose sum does not exceed the maximum
choices.why: Regions cannot collectively spend more authority than issued.

choices.text: Give each region the full 1,000 budget
choices.why: The total can multiply.
That does not preserve the hard cap.

choices.text: Use eventual counts with no admission bound
choices.why: Concurrent increments can exceed available budget.

questions.explanation: Escrow-style allocation trades flexible utilization for independent safety. Each region receives a bounded amount of spending authority, and the sum of issued authority stays within the campaign maximum. Transfers must revoke or debit one allocation before the same authority becomes spendable elsewhere, otherwise rebalancing can duplicate budget.
questions.tradeoff: Unused regional quota can strand capacity until reallocated.
questions.followup: How would quota transfer avoid being spent twice?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A promotion allows 1,000 total redemptions and one redemption per user. Multiple API replicas handle claims concurrently.

questions.title: Campaign correction
questions.prompt: A bug granted 20 excess coupons. Which response is engineering-sound?

choices.why: Customers and accounting lose a coherent history.

choices.text: Pretend eventual consistency guarantees later correction
choices.why: The effects need explicit policy.

choices.text: Restart all replicas and declare resolved
choices.why: Past excess grants remain.

choices.text: Contain new grants, reconcile affected users and execute a reviewed business remedy
choices.why: Recovery distinguishes technical containment from customer policy.

questions.explanation: Invariant violation requires both scope evidence and an accountable remedy. First stop the path that issues excess grants, then determine the exact affected claims and their business effects. Customer cancellation, honoring coupons or other remedies are explicit product decisions that should preserve audit history instead of silently rewriting records.
questions.tradeoff: Customer remediation may cost more than the coupon budget.
questions.followup: What evidence proves the bug is no longer issuing excess claims?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A promotion allows 1,000 total redemptions and one redemption per user. Multiple API replicas handle claims concurrently.

questions.title: Count once
questions.prompt: What identifies one billable usage occurrence?

choices.why: Replays have different arrival times.

choices.text: A stable source event identity with scoped deduplication
choices.why: Repeated delivery maps to one occurrence.
A customer legitimately makes many calls.
It lacks per-event correction evidence.

questions.explanation: Billing identity must survive replay and retry. Arrival time changes on replay, while a customer can generate many valid usage occurrences. Use a stable source event key and payload semantics to distinguish duplicate delivery from a new billable action, with retention aligned to the accepted replay horizon.
questions.tradeoff: Deduplication retention must match late-arrival policy.
questions.followup: How would source retries with changed quantities be handled?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service bills API usage monthly. Events have stable IDs, event time and arrival time. Events can arrive late or be replayed. Prices are versioned by effective interval.

questions.title: Price selection
questions.prompt: Which price should a usage event use under event-time billing?

choices.text: Whatever price is current when replayed
choices.why: Replays would change historical charges.
That is not the stated contract.

choices.text: The price version effective for the event's billable time and contract
choices.why: Reprocessing remains reproducible.

choices.text: A price inferred from current server region
choices.why: Region alone does not identify the contract.

questions.explanation: Reproducible billing needs historical price context. Persist or reconstruct the price version that applied under the customer's contract at the event's billable time. Replaying old usage through today's price would change historical charges, making invoices nonreproducible even if usage totals remain identical.
questions.tradeoff: Versioned pricing increases retained metadata.
questions.followup: How would customer-specific contract overrides be represented?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service bills API usage monthly. Events have stable IDs, event time and arrival time. Events can arrive late or be replayed. Prices are versioned by effective interval.

questions.title: Late after close
questions.prompt: Usage arrives after an invoice is finalized. What is necessary?

choices.text: A defined adjustment or next-invoice policy with audit linkage
choices.why: Finalized history and late facts are reconciled explicitly.

choices.text: Silently edit the sent invoice without trace
choices.why: Customer-visible history changes invisibly.

choices.text: Drop every late event without disclosure
choices.why: That may violate the billing contract.

choices.text: Issue a new full invoice for all historical usage
choices.why: Prior charges can be duplicated.

questions.explanation: Financial close requires a policy for facts that arrive after the boundary. Finalization creates a customer-visible accounting boundary, not a guarantee that every source event has arrived. Handle late facts through a documented adjustment policy linked to the original period, avoiding invisible edits or a second full charge for already billed usage.
questions.tradeoff: Adjustments complicate customer explanations and reconciliation.
questions.followup: How would disputes trace a line item back to source events?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service bills API usage monthly. Events have stable IDs, event time and arrival time. Events can arrive late or be replayed. Prices are versioned by effective interval.

questions.title: Pipeline completeness
questions.prompt: What distinguishes zero usage from missing telemetry?

choices.text: Both appear as no records, so treat them identically
choices.why: Missing input is not proof of no activity.
It does not prove source coverage.
The job may process incomplete input.

choices.text: Source progress evidence, expected partitions and gap detection
choices.why: Completeness is evaluated independently of the sum.

questions.explanation: A correct aggregation over incomplete input still yields an incorrect bill. No rows can mean genuine inactivity, source failure or an unprocessed partition. Track source progress and expected coverage independently from aggregation, and delay or explicitly estimate an invoice when completeness evidence does not support a final amount.
questions.tradeoff: Coverage tracking adds operational metadata.
questions.followup: When should an invoice be delayed rather than estimated?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service bills API usage monthly. Events have stable IDs, event time and arrival time. Events can arrive late or be replayed. Prices are versioned by effective interval.

questions.title: Compensation boundaries
questions.prompt: Match each completed business effect to the most appropriate recovery category. Use each choice once.

items.text: An inventory reservation is held but no item was shipped.
A payment was captured by an external provider.
A physical parcel has left the warehouse.
A promotional email has already been read.

choices.text: Release the reservation through an idempotent state transition.
choices.why: Uncommitted inventory authority can be returned if release wins against finalization.

choices.text: Request and reconcile a refund under the provider's contract.
choices.why: Refund is a new financial operation, not erasure of the original capture.

choices.text: Use a return, interception or other explicit fulfillment remedy.
choices.why: Physical movement is not rolled back by undoing a database row.

choices.text: Treat the disclosure as irreversible and use a corrective communication policy if needed.
choices.why: A recipient cannot be made to unread an already disclosed message.

questions.explanation: Compensation is domain-specific and does not mean that history never happened. Some effects can be offset by a controlled state transition, others need a new external operation, and some cannot be reversed. A saga must represent both failed compensation and irreversibility instead of promising distributed rollback.
questions.tradeoff: Business remedies can cost money, time and customer trust even when software recovery is correct.
questions.followup: Which irreversible action should be delayed until other prerequisites are verified?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Order creation, inventory reservation and payment use separate services without a shared database transaction. Each supports idempotent commands and explicit state.

questions.title: Durable orchestration
questions.prompt: What should the orchestrator persist?

choices.text: Workflow identity, completed steps and pending action state
choices.why: Recovery can resume after a crash.
A process crash loses progress.
Intermediate uncertainty is unrecoverable.
It does not identify workflow progress.

questions.explanation: A long-running transaction is a durable state machine. Persist the workflow's identity, step results and pending commands so another worker can resume after a crash. Dispatching a command and recording its outcome can themselves be ambiguous, requiring idempotent commands and reconciliation rather than reliance on one live thread.
questions.tradeoff: State retention and schema evolution become responsibilities.
questions.followup: How would command retries remain idempotent after orchestration failover?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Order creation, inventory reservation and payment use separate services without a shared database transaction. Each supports idempotent commands and explicit state.

questions.title: Compensation failure
questions.prompt: Inventory release fails during cancellation. What should happen?

choices.why: The release has not completed.

choices.text: Persist unresolved compensation, retry safely and escalate by policy
choices.why: The exception remains visible and recoverable.

choices.text: Forget the reservation to reduce backlog
choices.why: Stock can remain unavailable indefinitely.

choices.text: Repeat payment capture to restore symmetry
choices.why: That creates a new wrong effect.

questions.explanation: A compensation can fail, so recovery itself needs a state machine. A failed compensation leaves the workflow partially recovered and must remain visible as such. Persist the outstanding action, retry within the recipient's idempotency contract and escalate by age or business impact instead of marking the entire saga cancelled prematurely.
questions.tradeoff: Exception queues need staffing and deadlines.
questions.followup: How would you detect a reservation that is stuck despite successful retry acknowledgements?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Order creation, inventory reservation and payment use separate services without a shared database transaction. Each supports idempotent commands and explicit state.

questions.title: Irreversible step placement
questions.prompt: Shipping a physical parcel is irreversible in the software transaction sense. What follows?

choices.text: Treat shipping like a local rollback
choices.why: The parcel has already moved.

choices.text: Ship first to reduce orchestration latency
choices.why: Later failures become harder to remedy.
Those remain business prerequisites.

choices.text: Gate shipment on verified prerequisites and define post-shipment remedies
choices.why: Workflow order follows irreversibility and risk.

questions.explanation: Not all saga steps have equal recovery cost. Complete the required payment, inventory and review decisions before crossing a costly irreversible boundary. After physical shipment, recovery becomes a return, refund or other business remedy rather than a software rollback, so its policy belongs in the design.
questions.tradeoff: Waiting for stronger evidence can delay fulfillment.
questions.followup: How would fraud review alter the commitment point?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Order creation, inventory reservation and payment use separate services without a shared database transaction. Each supports idempotent commands and explicit state.

questions.title: Bid arbitration
questions.prompt: What determines whether concurrent bids are accepted?

choices.text: The earliest client-reported click time after clock correction
choices.why: The stated authority is the server state machine; client time does not arbitrate its current price and close state.

choices.text: The state machine's serialized eligibility transition
choices.why: Price and close checks apply to one ordered state.
Client clocks are not trusted.

choices.text: Whichever bid's payment authorization finishes first
choices.why: Payment latency is not the defined auction ordering or eligibility boundary.

questions.explanation: Bid validity is a state transition under a defined ordering contract. The state machine evaluates price and deadline against one authoritative current state, assigning a coherent order to competing bids. Client animation timing and unsynchronized device clocks cannot establish which claim legitimately became the next accepted bid.
questions.tradeoff: A hot auction can become a coordination bottleneck.
questions.followup: How would you scale read traffic without weakening bid arbitration?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A live auction accepts bids through one authoritative state machine per auction. A bid must exceed the current price and arrive before the server-defined close boundary. Clients have skewed clocks.

questions.title: Deadline authority
questions.prompt: Which clock should the acceptance contract reference?

choices.why: Clients can understand which observed event counts.
Skew and manipulation create disagreement.
Notifications can be delayed.
Backups do not represent live acceptance.

questions.explanation: Specify whether receipt, validation or commit before the deadline is required. Define whether the deadline applies to receipt, validation or commit and make that boundary observable. Network delay may still disappoint a user, but the system can explain decisions consistently instead of allowing every bidder's clock to define a separate close time.
questions.tradeoff: Strict definitions may disappoint users under network delay.
questions.followup: How would a soft-close extension policy be represented?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A live auction accepts bids through one authoritative state machine per auction. A bid must exceed the current price and arrive before the server-defined close boundary. Clients have skewed clocks.

questions.title: Leader failover
questions.prompt: The previous auction leader resumes after replacement. What must prevent stale acceptance?

choices.text: Send a shutdown message to the former leader and immediately allow the replacement
choices.why: The former leader may be paused or partitioned and later resume without receiving the message.

choices.text: Rely on each leader's local lease-expiry check immediately before computation
choices.why: A pause can occur after the check and before the external commit.

choices.text: Fencing or equivalent authority checks on state transitions
choices.why: Old leaders cannot commit accepted bids.

choices.text: Route new clients only to the replacement while leaving old connections active
choices.why: Existing connections can still reach the stale leader, so write authority must be fenced.

questions.explanation: Leadership detection alone does not prevent a paused old leader from acting. A paused old leader can resume with stale beliefs after a replacement has taken over. The durable acceptance boundary must reject its obsolete generation, since detecting lease loss or requesting shutdown is not equivalent to preventing a later commit.
questions.tradeoff: Fencing adds persistent version coordination.
questions.followup: How would an accepted bid's evidence survive failover?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A live auction accepts bids through one authoritative state machine per auction. A bid must exceed the current price and arrive before the server-defined close boundary. Clients have skewed clocks.

questions.title: Dispute evidence
questions.prompt: Which audit record supports a close-time dispute?

choices.why: It omits acceptance history.
They do not establish server order.
Counts cannot reconstruct eligibility.

choices.text: Bid identity, authoritative order, validation result and close-state version
choices.why: The decision can be reconstructed under the contract.

questions.explanation: Explain outcomes from durable state-machine evidence. Record the input identity, authoritative sequence, relevant auction-state version and acceptance decision so the eligibility calculation can be reconstructed. Notifications and screenshots are useful context but cannot replace the durable ordering evidence for a close-time dispute.
questions.tradeoff: Detailed records need retention and privacy controls.
questions.followup: What if notification says accepted but no authoritative commit exists?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A live auction accepts bids through one authoritative state machine per auction. A bid must exceed the current price and arrive before the server-defined close boundary. Clients have skewed clocks.

questions.title: Lease limit
questions.prompt: Why is a lease alone insufficient to prevent duplicate charge effects?

choices.why: They expire by design.

choices.text: Only one process can ever pause
choices.why: Several can pause or partition.

choices.text: An old worker may act after losing ownership
choices.why: Ownership must be checked at the effect boundary.

choices.text: The scheduler name is too short
choices.why: Names do not enforce exclusivity.

questions.explanation: Scheduling ownership and external-effect identity are separate concerns. A lease determines who should work now, but a paused process can act after that ownership expires. Use stable business-operation identity at the external effect boundary, and fencing where supported, rather than relying on scheduler exclusivity alone.
questions.tradeoff: Fencing may not be supported by the external provider.
questions.followup: Which stable key would identify one subscription billing period?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A monthly subscription job may run on several workers. A worker can pause past its lease and resume. The external charge API supports operation-key deduplication for a finite window.

questions.title: Monthly identity
questions.prompt: Which operation identity fits one charge per subscription period?

choices.text: A fresh UUID per worker attempt
choices.why: Retries become distinct charges.

choices.text: Subscription plus billing-period identity, under a defined adjustment policy
choices.why: Attempts converge on one scheduled obligation.
Future months would be suppressed.
Worker replacement changes identity.

questions.explanation: A job's business occurrence must outlive worker assignment. One subscription and billing period represent one scheduled obligation even if several workers attempt it. Worker hostnames and attempt UUIDs change during recovery, while customer ID alone is too broad because it would suppress legitimate future billing periods.
questions.tradeoff: Corrections and prorations need separate explicit identities.
questions.followup: How would a plan change halfway through the month be modeled?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A monthly subscription job may run on several workers. A worker can pause past its lease and resume. The external charge API supports operation-key deduplication for a finite window.

questions.title: Long outage replay
questions.prompt: The backlog exceeds provider deduplication retention. What is required before blindly retrying?

choices.text: Reconcile authoritative outcomes and preserve local obligation state
choices.why: Provider key expiry can make an old retry a new charge.

choices.text: Reuse the old key and assume eternal protection
choices.why: The retention window is finite.

choices.text: Generate new keys for all jobs
choices.why: That can duplicate prior effects.
That violates billing intent.

questions.explanation: A finite external dedupe window bounds retry safety. Once the provider forgets an old key, replaying it may create a fresh charge even though a prior attempt succeeded. Reconcile the unresolved obligation from durable local state and authoritative provider evidence before granting a new external attempt.
questions.tradeoff: Historical reconciliation may need manual exceptions.
questions.followup: Which local evidence can distinguish never-dispatched from outcome-unknown jobs?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A monthly subscription job may run on several workers. A worker can pause past its lease and resume. The external charge API supports operation-key deduplication for a finite window.

questions.title: Operational completion
questions.prompt: Which metric is better than scheduler success count?

choices.text: Count tasks removed from the worker queue
choices.why: Removal can precede an external effect or follow a dropped task without verified completion.

choices.text: Count successful lease acquisitions for scheduled periods
choices.why: A worker can acquire ownership and fail before producing the business effect.

choices.text: Report queue depth without distinguishing pending and outcome-unknown obligations
choices.why: A shallow queue does not prove that uncertain external charges have been reconciled.

choices.text: Obligations reconciled to final outcomes, with overdue unknown states
choices.why: It measures the business workflow boundary.

questions.explanation: Job execution should be tracked to authoritative effects. Lease acquisition or job completion only describes local execution progress. Track whether each billing obligation has a verified final business outcome, distinguishing overdue unknown results from never-started work and from confirmed failures that can safely retry.
questions.tradeoff: Outcome tracking requires cross-system correlation.
questions.followup: How would you alert differently on delayed versus duplicate obligations?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A monthly subscription job may run on several workers. A worker can pause past its lease and resume. The external charge API supports operation-key deduplication for a finite window.

questions.title: Refund budget
questions.prompt: What must competing refunds reserve atomically?

choices.text: A portion of the remaining refundable amount
choices.why: Concurrent attempts cannot each spend the same remainder.
Connections do not control money.
Notification capacity is unrelated.

choices.text: Only the original order ID without amount state
choices.why: Identity alone does not enforce the budget.

questions.explanation: Pending external refunds need to consume controlled budget until their outcome is known. Concurrent partial refunds compete for the same remaining amount, including funds reserved for unresolved external attempts. Atomically reserve authority before dispatch and release it only after a safe terminal outcome, so two requests cannot each spend the same remainder.
questions.tradeoff: Unknown outcomes can temporarily reduce available refund capacity.
questions.followup: When can a failed reservation safely release its amount?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An order captured 100 currency units. Partial refunds are allowed, but total successful refunds must not exceed captured funds. Requests and provider callbacks can repeat.

questions.title: Callback repetition
questions.prompt: How should repeated success callbacks affect the order total?

choices.text: Add the amount on every callback
choices.why: Delivery duplication inflates refunded totals.
External outcomes remain unknown.

choices.text: Apply a conditional terminal transition for the identified refund
choices.why: The same outcome is incorporated once.
Different events can share a second.

questions.explanation: State transitions, not transport counts, drive financial totals. Repeated callbacks should converge on one refund state, not each add another amount to the order total. Verify the identified refund and condition the state change so delayed pending events cannot reverse an already established terminal success.
questions.tradeoff: Provider event identity and refund identity may both be needed.
questions.followup: How would out-of-order pending and success events be handled?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An order captured 100 currency units. Partial refunds are allowed, but total successful refunds must not exceed captured funds. Requests and provider callbacks can repeat.

questions.title: Unknown external result
questions.prompt: A refund timed out. Why not immediately release its reserved budget?

choices.why: Success is not known either.

choices.text: It may have succeeded externally, so another refund can overspend
choices.why: Outcome ambiguity affects remaining authority.

choices.text: Reservation state is impossible to persist
choices.why: It can be durable.
Partial refunds are explicitly allowed.

questions.explanation: Hold or reconcile uncertainty before granting replacement authority. The first provider call may already have refunded money even though its response was lost. Returning that budget to the available pool can authorize a second refund against the same captured funds; retain uncertainty until authoritative evidence safely resolves it.
questions.tradeoff: Conservative reservation delays legitimate refunds.
questions.followup: Which evidence safely closes a timed-out refund as failed?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An order captured 100 currency units. Partial refunds are allowed, but total successful refunds must not exceed captured funds. Requests and provider callbacks can repeat.

questions.title: Accounting repair
questions.prompt: Local totals disagree with provider settlements. Best workflow?

choices.text: Force the local total to the user's requested amount
choices.why: Intent is not settlement evidence.
Reconciliation evidence disappears.
Arrival order does not determine authority.

choices.text: Reconcile each refund identity, classify discrepancies and post auditable adjustments
choices.why: The repair follows actual effects.

questions.explanation: Aggregate differences should be traced to individual state transitions. Trace the aggregate discrepancy to individual refund identities and settlement states before posting corrections. This distinguishes missed callbacks, duplicate local application and genuinely different external effects, allowing auditable repair instead of assigning authority to whichever response arrived last.
questions.tradeoff: Reconciliation costs time but prevents compounding errors.
questions.followup: Which mismatches require human review rather than automatic adjustment?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An order captured 100 currency units. Partial refunds are allowed, but total successful refunds must not exceed captured funds. Requests and provider callbacks can repeat.

questions.title: Locate the invariant
questions.prompt: Where should the rule 'only live Held can become Confirmed' be enforced?
questions.explanation: The state owner must validate the current state and deadline at the mutation boundary. A prior read is not sufficient when expiry can race. Expose transition results instead of arbitrary setters so timers, callbacks, and user commands all pass through the same rule and observe the same winning outcome.
questions.tradeoff: A central transition API limits arbitrary mutation.
questions.followup: What storage operation implements this atomic transition?

choices.text: Inside one atomic transition operation that owns reservation state
choices.why: Callers cannot bypass the state predicate.
Callbacks and timers bypass the UI.

choices.text: Only in documentation for each caller
choices.why: Independent callers can race or omit checks.

choices.text: In an asynchronous audit after confirmation
choices.why: That detects violations after they happen.

questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A reservation can be Held, Confirmed, Expired, or Cancelled. Only a live Held reservation can be confirmed. A confirmed reservation cannot expire. Payment callbacks and expiry timers can race.

questions.title: A race winner
questions.prompt: Confirmation and expiry concurrently attempt to change the same Held record. What outcome preserves the model?
questions.explanation: Model the race as competing conditional transitions, not independent field setters. The losing path needs a domain-specific response. Use a row version, conditional write, or equivalent serialization boundary. The financial outcome may need reconciliation even when the reservation transition itself has one clear winner.
questions.tradeoff: Rejected confirmation may require payment reconciliation.
questions.followup: What should happen if payment succeeded after expiry won?

choices.text: Both succeed and last arrival decides silently
choices.why: That permits contradictory acknowledged outcomes.

choices.text: Payment callback always overrides Expired without a rule
choices.why: That adds an undocumented transition.

choices.text: Timers overwrite any state because they run later
choices.why: Confirmed reservations must not expire.

choices.text: Exactly one conditional transition wins; the loser observes the new state
choices.why: Both must compare against the same expected version or state.

questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A reservation can be Held, Confirmed, Expired, or Cancelled. Only a live Held reservation can be confirmed. A confirmed reservation cannot expire. Payment callbacks and expiry timers can race.

questions.title: Represent the lifecycle
questions.prompt: Which design choices support the stated rules? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A state machine is useful because behavior depends on state and event combinations. Merely naming an enum does not enforce transitions. Include duplicate events and events arriving in terminal states. These cases determine whether retries are harmless, rejected, or require reconciliation rather than merely exercising the happy path.
questions.tradeoff: A richer result model requires callers to handle more cases.
questions.followup: How would you generate transition coverage from the table?

choices.text: An explicit transition table with guards
choices.why: It makes allowed paths reviewable.

choices.text: Typed transition results for already-final versus invalid operations
choices.why: Callers can handle meaningful outcomes.

questions.title: Repository contract
questions.prompt: Which method best exposes the required invariant?
questions.explanation: The abstraction should name the domain operation, not merely expose storage primitives. Its atomicity requirement must be part of the contract. The return value should distinguish a durable reservation, a business rejection, and an uncertain infrastructure outcome. questions.title: Identity versus mutable state
questions.prompt: A reservation object is placed in a hash set. Which equality design is safest if status changes?
questions.explanation: Entity identity and current state are different concepts. Hash-based collections need stable equality-relevant values while an object is stored. A stable reservation ID supports entity identity, while an immutable snapshot can separately compare complete values. questions.title: A dual-write gap
questions.prompt: The order commits, then the process crashes before publishing. What is missing?
questions.explanation: Separate durable effects leave a failure window unless their intent is recorded atomically. Persist the intention to publish in the same transaction as the order so a recovery worker can discover it after a crash. Reordering two independent external writes merely moves the failure window; it does not make their outcomes atomic.

questions.title: Choose the transaction
questions.prompt: What belongs in one local SQL transaction?
questions.explanation: The outbox records intent locally; it does not make the external broker part of the database commit. A network publish remains outside it, and a relay later turns the durable intent into broker traffic under an explicit retry policy.

questions.title: Relay uncertainty
questions.prompt: The relay publishes then crashes before marking the row sent. Which statements hold? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Outbox atomicity prevents lost intent; duplicate-safe consumers complete the end-to-end design. The broker may have accepted the event even though the relay did not persist that fact. Re-publishing avoids lost intent but can duplicate delivery, so carry stable event identity through the relay and make each consumer's durable effect duplicate-safe.

questions.title: Bound lag
questions.prompt: The outbox grows during a broker outage. Which operating plan is strongest?
questions.explanation: Publication backlog is customer-visible deferred work, not merely an internal table size. Track how long the oldest unpublished business intent has waited, not just how many rows exist. Plan storage and relay throughput for outages, and define when accepting more orders would violate the downstream delivery promise rather than deleting unsent evidence.

questions.title: Order within an aggregate
questions.prompt: Two events for one order carry versions 7 and 8. What protects a projection from applying 7 after 8?
questions.explanation: Event identity and aggregate sequence solve different problems: duplicate detection versus ordering. An event ID distinguishes repeated attempts, while an aggregate version distinguishes sequence. Preserve per-order ordering or reject stale application at the projection, and explicitly handle version gaps rather than assuming a newer arrival proves all earlier effects were processed.

questions.title: Atomic consumer effects
questions.prompt: A consumer updates a SQL projection and records the event as processed. What arrangement prevents a crash gap between them?
questions.explanation: A processed marker must describe a durable effect, not just an attempt. Writing the inbox marker first can suppress an effect that never committed; writing the effect first can repeat it after a crash. One transaction for both establishes a durable duplicate decision for SQL-local effects, but not for arbitrary external calls.

questions.prompt: A new team replays six months of events into a new projection. What must be decided before replay?
questions.explanation: Separate rebuilding state from re-executing business actions and validate retained schema compatibility. Reconstruction should build the new projection without re-triggering payments, notifications, or other irreversible actions. questions.title: Ambiguous payment response
questions.prompt: The provider times out after receiving a charge request. What is the correct interpretation?
questions.explanation: Transport uncertainty must not be turned into a new business operation. The provider could have charged successfully and lost only its response, or it could have failed before committing. Record an explicit unknown state and resolve it through the provider's stable operation identity instead of interpreting the timeout as permission for a new charge.

questions.title: Operational ownership
questions.prompt: Who should own unresolved payment outcomes?
questions.explanation: Financial uncertainty is a domain state with accountable recovery, not just a transient exception. Unknown financial outcomes can survive worker restarts and queue lease changes, so they need durable state, age monitoring, and an accountable resolver. The customer should see an honest pending or uncertain status while reconciliation proceeds, not a guessed success or failure.

questions.title: When to acknowledge
questions.prompt: When is queue acknowledgement safe in this workflow?
questions.explanation: Acknowledgement transfers responsibility away from the queue; another durable owner must already exist. Acknowledgement means the queue may stop redelivering, so another durable mechanism must already own any unfinished reconciliation. A worker's local promise or an in-flight HTTP call is not enough because both can disappear when the process crashes.

questions.title: Classify retry decisions

questions.explanation: Retry handling follows failure semantics and durable state, not a single catch-all exception path. questions.title: A queue is not infinite capacity

questions.title: Two clocks describe different facts
questions.prompt: Why retain both event_time and receive_time?

choices.text: They are redundant whenever devices reconnect
choices.why: Late delivery makes them meaningfully different.

choices.text: They distinguish occurrence time from ingestion delay
choices.why: Queries and lag diagnosis need different temporal meanings.

choices.text: Receive time is guaranteed to equal physical measurement time
choices.why: Network delay contradicts that.

choices.text: Event time proves device clocks are correct
choices.why: Device timestamps can be skewed.

questions.explanation: Event time describes when the device says the measurement occurred; receive time describes when the platform observed it. questions.title: Replay without external effects

choices.why: That corrupts authoritative history.

questions.title: Partial header
questions.prompt: A read returns only two header bytes. What should the decoder do?

choices.why: The length is incomplete.

questions.explanation: TCP delivers an ordered sequence of bytes, but a read call can stop in the middle of the four-byte length field. Keep the two bytes in bounded decoder state and wait for the remainder. Treating a partial read as malformed would reject ordinary valid network behavior.

choices.why: The SQL text can be identical while parameters and data distributions change optimal access paths.

questions.explanation: Averages hide parameter-sensitive workloads. A large tenant may justify a scan or different join strategy while a tiny tenant benefits from an index-driven path. Forcing one plan can transfer the regression to another population; evaluate parameter distributions rather than only the incident example.
questions.tradeoff: More targeted tuning complicates operations.
questions.followup: What evidence would justify tenant-specific routing or statistics?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A PostgreSQL 18 query estimated 100 matching rows but actually emitted 500,000. A nested-loop plan became expensive after tenant data skew increased.

questions.title: Rollout gate
questions.prompt: Which gate is appropriate for adding the candidate index?

choices.why: It misses performance and write costs.
That misses skew and sustained updates.
Successful creation is not a net workload win.

choices.text: Representative read plans plus write latency, storage and build impact
choices.why: The tradeoff is measured across the workload.

questions.explanation: An index optimizes some reads while taxing writes and maintenance. Assess the index as a workload change, including its build pressure, maintenance writes and storage. A faster warm-cache read is only one benefit and may be outweighed by sustained write latency or a disruptive construction process.
questions.tradeoff: Building it safely may take time and temporary space.
questions.followup: How would you detect an index that is rarely used but expensive to maintain?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A PostgreSQL 18 query estimated 100 matching rows but actually emitted 500,000. A nested-loop plan became expensive after tenant data skew increased.

questions.title: Bottleneck mismatch
questions.prompt: What best explains the unchanged p99?

choices.why: A local improvement can be genuine but immaterial.

choices.text: The optimized component may not dominate the critical path
choices.why: Other work or waiting controls user latency.
No such relationship exists.
They can, with suitable measurement.

questions.explanation: Component speedup does not imply proportional end-to-end improvement. The API's critical path contains other computation and waiting that the parser change does not shorten. Measure the parser's share under representative traffic before translating a local twofold speedup into a service-level expectation.
questions.tradeoff: Microbenchmarks remain useful for isolated design choices.
questions.followup: Which profile would show the parser's real request contribution?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A Java parser is twice as fast in a tight benchmark, but API p99 is unchanged. Parsing was only a small part of end-to-end latency.

questions.title: Benchmark validity
questions.prompt: Which practices help? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Account for warmup and consume computed results
choices.why: This reduces compilation and dead-code artifacts.

choices.text: Benchmark only a constant that the compiler can fold
choices.why: The measured operation may disappear.

choices.text: Use multiple forks and representative inputs
choices.why: This reduces process-history bias and unrealistic data effects.

choices.text: Assume using JMH removes the need for review
choices.why: Harnesses do not prove workload relevance.

questions.explanation: A harness helps measurement but cannot choose a representative experiment for you. JVM optimization can remove unused work or specialize constant inputs, and compilation history can distort short runs. Warmup, forks, consumed results and realistic input distributions reduce those artifacts but do not make a benchmark automatically representative of production.
questions.tradeoff: Rigorous runs take longer and need stable environments.
questions.followup: How would cold-start performance be measured separately?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A Java parser is twice as fast in a tight benchmark, but API p99 is unchanged. Parsing was only a small part of end-to-end latency.

questions.title: Investment choice
questions.prompt: Parsing is 2 percent of CPU and a queue dominates latency. Best next effort?

choices.text: Rewrite the parser repeatedly for headline speedups
choices.why: The potential system gain is bounded.

choices.text: Publish the local factor as API improvement
choices.why: That overstates the evidence.
That hides the actual bottleneck.

choices.text: Investigate queue demand and service capacity first
choices.why: It targets the measured limiting component.

questions.explanation: Optimization priority should follow impact, not isolated benchmark excitement. A component using two percent of CPU has a limited direct contribution to total CPU cost, and the observed latency is queue-driven. Investigate why work arrives or completes too slowly before investing more effort in a component outside the bottleneck.
questions.tradeoff: Maintainability may outweigh tiny CPU gains.
questions.followup: What would make a parser optimization strategically worthwhile despite small current impact?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A Java parser is twice as fast in a tight benchmark, but API p99 is unchanged. Parsing was only a small part of end-to-end latency.

questions.title: Production claim
questions.prompt: Which statement is evidence-calibrated?

choices.text: The parser improved in this benchmark; API benefit remains unproven
choices.why: It separates local evidence from system behavior.

choices.text: The service should deliver the same speedup because it calls the parser
choices.why: The parser's share of the critical path limits how much a local speedup affects the whole request.

choices.text: The optimization has no value because API p99 did not change
choices.why: It may reduce CPU cost or help another workload even though this API tail has not improved.

choices.text: The benchmark alone is enough to justify fleet-wide rollout
choices.why: Correctness, integration effects and operational benefit still need proportionate validation.

questions.explanation: State the measured boundary and avoid extrapolating beyond it. Report the workload, environment and measured component boundary with the result. The unchanged API tail is separate evidence; a production claim requires an end-to-end experiment showing that the local improvement affects the relevant user path.
questions.tradeoff: A rollout experiment may still be justified.
questions.followup: How would you define a measurable production success threshold?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A Java parser is twice as fast in a tight benchmark, but API p99 is unchanged. Parsing was only a small part of end-to-end latency.

questions.title: Warm versus cold capacity
questions.prompt: What assumption failed?

choices.why: Runtime state differs.
Local caches were explicitly emptied.

choices.text: The origin was sized only for warm-cache demand
choices.why: Cold misses create a different load profile.
No evidence indicates data loss.

questions.explanation: Cache state is part of the operational workload. A warm-cache plan assumes most requests do not reach the origin. Fleet replacement changes that assumption even with identical binaries, so capacity planning and deployment procedures must include the transient miss rate and origin load.
questions.tradeoff: Provisioning for full misses can be costly.
questions.followup: Which miss surge can controlled warmup realistically bound?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A fleet replacement empties local caches. Database traffic spikes and API latency deteriorates even though the new code is unchanged.

questions.title: Safer replacement
questions.prompt: Which actions can reduce the surge? Select all that apply.

choices.why: That maximizes correlated misses.

choices.text: Stage replacement and warm known hot data cautiously
choices.why: This spreads origin load.
The database can receive unbounded demand.

choices.text: Coalesce concurrent requests for the same missing key
choices.why: One load can satisfy many waiters.

questions.explanation: Spread cold-start demand and suppress duplicate fills. Staging keeps some warm capacity online while replacement instances learn the working set. Coalescing duplicate fills reduces concurrent origin reads for the same key, but warmup itself still needs a budget so background prefetching does not overwhelm the database.
questions.tradeoff: Warmup must not become a background overload source.
questions.followup: How would you choose hot keys without leaking tenant data?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A fleet replacement empties local caches. Database traffic spikes and API latency deteriorates even though the new code is unchanged.

questions.title: Autoscaling feedback
questions.prompt: Why can adding many new instances briefly worsen latency?

choices.text: Each new instance can add cold-miss demand before useful cache capacity
choices.why: Scale-out has a transient cost.

choices.text: The load balancer always divides traffic perfectly, so cache warmup is irrelevant
choices.why: Even balanced new replicas can all miss and increase origin demand.

choices.text: Scale-out immediately lowers database demand in proportion to replica count
choices.why: Cold local caches can initially produce the opposite effect.

choices.text: The new replicas must contain a slower binary
choices.why: The scenario specifies unchanged code; runtime cache state provides a direct alternative explanation.

questions.explanation: Evaluate scale-out transients, not just steady-state throughput. A new replica can increase origin demand before its cache becomes useful, producing a temporary negative feedback effect from scale-out. Model startup and warmup behavior alongside steady-state capacity, and ramp traffic based on downstream health.
questions.tradeoff: Slow ramps trade recovery speed for origin protection.
questions.followup: What signal should govern the ramp rate?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A fleet replacement empties local caches. Database traffic spikes and API latency deteriorates even though the new code is unchanged.

questions.title: Recovery evidence
questions.prompt: Which evidence confirms healthy recovery?

choices.why: New replicas can still be cold.
A high hit rate can coexist with harmful residual misses.
User errors and queueing may persist.

choices.text: Origin demand, cache-fill latency and user success/tail latency
choices.why: It observes both cause and outcome.

questions.explanation: A recovery claim needs the constrained dependency and user path to improve. Observe the origin's admitted demand and fill latency together with user errors and tail latency. Hit rate alone can look healthy when traffic is being rejected, while replica count only indicates scheduled capacity rather than warmed useful capacity.
questions.tradeoff: Multi-layer telemetry requires consistent time windows.
questions.followup: How would you avoid misreading hit rate when traffic is being rejected?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A fleet replacement empties local caches. Database traffic spikes and API latency deteriorates even though the new code is unchanged.

questions.title: Batch trigger
questions.prompt: Which policy balances size and latency?

choices.text: Flush at a maximum size or a maximum waiting time
choices.why: Neither low traffic nor high traffic waits without a bound.

choices.text: Flush only when a huge batch fills
choices.why: Low-rate requests may wait indefinitely.
The deadline is violated.
Users still experience the wait.

questions.explanation: Batch waiting is part of end-to-end latency, not free throughput. A maximum wait timer ensures a low-volume request does not wait indefinitely for companions, while a size bound limits high-volume batch growth. Include all accumulation time in the caller's deadline budget rather than measuring only execution after flush.
questions.tradeoff: Smaller batches reduce amortization benefits.
questions.followup: How would per-request deadlines affect batch composition?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service can process items more efficiently in batches. Clients require a 100 ms response deadline. Waiting to fill a large batch can itself consume most of that budget.

questions.title: Measure the gain
questions.prompt: Which metrics should be compared? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Useful throughput and total latency including batch wait
choices.why: This captures both efficiency and user cost.
It hides accumulation delay.

choices.text: CPU per item and deadline-miss rate
choices.why: These expose the resource and quality tradeoff.
Capacity settings are not observed outcomes.

questions.explanation: A faster batch execution can still worsen user latency. Compare resources per useful item and complete request latency under the same arrival distribution. Batch execution may become faster per item while users wait longer to form a batch, so throughput and deadline misses must be evaluated together.
questions.tradeoff: Measurements need representative arrival patterns.
questions.followup: How would bursty arrivals differ from steady arrivals?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service can process items more efficiently in batches. Clients require a 100 ms response deadline. Waiting to fill a large batch can itself consume most of that budget.

questions.title: Head-of-line risk
questions.prompt: One large item stalls the whole batch. Best design consideration?

choices.why: That may magnify the stall.

choices.text: Separate costly classes or cap per-item work where semantics allow
choices.why: Heavy items stop delaying unrelated small work.
Unbounded work increases the tail.
That hides stalled requests.

questions.explanation: Batching couples items into a shared completion and failure domain. One expensive item can couple the completion of many otherwise cheap requests when they share a batch. Use cost-aware lanes or work bounds where semantics allow, then check that isolation does not permanently starve the expensive class.
questions.tradeoff: Separate lanes reduce pooling efficiency.
questions.followup: How would fairness prevent the expensive lane from starving?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service can process items more efficiently in batches. Clients require a 100 ms response deadline. Waiting to fill a large batch can itself consume most of that budget.

questions.title: Mixed tenant workload
questions.prompt: A large tenant monopolizes batch slots. What should staff-level policy define?

choices.why: Other tenants can starve.
Averages hide tenant harm.

choices.text: Unlimited dedicated hardware for every user
choices.why: That ignores cost constraints.

choices.text: Explicit fairness, per-tenant bounds and cost attribution
choices.why: The efficiency optimization has an allocation contract.

questions.explanation: Throughput optimization does not decide who deserves scarce slots. An efficient global batcher can allocate nearly all slots to the loudest tenant unless fairness is explicit. Define the resource unit being shared and measure per-tenant wait and completion, not only total throughput or accelerator occupancy.
questions.tradeoff: Fairness can reduce peak aggregate throughput.
questions.followup: Which fairness unit fits variable-cost items?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service can process items more efficiently in batches. Clients require a 100 ms response deadline. Waiting to fill a large batch can itself consume most of that budget.

questions.title: Resource boundary
questions.prompt: Why can spare host CPU coexist with container stalls?

choices.text: Host-average CPU is sufficient evidence that this container is not CPU-constrained
choices.why: An enforced container quota can bind while the host has spare capacity.

choices.text: Increase only the application thread count because idle host cores are available
choices.why: More runnable threads do not bypass the container's CPU bandwidth policy.

choices.text: The container can exhaust its allowed CPU quota
choices.why: Host capacity and cgroup allowance are different boundaries.

choices.text: Treat the spikes as a database problem without checking container metrics
choices.why: The explicit CPU limit is a plausible local cause that should be tested first.

questions.explanation: Measure the resource policy actually constraining the workload. The container's quota can be exhausted even while other host cores are idle, because scheduling policy limits its permitted CPU use. Diagnose at both container and host scope rather than treating host-average utilization as proof of available application capacity.
questions.tradeoff: Higher limits can affect neighboring workloads.
questions.followup: Which cgroup statistics would support throttling as the cause?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A container experiences periodic latency spikes. The physical host has spare CPU, but the container has a cgroup CPU bandwidth limit.

questions.title: Diagnostic comparison
questions.prompt: Which evidence is most direct?

choices.why: It hides the container boundary.

choices.text: Throttling counters aligned with latency and container CPU demand
choices.why: This connects enforced limits with observed stalls.
It does not identify CPU throttling.
They omit timing and resource state.

questions.explanation: Correlated counters support a hypothesis but a controlled change strengthens causality. Align enforced throttling counters with bursts, queue delay and request latency to test the proposed mechanism. A controlled quota adjustment can strengthen causal evidence, whereas unrelated memory or success-count graphs cannot locate the time spent stalled.
