questions.tradeoff: Detailed metrics can be noisy at short windows.
questions.followup: How would a quota adjustment test be isolated safely?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A container experiences periodic latency spikes. The physical host has spare CPU, but the container has a cgroup CPU bandwidth limit.

questions.title: Raise every quota
questions.prompt: Why is a fleet-wide unlimited-quota change risky?

choices.text: It can move contention to shared hosts and reduce isolation
choices.why: One noisy workload can consume more shared capacity.
More consumption need not be cheaper.
They can throttle bursts.

choices.text: Removing quotas changes application correctness automatically
choices.why: The primary concern here is resource contention.

questions.explanation: Removing one bottleneck can expose another shared-resource boundary. Removing quotas expands how much a workload may consume from its neighbors and can relocate the bottleneck to host scheduling. Consider reservations, placement, burst allowance and tenant isolation together rather than optimizing one service without a shared-capacity policy.
questions.tradeoff: Burst capacity and tenant isolation need explicit balancing.
questions.followup: How would requests and scheduling placement complement limits?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A container experiences periodic latency spikes. The physical host has spare CPU, but the container has a cgroup CPU bandwidth limit.

questions.title: Capacity contract
questions.prompt: What should a service performance target specify?

choices.why: Quota and workload shape also matter.
Burstiness changes instantaneous demand.
Threads are not guaranteed CPU capacity.

choices.text: Workload distribution, allocated resources and tail/error objectives
choices.why: The benchmark corresponds to the deployed environment.

questions.explanation: A throughput number without its resource and latency envelope is incomplete. A performance result depends on request shape, concurrency, CPU quota and quality objectives. Record those conditions so a deployment with different resource limits is not incorrectly assumed to inherit the benchmark's throughput and latency envelope.
questions.tradeoff: Maintaining representative benchmarks requires effort.
questions.followup: How would autoscaling change the valid operating envelope?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A container experiences periodic latency spikes. The physical host has spare CPU, but the container has a cgroup CPU bandwidth limit.

questions.title: Leak or churn
questions.prompt: What does stable post-collection occupancy suggest?

choices.why: Longer observations may reveal retained growth.

choices.text: Allocation churn is plausible even without obvious retained growth
choices.why: High allocation can stress collection without a growing live set.
Temporary objects can consume CPU and collection work.
Heap observations do not prove network behavior.

questions.explanation: Distinguish retained memory growth from allocation rate and pause behavior. A stable live set after collections suggests objects are being reclaimed rather than accumulating continuously. High creation rates can still consume CPU and trigger collection work; longer observation and allocation profiles are needed before ruling out all retention problems.
questions.tradeoff: Heap summaries alone do not locate allocations.
questions.followup: Which profile would identify hot allocation sites?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. API traces show latency spikes aligned with JVM garbage collection. A serializer allocates many short-lived objects. Heap occupancy after collection is stable.

questions.title: Memory evidence map
questions.prompt: Match each observation to the most directly supported hypothesis. Use each choice once; these are investigation leads, not final diagnoses.

items.text: Allocation rate is high, while the post-collection live set stays stable.
The post-collection live set grows across comparable workload cycles.
Request pauses align with recorded stop-the-world intervals.
Latency rises mostly before a database connection is acquired.

choices.why: Many temporary objects can create collection pressure without persistent live-set growth.
Growing surviving state suggests retention that needs object-lifetime investigation.
Aligned pause intervals can account for part of request elapsed time.
The measured delay occurs before query execution rather than inside garbage collection.

questions.explanation: Match each signal to the boundary it actually measures. Stable retained memory does not mean low allocation, and a slow request is not automatically a GC problem. These observations guide targeted profiles and controlled experiments; correlation alone is not a complete causal diagnosis.
questions.tradeoff: Multiple profiles and traces cost instrumentation effort but prevent tuning the wrong resource.
questions.followup: Which two signals would you collect together to distinguish a leak from bursty temporary allocation?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. API traces show latency spikes aligned with JVM garbage collection. A serializer allocates many short-lived objects. Heap occupancy after collection is stable.

questions.title: Heap increase
questions.prompt: Why is simply doubling heap not a complete diagnosis?

choices.why: It can affect frequency and behavior.
Stable live-set data does not establish that.

choices.text: It changes symptoms without proving the allocation bottleneck or pause tradeoff
choices.why: The causal workload remains to be measured.
There is no such universal relationship.

questions.explanation: Resource changes need a hypothesis and outcome measurements. A larger heap may alter collection frequency and pause characteristics without changing why the serializer allocates so much. Use the change as a hypothesis-driven experiment and measure total memory cost and latency rather than calling symptom relief a diagnosis.
questions.tradeoff: More memory costs money and can alter pause behavior.
questions.followup: What experiment separates reduced collection frequency from longer pauses?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. API traces show latency spikes aligned with JVM garbage collection. A serializer allocates many short-lived objects. Heap occupancy after collection is stable.

questions.title: Service-wide investment
questions.prompt: Which evidence justifies a broad serializer migration?

choices.text: One tiny benchmark on constant input
choices.why: It lacks production distribution and compatibility coverage.
Serialization semantics can still change.
Reputation is not workload evidence.

choices.text: Representative payload correctness, allocation reduction and tail/cost improvement
choices.why: It validates the intended system benefit.

questions.explanation: A widespread dependency migration carries compatibility and operational costs. A serializer is a compatibility boundary shared by payload producers and consumers. Verify output semantics and edge cases, then establish resource or tail improvement under representative traffic before imposing migration risk across many services.
questions.tradeoff: A narrow hot-path change may deliver most benefit with less risk.
questions.followup: How would schema edge cases enter the migration test corpus?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. API traces show latency spikes aligned with JVM garbage collection. A serializer allocates many short-lived objects. Heap occupancy after collection is stable.

questions.title: Reuse opportunity
questions.prompt: What should be evaluated first?

choices.why: That increases setup work.
It does not address connection overhead.

choices.text: Reuse appropriately scoped channels and stubs
choices.why: This amortizes setup while preserving service boundaries.
That reduces concurrency unnecessarily.

questions.explanation: Connection reuse removes repeated setup but does not create infinite stream capacity. Repeated channel creation can put connection and transport setup on every request's critical path. Reuse channels at an appropriate scope, then measure whether per-connection stream limits or server capacity become the next bottleneck rather than assuming one channel is limitless.
questions.tradeoff: A channel can become a shared contention point.
questions.followup: Which measurements reveal a stream-concurrency bottleneck?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service creates a new gRPC channel for each request. Profiling shows repeated connection setup and request queuing; the server supports concurrent streams with a finite limit.

questions.title: Queue visibility
questions.prompt: Server execution is fast, but client latency is high. Which timing is needed?

choices.text: Client-side queue and connection/stream wait time
choices.why: The delay may occur before server execution.
That excludes client waiting.
Size does not locate delay.
It cannot account for all queueing.

questions.explanation: An RPC spans client admission, transport and server work. A server span starts too late to explain time spent waiting for a client connection or stream slot. Instrument the complete client path so deadline consumption before dispatch is visible and can be distinguished from network and handler execution.
questions.tradeoff: Cross-boundary tracing adds instrumentation.
questions.followup: How would deadline propagation account for time already spent queued?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service creates a new gRPC channel for each request. Profiling shows repeated connection setup and request queuing; the server supports concurrent streams with a finite limit.

questions.title: More channels decision
questions.prompt: When is adding channels justified?

choices.text: When average client latency exceeds the target, regardless of where time is spent
choices.why: Latency is a useful symptom, but extra connections only help a transport-concurrency bottleneck.

choices.text: When measured per-connection limits constrain safe concurrency
choices.why: It targets an identified bottleneck.

choices.text: Whenever the server reports low CPU, without measuring client queueing
choices.why: Low CPU can also reflect other waiting; it does not establish a per-connection stream limit.

choices.text: Use one short-lived connection per request to maximize independence
choices.why: That removes sharing but reintroduces setup churn and does not bound total concurrency.

questions.explanation: Pool size should follow actual limits, workload and server capacity. Add connections only when measurements identify a per-connection limit and downstream capacity can use the additional concurrency. Otherwise more channels add sockets, handshakes and balancing complexity without addressing the real constrained resource.
questions.tradeoff: More connections consume resources and can disturb balancing.
questions.followup: How would the pool behave during server failover?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service creates a new gRPC channel for each request. Profiling shows repeated connection setup and request queuing; the server supports concurrent streams with a finite limit.

questions.title: Deadline policy
questions.prompt: What should happen to queued work after its deadline expires?

choices.text: Keep executing everything to preserve throughput
choices.why: Expired work consumes capacity without serving its caller.

choices.text: Reset its deadline at every hop
choices.why: End-to-end latency becomes unbounded.
Clients need an honest outcome.

choices.text: Cancel or avoid dispatch where safe, while handling ambiguous side effects
choices.why: Capacity is reclaimed without assuming cancellation undoes commits.

questions.explanation: Deadline expiry and business rollback are different events. An expired request may still occupy a queue or execute on a backend unless cancellation is propagated and honored. Stop unnecessary work where safe, but reconcile uncertain writes through their business identity because cancellation cannot promise to reverse a committed effect.
questions.tradeoff: Cancellation support varies across execution boundaries.
questions.followup: How would an idempotent write recover after a transport deadline?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service creates a new gRPC channel for each request. Profiling shows repeated connection setup and request queuing; the server supports concurrent streams with a finite limit.

questions.title: Feedback in the generator
questions.prompt: What can this closed-loop test conceal?

choices.text: Queue growth under an externally fixed arrival rate
choices.why: The generator self-throttles when responses slow.
Some regressions still appear.
Load generation does not determine semantic tests.

choices.text: The exact number of CPU cores
choices.why: That is a separate measurement.

questions.explanation: Model arrival behavior explicitly; different client populations need different load models. A response-paced generator reduces demand precisely when the service slows, unlike an external population continuing to arrive. Specify which arrival model matches the intended users and use complementary tests to expose queue growth under fixed offered load.
questions.tradeoff: Open-loop tests can overload systems and need safety limits.
questions.followup: Which real user behavior is best represented by closed-loop clients?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new release appears faster in a load test, but the generator waits for each response before sending the next. When the service slows, offered load drops.

questions.title: Outcome accounting
questions.prompt: Which results should be reported together? Select all that apply.

choices.why: It hides errors and slow tails.

choices.text: Offered, accepted and completed request rates
choices.why: They reveal where work is rejected or accumulates.

choices.text: Latency distribution plus timeouts and errors
choices.why: This prevents apparent wins from omitted failures.
Configuration is not achieved load.

questions.explanation: A performance result needs workload and outcome denominators. Distinguish requests the generator intended, those admitted by the service and those completed successfully. Include failures and timeouts in the interpretation so a system that quickly rejects half its traffic is not advertised as a latency improvement.
questions.tradeoff: Detailed accounting complicates reports but makes comparisons defensible.
questions.followup: How would timed-out work still running on servers be counted?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new release appears faster in a load test, but the generator waits for each response before sending the next. When the service slows, offered load drops.

questions.title: Comparability gate
questions.prompt: What should remain comparable between old and new versions?

choices.why: Different data and load can dominate.

choices.text: Keep only the same nominal requests per second
choices.why: Different payloads, skew and arrival feedback can make nominally equal rates incomparable.

choices.text: Arrival model, data distribution, resources and success criteria
choices.why: These control major confounders.

choices.text: Run both binaries on the same machine but leave cache state uncontrolled
choices.why: Hardware identity alone does not control a major source of workload variation.

questions.explanation: Change one hypothesis-relevant factor while documenting unavoidable differences. Control the inputs most likely to change resource demand, including skew, payload sizes, cache state and allocated resources. Document unavoidable variability and repeat runs so a favorable environment is not mistaken for a better implementation.
questions.tradeoff: Strict control may reduce production realism; use complementary tests.
questions.followup: Which variability should be randomized rather than held constant?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new release appears faster in a load test, but the generator waits for each response before sending the next. When the service slows, offered load drops.

questions.title: Capacity claim
questions.prompt: A test reached 10,000 requests per second with 30 percent errors. What is the accurate conclusion?

choices.text: Safe capacity is 10,000 successful requests per second
choices.why: The success rate contradicts that.

choices.text: The service can handle any lower workload
choices.why: Distribution and tails may differ.

choices.text: Errors can be omitted from capacity reports
choices.why: They are user-visible outcomes.

choices.text: The offered rate exceeded the tested quality envelope; safe capacity remains to be established
choices.why: Capacity must include error and latency objectives.

questions.explanation: A rate without quality constraints is not a service-capacity guarantee. The observed rate is offered demand, not a successful operating capacity, when nearly a third of requests fail. Find the sustained rate that meets the stated latency and success objectives, then reserve appropriate failure and burst headroom.
questions.tradeoff: Finding the sustainable envelope takes multiple controlled runs.
questions.followup: How would headroom for failures change the final production limit?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new release appears faster in a load test, but the generator waits for each response before sending the next. When the service slows, offered load drops.

questions.title: Isolation claim
questions.prompt: What is accurate about database failure isolation?

choices.text: Eight API groups imply eight independent database failure domains
choices.why: The shared cluster remains common.

choices.text: The database remains a cross-cell failure dependency
choices.why: Serving separation alone does not isolate shared state.

choices.text: Only the smallest cell can be affected
choices.why: No such routing property was given.

choices.text: More routers remove the shared database dependency
choices.why: Routers do not replicate database authority.

questions.explanation: Draw the dependency graph rather than counting deployment groups. Every synchronous path through the shared database crosses the claimed isolation boundary. Test loss of that shared cluster explicitly; cell-local health does not establish availability when every useful request still needs the same database authority.
questions.tradeoff: Independent state can require migration and cross-cell workflow design.
questions.followup: Which shared control services can fail without stopping established traffic?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A SaaS platform has eight serving cells. Each cell has separate API and worker instances, but all cells synchronously depend on one database cluster.

questions.title: Partition key fit
questions.prompt: Tenants mostly operate on their own data. Which cell key deserves first evaluation?

choices.why: It aligns most requests with one natural data boundary.

choices.text: A random cell selected independently for every request
choices.why: This distributes traffic but makes tenant state access cross cells frequently.

choices.text: The current least-loaded cell, without a durable tenant placement map
choices.why: Request-level balancing alone does not preserve stable state ownership.

choices.text: Separate read cells and write cells for every tenant
choices.why: This can create cross-cell dependencies for most operations rather than matching tenant locality.

questions.explanation: A cell key should minimize cross-cell work and be available to routing. Tenant ID fits the given locality, but large tenants still need capacity planning. Check large tenants and cross-tenant operations separately, because a natural locality key can still create hot cells or expensive exceptions to the common path.
questions.tradeoff: Tenant-size skew can leave cells uneven.
questions.followup: How would a tenant too large for one cell be handled?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A SaaS platform has eight serving cells. Each cell has separate API and worker instances, but all cells synchronously depend on one database cluster.

questions.title: Cell-size decision
questions.prompt: What should determine a cell's maximum tested size?

choices.text: The largest instance offered by the vendor
choices.why: Instance size does not prove service behavior.
Its workload distribution can differ.

choices.text: Load-test envelope, recovery time and acceptable customer blast radius
choices.why: It connects scale limits with operational risk.

choices.text: Only total company traffic divided evenly
choices.why: Tenants need not have equal demand.

questions.explanation: A bounded cell is useful only if its limits are exercised. Recovery and overload behavior matter alongside steady-state throughput. Specify the workload shape behind the limit, including tenant skew and failure recovery, rather than treating a tenant count as a universal capacity unit.
questions.tradeoff: Smaller cells reduce blast radius but increase fleet overhead.
questions.followup: Which metrics tell you to split before a cell becomes unsafe?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A SaaS platform has eight serving cells. Each cell has separate API and worker instances, but all cells synchronously depend on one database cluster.

questions.title: Control-plane outage
questions.prompt: Existing tenant mappings are cached and versioned. What design can preserve serving during a provisioning outage?

choices.text: Make every data request create a fresh placement record
choices.why: Serving now requires the failed control operation.

choices.text: Route all tenants randomly until recovery
choices.why: Requests may reach cells without their data.

choices.text: Reject all reads even when verified mappings remain valid
choices.why: That imposes an unnecessary dependency if the contract allows cached routing.

choices.text: Continue established routing under explicit validity bounds while pausing changes
choices.why: Serving and administration have different dependency needs.

questions.explanation: Separate steady-state data access from topology mutation. Cached authority needs a stated freshness and migration protocol, not indefinite blind trust. Placement changes and revocations may need newer state than ordinary reads, so define which operations pause rather than silently applying one cache policy everywhere.
questions.tradeoff: Longer autonomy delays some placement changes.
questions.followup: How would emergency tenant suspension reach isolated cells?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A SaaS platform has eight serving cells. Each cell has separate API and worker instances, but all cells synchronously depend on one database cluster.

questions.title: Namespace limit
questions.prompt: What should be said about namespaces?

choices.text: They alone guarantee every security and resource boundary
choices.why: Other controls are still necessary.
Namespaces are not a full host-isolation proof.

choices.text: They organize scope but require access, network and resource controls
choices.why: Isolation spans multiple layers.
Operations still need authorization.

questions.explanation: A naming boundary is not a complete threat model. Define what tenants can do and which shared components remain attack or contention surfaces. Review control-plane permissions, network reachability, host sharing and sensitive storage together; strong controls at one layer do not automatically close another tenant boundary.
questions.tradeoff: Stronger isolation often reduces packing efficiency.
questions.followup: When would separate clusters or virtual control planes be justified?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A platform hosts workloads from different organizations in Kubernetes. Tenants should not read each other's data or exhaust all shared resources.

questions.title: Resource protection
questions.prompt: Which controls address noisy-neighbor risk? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Per-tenant resource quotas and meaningful requests/limits
choices.why: They constrain aggregate and workload resource claims.

choices.text: One administrator credential shared by every tenant
choices.why: That broadens authority rather than bounding resources.
A tenant can still request excessive resources.

choices.text: Admission and concurrency limits on expensive shared services
choices.why: Not all contention is captured by pod CPU limits.

questions.explanation: Resource isolation includes both scheduled compute and shared APIs or storage. A tenant can overwhelm a dependency without exceeding one container limit. Measure whether quotas actually preserve other tenants' useful throughput during a burst; configured limits alone do not establish fair behavior across shared dependencies.
questions.tradeoff: Limits can reject legitimate bursts.
questions.followup: How would burst credits preserve fairness without unlimited borrowing?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A platform hosts workloads from different organizations in Kubernetes. Tenants should not read each other's data or exhaust all shared resources.

questions.title: Hard isolation request
questions.prompt: One customer requires protection against hostile neighboring workloads. Best next step?

choices.text: Promise existing namespace separation without a threat review
choices.why: The stated adversary is stronger than organizational isolation.

choices.text: Map the threat model to runtime, host and control-plane isolation choices
choices.why: The design must cover the required boundary.
Labels do not change execution isolation.

choices.text: Disable quotas to give the customer priority
choices.why: Priority does not protect confidentiality.

questions.explanation: Translate the contractual word isolation into concrete adversary capabilities. Choose deployment boundaries only after those capabilities are explicit. Name the capabilities of the hostile neighbor, such as arbitrary code execution or control-plane access, before choosing which infrastructure boundaries must be independent.
questions.tradeoff: Dedicated infrastructure can increase cost and operational burden.
questions.followup: Which residual shared services remain in a dedicated-cluster design?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A platform hosts workloads from different organizations in Kubernetes. Tenants should not read each other's data or exhaust all shared resources.

questions.title: Tenant escape incident
questions.prompt: What should an incident inventory include?

choices.text: Shared identities, hosts, control services and data paths reachable from the affected boundary
choices.why: Scope follows possible authority and connectivity.
Spend does not define exposure.
It omits shared dependencies.

choices.text: All company systems declared compromised without analysis
choices.why: That may be unnecessarily broad and uninformative.

questions.explanation: Containment starts from actual reachability and permissions. Distinguish confirmed access from plausible exposure while investigating. Use that inventory to bound containment and identify missing evidence; a shared component may be exposed even when its customer-facing namespace appears unaffected.
questions.tradeoff: Complete inventories are expensive to maintain but valuable during incidents.
questions.followup: How would you verify that a remediation closes the original path?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A platform hosts workloads from different organizations in Kubernetes. Tenants should not read each other's data or exhaust all shared resources.

questions.title: Classify the bottleneck
questions.prompt: Which intervention targets the shared admission boundary?

choices.text: Add unlimited retries to every controller
choices.why: This multiplies demand.

choices.text: Classify flows and bound concurrent expensive requests
choices.why: One source cannot consume the whole API capacity.
That pushes more work into the bottleneck.

choices.text: Reduce all request timeouts to zero
choices.why: Useful work is rejected indiscriminately.

questions.explanation: The shared resource needs allocation, not just more waiting rooms. Classification should distinguish critical flows and avoid starving legitimate background reconciliation. Limit work before it consumes the expensive shared resource, and include recovery controllers in the policy so background starvation does not prevent convergence indefinitely.
questions.tradeoff: Fairness can reduce aggregate throughput.
questions.followup: What cost measure should distinguish a small GET from a large LIST?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A management API serves user changes and reconciliation controllers. One controller repeatedly lists large resource collections, delaying critical operations.

questions.title: Controller efficiency
questions.prompt: What reduces repeated full-list pressure while preserving reconciliation?

choices.text: Poll the entire collection more frequently
choices.why: Pressure increases.

choices.text: Cache forever with no update stream
choices.why: State becomes stale indefinitely.

choices.text: Use supported incremental watch/cache patterns with resync recovery
choices.why: Most changes need not reread all objects.
Desired state may no longer converge.

questions.explanation: Incremental observation reduces routine work, but reconnect gaps and cache rebuilds still need bounded recovery. Treat full resync as a load event. Rate-limit cache rebuilds and replay after disconnection, because a normally efficient incremental design can still generate synchronized full-list storms during recovery.
questions.tradeoff: Watch state adds lifecycle and memory complexity.
questions.followup: How would many controllers reconnecting together be staggered?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A management API serves user changes and reconciliation controllers. One controller repeatedly lists large resource collections, delaying critical operations.

questions.title: Priority inversion
questions.prompt: Critical requests share a FIFO queue behind huge background jobs. What should policy address?

choices.text: Separate bounded queues or concurrency shares by class
choices.why: Critical work can receive capacity without waiting for every background item.

choices.text: Only increase the FIFO queue length
choices.why: That extends waiting.
The server's scheduling policy remains unchanged.

choices.text: Give one privileged user unlimited requests
choices.why: That creates another starvation path.

questions.explanation: Priority needs capacity isolation as well as labels. Keep some progress for background work because convergence can itself become critical over time. Define minimum progress and borrowing rules explicitly; an urgent queue without a bounded service allocation can still wait behind already admitted expensive work.
questions.tradeoff: Reservations can leave capacity temporarily unused.
questions.followup: How would borrowing work without letting background work block urgent requests?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A management API serves user changes and reconciliation controllers. One controller repeatedly lists large resource collections, delaying critical operations.

questions.title: Fairness evidence
questions.prompt: Which dashboard best reveals whether the policy works?

choices.why: Large users can hide starvation.
Small classes can suffer unnoticed.
Configuration is not observed allocation.

choices.text: Per-class admission, queue wait, execution cost, errors and progress
choices.why: It links policy to actual service outcomes.

questions.explanation: Fairness is a distributional property, not a fleet average. Measure who waits and who completes work under overload. Compare classes under sustained overload and during recovery, since average healthy-state latency can hide one class receiving almost no useful service when demand spikes.
questions.tradeoff: High-cardinality dimensions need bounded aggregation.
questions.followup: Which labels can expose useful tenants without leaking sensitive identifiers?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A management API serves user changes and reconciliation controllers. One controller repeatedly lists large resource collections, delaying critical operations.

questions.title: Success metric
questions.prompt: Which metric most directly measures user value?

choices.text: Time and effort to safely deliver a supported change
choices.why: It measures the platform's intended developer outcome.
More files can mean more friction.
Activity is not adoption value.

choices.text: Only the count of central policies
choices.why: Policy quantity does not establish delivery quality.

questions.explanation: A platform is a product for its users. Pair delivery efficiency with reliability and security outcomes so speed does not hide transferred risk. Measure real application-team tasks from request to safe production outcome, including failed migrations and support tickets rather than counting platform-generated repositories alone.
questions.tradeoff: Measuring developer workflow requires representative tasks.
questions.followup: How would you distinguish platform delay from application review delay?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A platform team offers standardized deployment templates. Product teams currently maintain custom pipelines, some for legitimate regulated or latency-sensitive needs.

questions.title: Escape hatch
questions.prompt: What is a useful exception mechanism?

choices.why: They become invisible risk and support obligations.
Legitimate constraints may make adoption impossible.

choices.text: Documented time-bounded exceptions with owners and equivalent controls
choices.why: Special needs remain visible and accountable.

choices.text: Copy the entire platform per team
choices.why: Forks multiply maintenance without shared evolution.

questions.explanation: A paved path should cover common needs while making deviations explicit. Exceptions reveal product gaps rather than automatically proving disobedience. Set an expiry or review trigger and record the equivalent safeguards, so an exception can be renewed deliberately or converted into a supported standard feature.
questions.tradeoff: Reviewing exceptions adds coordination work.
questions.followup: Which repeated exception should become a supported capability?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A platform team offers standardized deployment templates. Product teams currently maintain custom pipelines, some for legitimate regulated or latency-sensitive needs.

questions.title: Migration incentive
questions.prompt: How should staff engineers drive adoption across teams?

choices.why: Teams inherit unknown risk.

choices.text: Pilot real workloads, measure outcomes and fund migration support
choices.why: Evidence and assistance address actual switching costs.

choices.text: Measure success only by emails announcing the platform
choices.why: Announcements do not move workloads.
Critical unsupported cases can break.

questions.explanation: Adoption competes with feature delivery and existing reliability commitments. A credible migration plan includes workload fit, ownership and rollback. Include the time product teams spend adapting code and learning operations, because central platform savings can otherwise conceal effort merely transferred to consumers.
questions.tradeoff: Support capacity can limit rollout speed.
questions.followup: Which teams provide the most informative initial pilot?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A platform team offers standardized deployment templates. Product teams currently maintain custom pipelines, some for legitimate regulated or latency-sensitive needs.

questions.title: Ownership boundary
questions.prompt: Who owns an outage caused by a standard template's default?

choices.text: Only the application team because it deployed
choices.why: The shared default has a platform owner too.

choices.text: Only the platform team for every application bug
choices.why: Application semantics still belong to service owners.

choices.text: Nobody because the template is open source
choices.why: Internal operational accountability remains.

choices.text: Define joint incident response with clear component ownership and repair duties
choices.why: Responsibility follows the shared contract and failure cause.

questions.explanation: Reusable defaults create shared operational obligations. Clear escalation prevents teams from discovering ownership during an outage. Specify who can mitigate immediately, who repairs the shared default and how existing deployments receive the fix; ownership should not depend on incident-time negotiation.
questions.tradeoff: Joint response can be slower without rehearsed interfaces.
questions.followup: How would a bad default be corrected across already-created services?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A platform team offers standardized deployment templates. Product teams currently maintain custom pipelines, some for legitimate regulated or latency-sensitive needs.

questions.title: Cost boundary
questions.prompt: What belongs in the comparison?

choices.why: Staffing, incidents and infrastructure are omitted.

choices.text: Total lifecycle cost including operations, durability and migration
choices.why: It compares equivalent responsibilities.
Prototype size does not capture production obligations.
Current needs are modest and semantics matter.

questions.explanation: A custom broker inherits recovery, upgrades, security and on-call work. Compare the cost of equivalent guarantees rather than one visible fee. Include restore drills, upgrades and on-call staffing in the custom option, while examining provider pricing, quotas and exit costs in the managed option.
questions.tradeoff: Managed services can have lock-in and pricing exposure.
questions.followup: Which workload change would make a custom system worth reconsidering?
questions.caseTitle: Build versus buy a queue service
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A company needs durable messaging with modest throughput. A managed service meets current semantics, but a team proposes a custom broker to avoid per-request fees.

questions.title: Semantic fit
questions.prompt: Which evidence should precede a performance comparison?

choices.text: A requirement matrix for ordering, retention, replay and failure behavior
choices.why: It establishes whether both candidates solve the same problem.

choices.text: The service with the largest community and best-known brand
choices.why: Ecosystem maturity matters, but it does not establish the required ordering and durability semantics.
It may omit durability and real payloads.

choices.text: A comparison of implementation languages and SDK convenience
choices.why: Integration effort matters, but it cannot replace the core behavior contract.

questions.explanation: Performance numbers are misleading when durability or ordering differ. First reject designs that fail the required contract. Retain examples of required failure behavior as executable tests, so later optimizations cannot quietly trade away the semantics that justified the selected service.
questions.tradeoff: A detailed matrix takes time but avoids false comparisons.
questions.followup: Which guarantee is easiest to accidentally weaken in a prototype?
questions.caseTitle: Build versus buy a queue service
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A company needs durable messaging with modest throughput. A managed service meets current semantics, but a team proposes a custom broker to avoid per-request fees.

questions.title: Exit strategy
questions.prompt: What reduces managed-service lock-in without premature rebuilding?

choices.text: Wrap every provider feature in a fake universal abstraction
choices.why: Important semantics can be hidden or lost.

choices.text: Export no data to simplify operations
choices.why: Migration becomes harder.

choices.text: Document semantics, retain recoverable data and test a realistic migration path
choices.why: Exit risk is made concrete.

choices.text: Build a second full broker before first adoption
choices.why: Cost may exceed the identified risk.

questions.explanation: Portability is about data, behavior and recovery, not just method names. Test the costly boundaries rather than claiming interchangeable APIs. Prioritize exporting recoverable history and exercising a realistic cutover over abstracting every API; behavior and data often dominate the true migration cost.
questions.tradeoff: An exit path has ongoing maintenance cost.
questions.followup: Which provider-specific feature delivers enough value to accept explicit coupling?
questions.caseTitle: Build versus buy a queue service
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A company needs durable messaging with modest throughput. A managed service meets current semantics, but a team proposes a custom broker to avoid per-request fees.

questions.title: Custom-service readiness
questions.prompt: What would make a custom proposal credible?

choices.why: It omits failure and operating costs.

choices.text: A higher throughput number with memory-only writes
choices.why: The durability contract differs.

choices.text: A promise to add recovery later
choices.why: Recovery is part of the core requirement.

choices.text: Measured contract parity, failure tests, staffing and staged migration economics
choices.why: The proposal addresses the whole service lifecycle.

questions.explanation: A broker is a long-lived operational commitment. Readiness evidence must include how it fails and recovers, not merely how it sends. Require the proposal to explain how durable acknowledgements survive faults and how a small team will maintain those guarantees over several years of changes.
questions.tradeoff: The evidence burden can outweigh expected savings.
questions.followup: What pilot would test the hardest assumption without risking critical traffic?
questions.caseTitle: Build versus buy a queue service
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A company needs durable messaging with modest throughput. A managed service meets current semantics, but a team proposes a custom broker to avoid per-request fees.

questions.title: Initial seam
questions.prompt: Which extraction best matches the stated phase?

choices.text: Move all billing and profile writes at once
choices.why: That expands the migration boundary.

choices.text: Create two independent profile writers immediately
choices.why: Authority becomes ambiguous.

choices.text: Route profile reads through a new service fed from the authoritative writer
choices.why: The read seam can evolve without dual ownership.

choices.text: Rewrite the entire monolith before any release
choices.why: It delays evidence and increases batch size.

questions.explanation: Choose a seam with a clear ownership boundary. A derived reader still needs freshness and reconciliation contracts. Declare the projection's freshness and read-your-write behavior, since changing where reads are served can alter user experience even while one writer remains authoritative.
questions.tradeoff: Read projections add lag and duplicate storage.
questions.followup: Which reads cannot tolerate the projection's lag?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A monolith owns customer profiles and billing. The team wants to extract profile reads first while keeping one authoritative writer during the initial phase.

questions.title: Routing correctness
questions.prompt: What must the facade preserve during mixed operation?

choices.text: Stable external behavior and explicit routing ownership
choices.why: Clients should not accidentally receive conflicting semantics.

choices.text: A random destination on every call
choices.why: State and compatibility may differ.

choices.text: Preserve URL paths while allowing response and retry semantics to diverge
choices.why: The external contract includes payloads, errors and effects, not only routing syntax.

choices.text: Expose the new service's storage schema directly as the public API
choices.why: Internal data representation can break old clients and bind them to migration details.

questions.explanation: A routing layer is a compatibility boundary, not merely a traffic splitter. Define how errors, retries and fallback behave. Test retries and partial failures at the facade, because an apparently harmless fallback can repeat a write or combine incompatible answers from both implementations.
questions.tradeoff: The facade can become a bottleneck or long-lived dependency.
questions.followup: Which fallback is unsafe after a new-path write partially succeeds?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A monolith owns customer profiles and billing. The team wants to extract profile reads first while keeping one authoritative writer during the initial phase.

questions.title: Write ownership transfer
questions.prompt: What evidence is needed before moving profile writes?

choices.why: Read performance does not prove write correctness.

choices.text: Data catch-up, invariant parity, cutover fencing and recovery plan
choices.why: The authoritative transition is controlled.

choices.text: Only team agreement in a meeting
choices.why: Agreement is not operational evidence.
It may contain incomplete or stale data.

questions.explanation: Write migration changes authority, not just routing. Prevent both old and new writers from independently accepting conflicting updates. Rehearse the authority handoff with stale clients and failed cutovers, not just a bulk copy, because data completeness alone does not fence the old writer.
questions.tradeoff: A brief write pause may simplify a high-risk cutover.
questions.followup: How would a no-pause migration establish one current writer?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A monolith owns customer profiles and billing. The team wants to extract profile reads first while keeping one authoritative writer during the initial phase.

questions.title: Retire the monolith path
questions.prompt: When is deleting the old profile path justified?

choices.why: No traffic or state evidence is implied.
Rare integrations may remain.

choices.text: When the monolith team wants fewer files
choices.why: Maintenance preference is not dependency proof.

choices.text: After supported consumers migrate and rollback/data-retention decisions are explicit
choices.why: Retirement follows dependency closure.

questions.explanation: A strangler migration is complete only when old obligations are closed. Hidden jobs and external clients often outlive interactive traffic. Use access telemetry and a consumer inventory together; no recent interactive traffic does not prove that a monthly export or recovery procedure no longer needs the old path.
questions.tradeoff: Long overlap costs resources and attention.
questions.followup: How would you discover consumers that run only quarterly?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A monolith owns customer profiles and billing. The team wants to extract profile reads first while keeping one authoritative writer during the initial phase.

questions.title: Different freshness needs
questions.prompt: Which policy is appropriate?

choices.why: Revocation cannot meet a freshness requirement.

choices.text: Classify settings by safety and freshness contract
choices.why: Tuning and authority changes need different failure behavior.

choices.text: Reject all work whenever any tuning value is stale
choices.why: That may unnecessarily reduce availability.

choices.text: Treat configuration as one undifferentiated blob
choices.why: Dependencies and risk remain hidden.

questions.explanation: A configuration cache is safe only relative to each setting's semantics. A stale thread-count hint differs from stale access permission. Document what cached state remains safe during a partition and which operations must stop, rather than letting every consumer invent a different default on failure.
questions.tradeoff: Classification increases configuration-system complexity.
questions.followup: Which settings should have mandatory expiry rather than defaults?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Thousands of workers fetch configuration every minute. A central outage lasts 20 minutes. Some settings control tuning; others revoke access to sensitive data.

questions.title: Restart storm
questions.prompt: Why can a restart during the outage be worse than steady operation?

choices.text: New workers may lack a validated last-known configuration
choices.why: Existing workers still have usable state.
The binary can be unchanged.
That depends on storage design.

choices.text: Configuration outages delete all customer data
choices.why: No such coupling was specified.

questions.explanation: Startup dependencies and steady-state dependencies can differ. Test recovery when the control service is unavailable, not only normal refresh. Validate persisted state against expected schema and age, then test cold startup during a control-plane outage so recovery does not depend on unavailable fresh configuration.
questions.tradeoff: Persisted config requires integrity and version checks.
questions.followup: How would an old persisted snapshot be rejected safely?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Thousands of workers fetch configuration every minute. A central outage lasts 20 minutes. Some settings control tuning; others revoke access to sensitive data.

questions.title: Rollout blast radius
questions.prompt: What contains a syntactically valid but harmful configuration?

choices.text: Validate types and allowed numeric ranges, then apply globally
choices.why: Valid values can still create harmful behavior under a particular workload.

choices.text: Publish one atomic global version with no canary cohort
choices.why: Atomicity avoids mixed versions but does not contain a semantically bad configuration.

choices.text: Versioned staged rollout with outcome guardrails and rollback
choices.why: Semantic effects are observed before broad adoption.

choices.text: Require two human approvals but omit automated outcome guardrails
choices.why: Review helps, yet mistakes that survive review still need bounded exposure and observable rollback criteria.

questions.explanation: Treat configuration changes as releases when they can change behavior materially. A rollback must restore a known compatible version. Observe user outcomes and resource saturation for each cohort, because a numerically valid setting can still trigger an overload cascade when applied to real demand.
questions.tradeoff: Staging delays global convergence.
questions.followup: Which settings require coordinated atomic change rather than independent rollout?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Thousands of workers fetch configuration every minute. A central outage lasts 20 minutes. Some settings control tuning; others revoke access to sensitive data.

questions.title: Ownership contract
questions.prompt: What should each setting declare?

choices.why: Meaning and failure behavior remain implicit.
That is insufficient operational ownership.
Human presentation is not a runtime contract.

choices.text: Owner, allowed range, default, freshness and failure behavior
choices.why: Consumers and operators share explicit semantics.

questions.explanation: Configuration values become APIs across teams and versions. Documentation should state what a consumer does when the value is missing or stale. Make incompatible setting changes follow a consumer migration plan, since old and new workers may interpret the same value under different versions of the contract.
questions.tradeoff: Rich schemas require maintenance.
questions.followup: How would deprecation work when old workers still read a setting?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Thousands of workers fetch configuration every minute. A central outage lasts 20 minutes. Some settings control tuning; others revoke access to sensitive data.

questions.title: Bottleneck location
questions.prompt: What should capacity planning recognize?

choices.text: Small metadata can dominate request rate and availability
choices.why: Byte volume is not the only scaling dimension.

choices.text: Metadata is free because it is small
choices.why: CPU, IOPS and coordination still matter.

choices.text: Blob size determines every lookup's cost exactly
choices.why: Lookup workload has separate structure.
Metadata sits on every access path.

questions.explanation: Capacity has operations, bytes and correctness dimensions. A tiny authoritative record can be the critical dependency for a very large object. Measure lookup rate, mutation contention and listing cost independently from blob throughput, because the smallest dataset can still dominate every request's critical path.
questions.tradeoff: Caching reduces reads but introduces freshness questions.
questions.followup: Which metadata fields can safely be cached longer?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Many services store large objects but consult a central metadata service for names, ownership and object locations. Metadata traffic grows faster than blob traffic.

questions.title: Location indirection
questions.prompt: Why separate a stable object identity from physical storage location?

choices.text: It removes the need to find the bytes
choices.why: A mapping is still required.
The mapping service can fail.

choices.text: Objects can move without changing their logical identity
choices.why: Clients need not encode placement permanently.
Identity is independent of access policy.

questions.explanation: Indirection supports migration and placement changes. The mapping update still needs consistency so readers find a valid location. During movement, readers need either a still-valid old location, a redirect or a retryable mapping update; stable identity does not eliminate migration races by itself.
questions.tradeoff: An extra lookup adds latency or cache complexity.
questions.followup: How would a reader handle a stale location during migration?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Many services store large objects but consult a central metadata service for names, ownership and object locations. Metadata traffic grows faster than blob traffic.

questions.title: Metadata partitioning
questions.prompt: Which partition decision is most relevant?

choices.text: Split only by payload byte size
choices.why: Metadata access locality may differ.

choices.text: Choose keys from lookup patterns, tenant boundaries and hot-key risks
choices.why: The partition aligns with dominant operations.

choices.text: Randomly choose a new shard for every lookup
choices.why: Stable ownership disappears.

choices.text: Put all frequently accessed metadata on one shard
choices.why: That can concentrate the bottleneck.

questions.explanation: Partitioning should follow operations and invariants, not just storage volume. Cross-partition listing and uniqueness costs must be made explicit. Evaluate secondary operations such as namespace listing and global uniqueness before committing to the key, because optimizing one point lookup may distribute another invariant awkwardly.
questions.tradeoff: A key that helps point lookups can complicate ordered listing.
questions.followup: How would globally unique names be allocated?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Many services store large objects but consult a central metadata service for names, ownership and object locations. Metadata traffic grows faster than blob traffic.

questions.title: Control/data separation
questions.prompt: Which failure policy is plausible for existing immutable-object reads?

choices.text: Require provisioning a new namespace for every read
choices.why: That adds unnecessary control-plane coupling.

choices.text: Guess random storage nodes when metadata is stale
choices.why: It does not preserve access or identity.

choices.text: Skip ownership checks whenever metadata is slow
choices.why: That weakens confidentiality.

choices.text: Use verified cached mappings within explicit authorization and validity bounds
choices.why: Established reads may survive some control failures.

questions.explanation: Autonomy is possible only for state whose cached meaning remains valid. Placement and access revocation may have different freshness bounds. Review the authorization bound separately from placement freshness, since an unchanged immutable blob may become forbidden even while its physical location remains perfectly accurate.
questions.tradeoff: More cached state complicates invalidation and recovery.
questions.followup: Which metadata changes invalidate an otherwise immutable object's read capability?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Many services store large objects but consult a central metadata service for names, ownership and object locations. Metadata traffic grows faster than blob traffic.

questions.title: User journey boundary
questions.prompt: What should be defined first?

choices.text: Set CPU objectives for every dependency before defining checkout behavior
choices.why: Resource targets help diagnosis but do not define the user's successful journey.

choices.text: Use the company-wide uptime metric as checkout's indicator
choices.why: Other products and paths can hide checkout-specific failures.

choices.text: The user-visible checkout success and latency indicators
choices.why: Dependencies can align to a shared outcome.

choices.text: Standardize dashboard formatting before agreeing on indicator semantics
choices.why: Consistent presentation does not make teams measure the same outcome.

questions.explanation: Start with what the customer experiences, then map contributing dependencies. Internal uptime can be high while the composed request fails. Classify expected business rejection separately from infrastructure failure, so an ordinary insufficient-funds decline does not distort the reliability indicator for the checkout system.
questions.tradeoff: Journey instrumentation requires consistent correlation.
questions.followup: How would expected business declines be separated from system errors?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A product promises an end-to-end checkout SLO. Five teams own synchronous dependencies, each reporting a different internal uptime metric.

questions.title: Dependency composition
questions.prompt: Why is giving every dependency exactly the end-to-end target insufficient?

choices.text: Several required dependencies can compound failure probability
choices.why: Individual objectives do not automatically compose to the same target.
Correlations must be investigated, not assumed.

choices.text: SLOs cannot be assigned to dependencies
choices.why: They can support planning when semantics are clear.
The scenario explicitly has five.

questions.explanation: Required calls introduce additional failure opportunities. Budgeting must consider call structure, correlated incidents and degraded modes. Use the actual call graph and correlations rather than multiplying uptime numbers mechanically, then consider whether optional work can leave the synchronous critical path.
questions.tradeoff: Stricter dependency objectives may cost more than removing a dependency.
questions.followup: Which optional calls could leave the synchronous path?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A product promises an end-to-end checkout SLO. Five teams own synchronous dependencies, each reporting a different internal uptime metric.

questions.title: Budget exhaustion decision
questions.prompt: The journey burns its reliability budget rapidly. What is staff-level coordination?

choices.text: Every team continues unrelated risky launches independently
choices.why: Shared user harm remains unmanaged.

choices.text: Use a pre-agreed policy to prioritize stabilization across owners
choices.why: The common outcome drives coordinated action.

choices.text: Blame the team with the largest dashboard
choices.why: Dashboard size is not causality.

choices.text: Change the SLO retroactively to erase the incident
choices.why: That removes accountability.

questions.explanation: An error budget is useful when it changes decisions through an agreed policy. Ownership should follow evidence about contributing causes. Make exceptions for necessary risk-reducing changes explicit, and track recovery against the shared user objective rather than asking each team to declare local success independently.
questions.tradeoff: Stabilization can delay feature work.
questions.followup: How would a necessary security release be handled during a freeze?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A product promises an end-to-end checkout SLO. Five teams own synchronous dependencies, each reporting a different internal uptime metric.

questions.title: Accountability
questions.prompt: Which contract reduces gaps between dependency teams?

choices.text: Each team owns only its code repository
choices.why: Runtime interactions fall between teams.

choices.text: The frontend owns every backend incident
choices.why: That misaligns expertise and control.
Communication does not define repair responsibility.

choices.text: Shared journey ownership plus explicit dependency escalation and change contracts
choices.why: Local and end-to-end duties are both visible.

questions.explanation: No single team may control the entire request path, but someone must coordinate its outcome. Interface contracts make local decisions legible to neighbors. Define escalation and change-notification duties at interfaces so teams can act before a local optimization consumes a neighbor's latency or reliability budget.
questions.tradeoff: Coordination has overhead and needs a lightweight cadence.
questions.followup: How would you resolve competing latency budgets across teams?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A product promises an end-to-end checkout SLO. Five teams own synchronous dependencies, each reporting a different internal uptime metric.

questions.title: Backup versus recovery
questions.prompt: What is currently demonstrated?

choices.text: The full application can recover within its target
choices.why: No restore test establishes that.
Restoring services has additional dependencies.
Daily backups imply a potential gap unless other mechanisms exist.

choices.text: Every credential works in the other region
choices.why: That was not tested.

questions.explanation: Backups are inputs to recovery, not proof of a working system. Restore, validation, routing and authority cutover are separate steps. Inventory every step from obtaining a usable backup to restoring authorized customer traffic; untested keys, routing or write ownership can defeat a successful file restore.
questions.tradeoff: Recovery drills consume resources and operational time.
questions.followup: Which data must be reconciled beyond the latest backup?
questions.caseTitle: Disaster recovery that has never run
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A platform has daily backups in another region. Leadership calls the design disaster-ready, but no restore has been tested and external dependencies are not inventoried.

questions.title: Recovery dependency map
questions.prompt: Match each recovery failure to the missing prerequisite it most directly reveals. Use each choice once.

items.text: Restored encrypted records cannot be decrypted.
The restored service is healthy, but clients still reach the failed region.
Both recovered and original regions accept conflicting writes.
Recent acknowledged operations are absent from restored state.

choices.why: Data bytes are unusable without authorized access to their decryption material.
A working destination does not help callers until routing directs them to it.
Recovery must prevent old and new regions from independently owning the same write authority.
Missing recent history requires evidence about backups, replication and replay progress.

questions.explanation: A disaster-recovery system must recover data, authority, reachability and a coherent history boundary. These failures can occur even when a database restore command succeeds. Diagnose the exact missing prerequisite instead of treating every recovery problem as a slow file copy or a generic networking issue. Run drills that exercise those distinct prerequisites, and report which were simulated versus actually recovered so one passing layer is not mistaken for end-to-end readiness.
questions.tradeoff: Independent recovery of control state adds complexity and must preserve security boundaries.
questions.followup: Which dependency is currently hosted only in the region whose failure you are planning for?
questions.caseTitle: Disaster recovery that has never run
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A platform has daily backups in another region. Leadership calls the design disaster-ready, but no restore has been tested and external dependencies are not inventoried.

questions.title: Recovery claim
questions.prompt: What justifies an RTO claim?

choices.why: Your full workflow may differ.

choices.text: The time to create a VM
choices.why: Most recovery work is omitted.

choices.text: A rehearsed representative recovery measured to validated service restoration
choices.why: It tests the actual boundary promised.
It remains a planning assumption.

questions.explanation: Recovery time ends when the required service is correct and usable, not when copying starts. State the tested scale and excluded conditions. Include data validation, external integration recovery and traffic cutover in the measured critical path, and document manual steps that limit repeatability under real incident pressure.
questions.tradeoff: Full-scale drills can be expensive.
questions.followup: Which partial drills provide useful evidence between full exercises?
questions.caseTitle: Disaster recovery that has never run
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A platform has daily backups in another region. Leadership calls the design disaster-ready, but no restore has been tested and external dependencies are not inventoried.

questions.title: Failback policy
questions.prompt: Why plan failback before an incident?

choices.why: State and authority may have diverged.

choices.text: The original region must be trusted immediately on return
choices.why: Old state may be stale.

choices.text: Failback cannot lose data by definition
choices.why: Poor cutover can create loss or conflicts.

choices.text: Reconciliation, writer fencing and traffic reversal need explicit steps
choices.why: Returning to normal is another migration.

questions.explanation: Recovery creates a new authoritative history that must not be overwritten by an old region's return. Treat failback as a controlled state transition. Reconcile the new region's accepted history before allowing the old region to resume authority, and test the case where both regions are reachable but hold different state.
questions.tradeoff: Delayed failback prolongs temporary cost and complexity.
questions.followup: What evidence proves the returning region is caught up?
questions.caseTitle: Disaster recovery that has never run
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A platform has daily backups in another region. Leadership calls the design disaster-ready, but no restore has been tested and external dependencies are not inventoried.

questions.title: Celebrity fan-out
questions.prompt: Which approach avoids a huge per-post write burst for celebrity authors?

choices.text: Fan out every celebrity post synchronously before acknowledging
choices.why: The author waits for millions of writes.

choices.text: Materialize ordinary feeds and merge celebrity posts at read time
choices.why: Write amplification is limited for extreme fan-out.

choices.text: Recompute every ordinary feed from all historical posts
choices.why: It discards the read-heavy workload advantage.

choices.text: Store celebrity posts only in process memory
choices.why: Durability is violated.

questions.explanation: Different fan-out distributions justify different read/write tradeoffs. A celebrity post may create millions of derived writes even though only a fraction of followers immediately read it. Keeping those posts in an author stream and merging them during reads trades some read work for a bounded publish path.
questions.tradeoff: Hybrid reads need merging, deduplication and pagination semantics.
questions.followup: How would an author crossing the threshold be migrated?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Most authors have hundreds of followers; a few have millions. Feed reads dominate. Five seconds of propagation delay is acceptable, but new posts must be durable.

questions.title: Durable acceptance
questions.prompt: When can the post API honestly acknowledge durable acceptance?

choices.text: After one follower-feed projection has been updated
choices.why: One derived copy does not necessarily satisfy the authoritative durability contract.

choices.text: After placing the post in a process-local fan-out queue
choices.why: A process crash can lose queued work if it is not covered by durable acceptance.

choices.text: After the authoritative post is durably recorded under its contract
choices.why: Feed projection may complete asynchronously.

choices.text: After every follower-feed projection has completed
choices.why: That provides a stronger visibility milestone than required and couples acknowledgement to extreme fan-out.

questions.explanation: Separate source-of-truth durability from projection freshness. Persist the authoritative post under the promised durability model, then let follower-feed materialization catch up within the freshness target. Acknowledge the milestone actually achieved rather than waiting for every reader or confusing visibility with durability.
questions.tradeoff: Asynchronous feeds need lag visibility.
questions.followup: How would the author immediately read their own accepted post?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Most authors have hundreds of followers; a few have millions. Feed reads dominate. Five seconds of propagation delay is acceptable, but new posts must be durable.

questions.title: Privacy change
questions.prompt: A public author becomes private. What must the feed design address?

choices.text: Eligibility on delivery plus removal or invalidation of stale projections
choices.why: Precomputed copies can outlive old permissions.
Existing cached posts remain accessible.
The exposure duration is uncontrolled.
That is not the requested privacy transition.

questions.explanation: Materialization cannot become permanent authorization. Precomputed feeds can retain posts created under an older privacy policy, so eligibility must remain enforceable at delivery. Cleanup or invalidation reduces stale copies, but a bounded revocation promise cannot depend only on feeds naturally aging out.
questions.tradeoff: Fresh checks add read cost; cleanup adds background work.
questions.followup: What revocation bound would the product promise?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Most authors have hundreds of followers; a few have millions. Feed reads dominate. Five seconds of propagation delay is acceptable, but new posts must be durable.

questions.title: Hybrid policy evidence
questions.prompt: What should determine the fan-out threshold?

choices.why: Its workload may differ.
Inactive followers and author frequency affect cost.
The distribution changes.

choices.text: Measured write amplification, read cost, author rate and freshness targets
choices.why: The threshold follows local workload economics.

questions.explanation: A hybrid boundary is an operational policy, not a universal constant. Follower count interacts with author posting rate, follower activity, cache behavior and feed-read frequency. Measure total materialization and merge cost under those distributions, then treat the threshold as a versioned policy with a safe migration path.
questions.tradeoff: Adaptive policy adds migration and observability complexity.
questions.followup: How would cost be attributed to dormant followers?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Most authors have hundreds of followers; a few have millions. Feed reads dominate. Five seconds of propagation delay is acceptable, but new posts must be durable.

questions.title: Resume cursor
questions.prompt: What should a reconnecting client provide?

choices.text: Its last durably received conversation sequence
choices.why: The server can replay the missing suffix.
Clock skew can skip or duplicate messages.

choices.text: The latest server timestamp observed, without a stable tie-breaker or sequence
choices.why: Timestamps can tie and do not define the specified conversation-log continuation.

choices.text: The number of messages currently visible in the interface
choices.why: Filtering, deletion or local display state can make this differ from the durable log position.

questions.explanation: Resume state should refer to the authoritative conversation history. The last received authoritative sequence identifies a precise history suffix the client still needs. A wall-clock timestamp is vulnerable to skew and ties, while a transport connection identifier has no durable relation to conversation progress.
questions.tradeoff: Cursor retention requires a fallback for expired history.
questions.followup: How would a gap beyond retention trigger resynchronization?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A chat server assigns a monotonic sequence within each conversation and durably stores messages before acknowledging. Clients reconnect after losing network access.

questions.title: Retry duplicate
questions.prompt: The server committed a message but the acknowledgement was lost. What prevents two visible messages?

choices.text: Assume the timeout means no commit
choices.why: The server may have committed.

choices.text: A stable client operation ID deduplicated durably
choices.why: Retries refer to one logical send.

choices.text: Generate a fresh operation ID for every retry
choices.why: That creates new logical sends.
Identical text can be intentional.

questions.explanation: Business identity survives transport ambiguity. Assign identity to the logical send before the first network attempt and persist deduplication with the resulting message. Reusing that identity after response loss returns the same send outcome, while text-based deduplication would suppress intentional repeated messages.
questions.tradeoff: Deduplication scope must include sender and conversation as appropriate.
questions.followup: How would altered payloads under the same operation ID be handled?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A chat server assigns a monotonic sequence within each conversation and durably stores messages before acknowledging. Clients reconnect after losing network access.

questions.title: Global ordering request
questions.prompt: Product asks for one total order across unrelated conversations. Best response?

choices.text: Implement it because all ordering is free
choices.why: Global coordination adds cost.

choices.text: Use client clocks and claim exact total order
choices.why: Clock order is not authoritative serialization.

choices.text: Clarify the user invariant and prefer per-conversation order if sufficient
choices.why: The required scope determines coordination.
Conversation usability still needs a clear contract.

questions.explanation: Avoid global coordination without a cross-conversation invariant. Per-conversation sequencing directly serves the chat invariant without forcing unrelated rooms through one global coordination point. Require a concrete cross-room use case before accepting the latency, availability and operational cost of a broader total order.
questions.tradeoff: A true global order may be justified for audit workflows.
questions.followup: Which product action would actually require cross-room order?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A chat server assigns a monotonic sequence within each conversation and durably stores messages before acknowledging. Clients reconnect after losing network access.

questions.title: Chat acknowledgement evidence
questions.prompt: Match each status to the strongest evidence it actually represents. Use each choice once.

items.text: Local pending
Server accepted
Device delivered
Read receipt

choices.text: The sender's client has recorded intent to send.
choices.why: Local intent can exist before any server receives or persists the message.

choices.text: The server persisted the message under its acknowledgement contract.
choices.why: Durable server acceptance does not establish recipient device delivery.

choices.text: A recipient device acknowledged receiving the identified message.
choices.why: Device receipt does not establish that a person opened or understood it.

choices.text: A recipient client emitted the product-defined read signal.
choices.why: This is evidence of the defined client action, not proof of human comprehension.

questions.explanation: Each status names a different observation boundary in the delivery workflow. Preserve those distinctions in APIs and the interface, especially across offline devices and retries. A server commit is durable progress, but it does not prove that any recipient device received the message or that a human read it.
questions.tradeoff: More precise states make client synchronization and customer support more complex.
questions.followup: How should read and delivery receipts merge across a person's phone and laptop?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A chat server assigns a monotonic sequence within each conversation and durably stores messages before acknowledging. Clients reconnect after losing network access.

questions.title: Snapshot pagination
questions.prompt: Which Elasticsearch strategy fits the export?

choices.text: Deep from/size on a changing index with no stable view
choices.why: Costs grow and result movement can affect pages.

choices.text: Sort only by a nonunique timestamp
choices.why: Ties can cause ambiguous continuation.

choices.text: Use a point-in-time view and stable search_after ordering
choices.why: The export advances within one bounded snapshot.

choices.text: Issue unrelated random queries for each page
choices.why: There is no coherent continuation.

questions.explanation: Snapshot identity and a deterministic cursor work together. The point-in-time view fixes the index state while a stable sort cursor identifies the next position in that view. Without both, document updates or tied sort values can shift results between pages and violate the export's exactly-once enumeration requirement.
questions.tradeoff: Long-lived snapshots consume resources and need expiry handling.
questions.followup: What should happen if the export's snapshot expires?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A catalog search changes continuously. An export requires every matching document exactly once from one snapshot; ordinary interactive search can show fresh approximate results.

questions.title: Read after index write
questions.prompt: An acknowledged index write is not immediately searchable. What concept explains this?

choices.text: Search visibility can depend on refresh
choices.why: Durability and searchable visibility are distinct.
Lack of search visibility is not proof of loss.
The API contract may acknowledge before refresh.
No authorization evidence was given.
