questions.context: Hypothetical archive: acknowledged documents must survive a single availability-zone loss. A regional disaster may lose at most five minutes of accepted data, and the service must resume within one hour. Backups exist but the team has never performed a full restore.

questions.title: Respond to a failed rehearsal
questions.prompt: The first realistic restore takes four hours. What is the responsible next step?

choices.text: Keep publishing the one-hour objective as verified
choices.why: The test contradicts that claim.

choices.text: Delete slow test phases from the report
choices.why: Those phases may be required during a real recovery.
Reporting alone does not close the recovery gap.

choices.text: Document the gap, prioritize the bottleneck, and retest or renegotiate the objective
choices.why: This turns the measured shortfall into an owned decision.

questions.explanation: A four-hour representative restore is evidence that the current design does not meet the one-hour target. Record the gap, identify the critical path and assign remediation or explicit business renegotiation. Do not exclude required steps merely to make a dashboard appear compliant.
questions.tradeoff: Meeting the original target may require preprovisioned capacity or higher spend.
questions.followup: Which restoration phases can safely run in parallel?
questions.caseTitle: Restore the archive, not just the service
questions.context: Hypothetical archive: acknowledged documents must survive a single availability-zone loss. A regional disaster may lose at most five minutes of accepted data, and the service must resume within one hour. Backups exist but the team has never performed a full restore.

questions.title: Consider encryption-key recovery
questions.prompt: Backups are intact but the only decryption-key service is in the lost region. What follows?

choices.text: The recovery design has an unresolved critical dependency
choices.why: Encrypted bytes are not usable without authorized key recovery.
Encryption does not disappear during an outage.

choices.text: File checksums can reconstruct the key
choices.why: Integrity metadata is not a decryption capability.

choices.text: A higher replica count fixes authorization
choices.why: More ciphertext copies do not restore key access.

questions.explanation: Encrypted backup bytes are unusable if authorized decryption capability is unavailable after the same disaster. Key-service recovery therefore belongs in the end-to-end restoration dependency graph. The solution must preserve both recoverability and protection against unauthorized emergency access; copying ciphertext alone addresses neither issue.
questions.tradeoff: Key recoverability must be balanced against misuse and unauthorized disclosure.
questions.followup: Who can authorize emergency key access, and how is it audited?
questions.caseTitle: Restore the archive, not just the service
questions.context: Hypothetical archive: acknowledged documents must survive a single availability-zone loss. A regional disaster may lose at most five minutes of accepted data, and the service must resume within one hour. Backups exist but the team has never performed a full restore.

questions.title: Sequence a constrained restore
questions.prompt: The documented procedure requires keys before decrypting, decryption before importing, and import before validation. Put those four actions in required order.
questions.explanation: The procedure states a strict dependency chain: decryption needs authorized keys, import needs decrypted records, and validation needs an imported application state. That establishes one required order for these actions. Other preparation can run in parallel if it does not depend on their outputs.
questions.tradeoff: Independent preparation work may run concurrently outside this chain.
questions.followup: What parallel work would reduce elapsed recovery time without breaking dependencies?

items.text: Restore authorized key access
Decrypt the backup
Import recovered records
Validate the restored application

questions.caseTitle: Restore the archive, not just the service
questions.context: Hypothetical archive: acknowledged documents must survive a single availability-zone loss. A regional disaster may lose at most five minutes of accepted data, and the service must resume within one hour. Backups exist but the team has never performed a full restore.

questions.title: Own the cost decision
questions.prompt: Warm standby meets the target at a cost the business disputes. What is the staff-level decision process?

choices.text: Choose the cheapest design regardless of lost orders
choices.why: That ignores accepted business risk constraints.

choices.text: Compare measured recovery capabilities, outage impact, recurring cost and accountable risk acceptance
choices.why: The trade-off should be explicit and owned.

choices.text: Let one storage engineer silently relax the target
choices.why: An individual implementation choice should not rewrite the business promise.

choices.text: Assume the worst disaster cannot occur
choices.why: The requirement explicitly includes regional disaster.

questions.explanation: Warm standby is justified only relative to the outage impact and recovery objectives the business accepts. Compare measured recovery time, data-loss exposure, recurring cost and operational readiness, then name the risk owner. A cheaper design may be valid after an explicit contract change, not a silent engineering shortcut.
questions.tradeoff: A relaxed objective saves money but may increase outage loss.
questions.followup: How would you record the accepted risk and its review trigger?
questions.caseTitle: Restore the archive, not just the service
questions.context: Hypothetical archive: acknowledged documents must survive a single availability-zone loss. A regional disaster may lose at most five minutes of accepted data, and the service must resume within one hour. Backups exist but the team has never performed a full restore.

questions.title: Scoped lookup
questions.prompt: Which lookup enforces isolation?

choices.why: Knowing an ID is not authorization.

choices.text: Invoice ID within a server-authorized tenant scope
choices.why: Membership constrains the object lookup.

choices.text: Invoice ID plus an unchecked tenant header
choices.why: The caller controls the header.

choices.text: Invoice ID hidden by the interface
choices.why: Direct API calls bypass navigation.

questions.explanation: Bind object retrieval to verified membership, including cache hits. The invoice ID selects an object, while verified membership establishes the caller's authority over that object. Apply the same scope to list, export and cache delivery paths so an alternate endpoint cannot bypass the rule.
questions.tradeoff: Scoped caches can have lower hit rates.
questions.followup: How would delegated membership in two tenants work?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An authenticated SaaS user supplies an invoice ID. Random IDs are not secret. Every invoice stores tenant_id.

questions.title: Regression coverage
questions.prompt: Which tests expose horizontal escalation? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Request another tenant's known ID using a valid session
choices.why: This removes obscurity from the test.
That tests authentication, not object access.

choices.text: Submit mixed-tenant IDs to bulk export
choices.why: Bulk paths may bypass individual checks.
Entropy does not prove enforcement.

questions.explanation: Test both individual and bulk paths with valid but insufficient authority. Use an authenticated account from tenant A against an existing tenant B object, then assert no content or export is returned. This tests the actual authorization boundary instead of relying on an attacker not guessing an identifier.
questions.tradeoff: Policy matrices need updates as endpoints grow.
questions.followup: What checks must the export worker repeat?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An authenticated SaaS user supplies an invoice ID. Random IDs are not secret. Every invoice stores tenant_id.

questions.title: Policy outage
questions.prompt: Confidentiality is mandatory and authorization cannot be established. What should a read do?

choices.why: That expands authority during failure.

choices.text: Trust the last browser tenant header
choices.why: Untrusted state is not evidence.
This preserves confidentiality at an availability cost.
The cached object may be outside the caller's scope.

questions.explanation: An authorizer outage grants no new permission. When permission cannot be established, returning a confidential invoice would invent authority from missing evidence. A previously validated decision is usable only under a deliberately approved scope and freshness contract, not merely because something is cached.
questions.tradeoff: A bounded, scoped decision cache can improve availability.
questions.followup: Which data could safely use a different outage policy?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An authenticated SaaS user supplies an invoice ID. Random IDs are not secret. Every invoice stores tenant_id.

questions.title: Cache migration
questions.prompt: The cache keys by invoice ID, and its hit path returns the object without checking the caller's current authorization. Which change closes that unsafe reuse during migration?

choices.text: Enforce current object authorization on every hit; migrate scoped/versioned response keys and retire old entries
choices.why: Per-hit authorization closes the bypass. The key migration prevents already-authorized response variants from being confused across scopes.
Existing authorization errors remain.
Unsafe reuse lasts longer.

choices.text: Check policy only on cache fill
choices.why: Later callers can have different rights.

questions.explanation: The defect is returning a cache hit without current object authorization, not the invoice identifier alone. A shared object cache can be safe when every delivery enforces the caller's current permission. Scoped or versioned response keys help migrate authorization-dependent representations, but historical scope labels do not themselves enforce later membership revocation.
questions.tradeoff: Scope changes require invalidation or fresh checks.
questions.followup: How would membership revocation affect cached entries?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An authenticated SaaS user supplies an invoice ID. Random IDs are not secret. Every invoice stores tenant_id.

questions.title: Wrong audience
questions.prompt: What must billing check beyond signature and expiry?

choices.why: Subjects do not identify intended recipients.

choices.text: Validate only the user's current account status after signature verification
choices.why: Account status does not establish that this token was issued for the billing API.
They bind acceptance to billing.

choices.text: Accept any token from the corporate issuer and rely on endpoint role checks
choices.why: Endpoint roles are still necessary, but they do not replace audience and token-purpose validation.

questions.explanation: Trusted issuers can mint tokens for different services. A valid signature establishes that the expected issuer signed the bytes, but the issuer can legitimately serve several audiences. Billing must reject a token whose purpose belongs to support, even when the subject is a real employee.
questions.tradeoff: Strict claims require issuer-consumer coordination.
questions.followup: How would multiple audiences alter the risk?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Billing and support share signing keys. Billing must reject support-only tokens even if their signatures are valid.

questions.title: Algorithm policy
questions.prompt: Who defines accepted verification algorithms?

choices.why: The sender controls that header.
Received metadata can select only approved behavior.

choices.text: Allow any algorithm supported by the installed JWT library
choices.why: Library capability is broader than the verifier's intended trust policy and may include inappropriate algorithms.

choices.text: Choose verification keys from an arbitrary token-provided URL after confirming it uses HTTPS
choices.why: HTTPS protects transport to that URL but does not make the sender's chosen key source trustworthy.

questions.explanation: Token metadata must not create verification policy. Treat the token's algorithm and key identifiers as untrusted selection hints within a preconfigured allowlist. Otherwise a caller can steer verification toward a weaker algorithm or a key source that the service never intended to trust.
questions.tradeoff: Rotation needs bounded overlap and monitoring.
questions.followup: How would unknown key IDs be handled safely?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Billing and support share signing keys. Billing must reject support-only tokens even if their signatures are valid.

questions.title: Migration deadline
questions.prompt: Billing wrongly accepts support tokens today. Best migration?

choices.why: That removes authenticity.
That prolongs exposure.

choices.text: Change every client instantly without inventory
choices.why: Unknown legitimate consumers may fail.

choices.text: Inventory use, issue scoped tokens and enforce by a deadline
choices.why: Compatibility work leads to a defined security boundary.

questions.explanation: Observation is a migration aid, not permanent permission to accept wrong-purpose tokens. First identify legitimate callers and their token issuers, then give them a supported billing-scoped path. Set an enforcement deadline and monitor failures; a permanent compatibility exception would preserve the original security defect.
questions.tradeoff: The transition window retains risk.
questions.followup: How would evidence of active abuse change sequencing?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Billing and support share signing keys. Billing must reject support-only tokens even if their signatures are valid.

questions.title: Revocation bound
questions.prompt: Tokens live an hour, but revocation must take effect in 30 seconds. What changes?

choices.text: Bound effective validity or consult fresh revocation state
choices.why: Acceptance can reflect the required deadline.
A revoked token remains signed.
Encryption does not refresh authorization.

choices.text: Rotate all keys on each logout
choices.why: Global disruption is excessive for one user's revocation.

questions.explanation: Revocation is a freshness requirement, not just a format choice. The one-hour offline acceptance window contradicts a 30-second revocation promise unless another fresh check limits it. Design the failure policy of that check explicitly, because an unavailable revocation store must not silently extend sensitive access forever.
questions.tradeoff: Online checks introduce latency and dependency failure.
questions.followup: What happens if revocation state is partitioned?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Billing and support share signing keys. Billing must reject support-only tokens even if their signatures are valid.

questions.title: Constrain reachability
questions.prompt: What most directly protects internal services?

choices.text: Isolated egress plus destination validation at connection time
choices.why: Both routing and actual target are constrained.
TLS destinations can still be internal.
DNS and redirects can change the target.
Authenticated input remains untrusted.

questions.explanation: A preview URL is not authority to exercise internal connectivity. Validate the address actually contacted, including redirects and name resolution, while also preventing the worker from routing into protected networks. Either layer alone can be weakened by parser ambiguity, rebinding or an overlooked fetch path.
questions.tradeoff: Private integration previews need a separate explicit path.
questions.followup: How would you support a customer-owned private endpoint?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Preview workers fetch user URLs, follow redirects and can currently reach internal services.

questions.title: Every redirect matters
questions.prompt: Which controls remain necessary? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Treat approval of the first URL as authorization for every redirect hop
choices.why: A public endpoint can redirect internally.
Each hop changes the network action.
A public destination can exhaust resources.

choices.text: Bound redirect depth and fetched bytes
choices.why: This limits resource amplification.

questions.explanation: Destination safety and resource bounds solve separate failure modes. A redirect creates a new server-side request with a new destination and therefore a new policy decision. Independently bound bytes, duration and redirect depth so an otherwise allowed public endpoint cannot monopolize worker capacity.
questions.tradeoff: Restrictions may reduce preview compatibility.
questions.followup: Where can DNS rebinding break validate-then-connect?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Preview workers fetch user URLs, follow redirects and can currently reach internal services.

questions.title: Immediate containment
questions.prompt: Which migration most directly reduces current blast radius?

choices.text: First improve the URL parser while leaving unrestricted worker egress unchanged
choices.why: Parser hardening is useful, but an overlooked fetch path or parser mismatch still retains broad internal reachability.

choices.text: Move previews to a dedicated autoscaling group with the same network permissions
choices.why: Process separation does not remove unintended network authority.

choices.text: Constrain worker egress and monitor denials
choices.why: Risk is reduced while broken dependencies become visible.

choices.text: Reduce request timeout while preserving internal reachability
choices.why: A shorter timeout can limit resource consumption but still allows fast unauthorized internal requests.

questions.explanation: Change the fetcher's authority before optimizing throughput. Restricting egress removes unintended reachability even before every historical preview is cleaned up. Observe denied destinations to distinguish unsupported legitimate integrations from malicious or malformed input, then handle exceptions through explicit policy.
questions.tradeoff: Expect undocumented egress dependencies.
questions.followup: How would denied legitimate requests be triaged?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Preview workers fetch user URLs, follow redirects and can currently reach internal services.

questions.title: Worker identity
questions.prompt: Which credential scope fits?

choices.why: Parser compromise inherits unrelated power.
The risky boundary receives only necessary permissions.

choices.text: Whatever credentials are on the host
choices.why: Ambient authority defeats isolation.
A destination cannot grant local authority.

questions.explanation: Untrusted-content workers should not inherit business-administration permissions. A file parser or remote fetch can be compromised even when its caller is authenticated. Give that execution boundary only the identity and network rights required for previews so a local failure cannot become ledger or account administration.
questions.tradeoff: Separate identities increase operational configuration.
questions.followup: Which credentials can be removed entirely?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Preview workers fetch user URLs, follow redirects and can currently reach internal services.

questions.title: Rotation dependencies
questions.prompt: Order the mandatory stages. New access must work before switching clients, and old access remains until adoption is verified.

items.text: Create and verify the new credential.
Switch clients to the new credential.
Verify old-credential use has ended.
Revoke the old credential.

questions.explanation: Overlap bridges different refresh times; publication alone does not prove adoption. Creating the replacement first makes it possible to test before switching consumers. Verify adoption at the database connection boundary, not only in the secret manager, because established sessions can continue using old credentials after refresh.
questions.tradeoff: Long overlap preserves availability but increases exposure if old access leaks.
questions.followup: What deadline prevents one broken client blocking rotation forever?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A database accepts old and new credentials simultaneously. Clients refresh periodically; planned rotation should not interrupt traffic.

questions.title: Pool observation
questions.prompt: The secret changed but old sessions remain. What should you measure?

choices.why: It does not update existing connections.
Connection lifetime determines safe retirement.
Count does not show which credentials are active.
Capacity does not establish adoption.

questions.explanation: Configuration and authenticated connection state have separate lifecycles. A secret-manager update confirms publication, not client adoption or connection renewal. Track which credential authenticates live sessions, then drain or renew pools at a controlled rate before revoking the old credential.
questions.tradeoff: Abrupt pool draining can cause connection storms.
questions.followup: How would renewal be rate-limited?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A database accepts old and new credentials simultaneously. Clients refresh periodically; planned rotation should not interrupt traffic.

questions.title: Active compromise
questions.prompt: The old credential is being abused. What changes?

choices.why: Attacker access continues.
The database still accepts it.
That does not contain old access.

choices.text: Revoke compromised access and execute recovery
choices.why: Containment can justify interruption.

questions.explanation: The planned overlap assumed an uncompromised old credential. The availability objective of a planned rotation changes when an attacker is actively exercising the old authority. Contain the compromised credential promptly, scope affected actions and recover lagging legitimate clients through a tested replacement path.
questions.tradeoff: Emergency revocation may break lagging clients.
questions.followup: Which evidence determines the compromised scope?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A database accepts old and new credentials simultaneously. Clients refresh periodically; planned rotation should not interrupt traffic.

questions.title: Lifecycle ownership
questions.prompt: Which contract makes rotation operable?

choices.text: Refresh bounds, owners, adoption alerts and emergency revocation
choices.why: It makes completion and response accountable.

choices.text: Let each team rotate independently without a shared maximum refresh bound
choices.why: Autonomy alone does not establish when the old credential is safe to revoke.

choices.text: Require an annual audit but omit continuous adoption signals
choices.why: Periodic review cannot establish live completion during each rotation or emergency.

choices.text: Use one shared credential to reduce the number of rotations
choices.why: This simplifies inventory but couples unrelated services into a larger breach and rotation boundary.

questions.explanation: Automation still needs measurable adoption and accountable owners. Each service needs a maximum refresh delay, an adoption signal and a person or team responsible for failure. Without those bounds, one forgotten client can keep an old credential valid indefinitely despite nominally automated rotation.
questions.tradeoff: Granularity adds management work.
questions.followup: How would rotation be tested during a regional outage?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A database accepts old and new credentials simultaneously. Clients refresh periodically; planned rotation should not interrupt traffic.

questions.title: Useful evidence
questions.prompt: What is the best audit record?

choices.why: The index exposes reusable authority.
Individual actions cannot be reconstructed.

choices.text: Actor, action, resource reference, outcome and correlation ID
choices.why: It captures investigation structure without credentials.
Secrets add exposure, not useful evidence.

questions.explanation: Record decision context while minimizing sensitive payloads. The record should reconstruct the actor, target, action and outcome without becoming a second credential store. Keep sensitive identifiers minimal and resolve them through separately controlled systems when an investigation requires more detail.
questions.tradeoff: Pseudonymous IDs require controlled lookup.
questions.followup: Which fields deserve shorter retention?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Support staff search payment audit records, but must not receive credentials or payment-execution authority.

questions.title: Untrusted log fields
questions.prompt: Customer notes contain newlines. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Structured encoding with bounded field values
choices.why: Notes cannot forge separate event boundaries.
Newlines can impersonate records.
That loses attribution without fixing encoding.
Storage does not sanitize output.

questions.explanation: Logging is an output-encoding boundary. A note is untrusted even after it has passed through a database. Encode it as data in a structured record and bound its size; otherwise newlines or delimiters can make one user input appear to be several authoritative events.
questions.tradeoff: Viewers also need safe rendering.
questions.followup: How would you test ingestion and dashboard behavior together?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Support staff search payment audit records, but must not receive credentials or payment-execution authority.

questions.title: Slow audit sink
questions.prompt: Balance changes require durable evidence. What decouples indexing safely?

choices.text: Drop events when the sink slows
choices.why: Evidence is lost.

choices.text: Atomically persist action and audit outbox
choices.why: Evidence survives while indexing catches up.
A crash can erase committed-action evidence.
Neither state nor evidence is durable.

questions.explanation: Separate durable evidence from searchable presentation. Commit the business mutation and an audit intent within one durable local boundary, then index asynchronously. If the index is unavailable, evidence remains recoverable; if the durable backlog fills, the service needs an explicit admission policy.
questions.tradeoff: Backlog capacity and replay need ownership.
questions.followup: When should backlog stop new sensitive actions?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Support staff search payment audit records, but must not receive credentials or payment-execution authority.

questions.title: Support permissions
questions.prompt: Which change limits index compromise?

choices.text: One role for logs and money movement
choices.why: Read compromise becomes execution authority.
Leak usefulness increases.

choices.text: Different subnet with identical broad roles
choices.why: Authority remains excessive.

choices.text: Redacted read views and separately authorized actions
choices.why: Investigation access stays distinct.

questions.explanation: Permission separation matters beyond physical placement. A search-index compromise should expose only the approved investigative view, not reusable tokens or execution permissions. Separate escalation workflows preserve the ability to help customers while preventing ordinary support sessions from moving money.
questions.tradeoff: Redaction can reduce diagnostic detail.
questions.followup: How should break-glass access expire?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Support staff search payment audit records, but must not receive credentials or payment-execution authority.

questions.title: Forwarded URL
questions.prompt: What happens if a valid link is forwarded?

choices.why: No such check exists.

choices.text: The recipient may download until effective expiry
choices.why: The URL carries delegated authority.
A scoped request does not imply public listing.

choices.text: The signature vanishes after one use
choices.why: Single-use behavior was not specified.

questions.explanation: Capability possession is different from identity-bound access. The store validates the capability, not the human holding it. Forwarding therefore transfers usable authority for the remaining lifetime unless the architecture adds an identity check, a redemption state machine or another revocation-aware boundary.
questions.tradeoff: Links reduce proxy load but can leak.
questions.followup: How would one-time redemption be implemented?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Anyone holding a valid signed URL can download a report until effective expiry. The store does not consult browser sessions.

questions.title: Reduce delegation risk
questions.prompt: Which controls help? Select all that apply.

choices.why: This bounds delegated actions.
Logs distribute authority.

choices.text: Rely only on random object names
choices.why: Name secrecy does not bound leaked-link lifetime.

choices.text: Use short expiry and avoid referrer leakage
choices.why: This limits duration and disclosure.

questions.explanation: Scope, lifetime and handling protect different dimensions. Limit what the signature authorizes, how long it remains acceptable and where the resulting URL can leak. A private object name alone is insufficient once the complete URL appears in logs, browser history or a forwarded message.
questions.tradeoff: Short lifetimes can inconvenience delayed users.
questions.followup: How should fresh links be issued safely?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Anyone holding a valid signed URL can download a report until effective expiry. The store does not consult browser sessions.

questions.title: Immediate revocation
questions.prompt: New policy requires revocation within five seconds; links last an hour. Best redesign?

choices.text: Shorten links only when the user next requests a download
choices.why: Previously issued one-hour capabilities remain valid beyond the new revocation deadline.

choices.text: Invalidate the application's cached metadata on revocation
choices.why: The object store validates the URL independently and does not consult that application cache.

choices.text: Use revocation-aware delivery or sufficiently bounded capabilities
choices.why: Enforcement now reflects the required freshness.

choices.text: Refresh the object's storage encryption key once per day
choices.why: Daily key handling does not establish five-second per-user access revocation and may have much broader effects.

questions.explanation: Independent capability validity limits revocation promises. The longest independently accepted link bounds how quickly access can be withdrawn from that path. A five-second promise requires correspondingly bounded acceptance or a current authorization decision at delivery; changing a UI button cannot revoke copied URLs.
questions.tradeoff: A proxy adds bandwidth and dependency cost.
questions.followup: What happens to an in-progress range download?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Anyone holding a valid signed URL can download a report until effective expiry. The store does not consult browser sessions.

questions.title: CDN delivery
questions.prompt: What must edge caching preserve?

choices.text: Authorization on delivery and correct resource-version identity
choices.why: Cached bytes do not imply public permission.

choices.text: Origin checks on the first miss only
choices.why: Later callers can bypass authority checks.

choices.text: One response for all signed URLs
choices.why: Different resources may collide.

choices.text: Permanent authority because signatures are cryptographic
choices.why: Signatures still have temporal scope.

questions.explanation: Byte reuse and access decisions are distinct. An edge can reuse immutable bytes while still making a fresh access decision for each delivery. Specify cache identity and authorization separately so a cache hit does not bypass expiry, resource scope or a policy change.
questions.tradeoff: Edge policy adds key-management work.
questions.followup: How do old cache entries behave during policy migration?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Anyone holding a valid signed URL can download a report until effective expiry. The store does not consult browser sessions.

questions.title: Contain the parser
questions.prompt: Which permission model fits?

choices.text: Workload identity scoped to export reads
choices.why: Compromise stays within granted operations.
Network presence is not business permission.
Parsing compromise becomes administration.

choices.text: Remove authentication behind the load balancer
choices.why: Caller identity disappears.

questions.explanation: Bind authority to workload and operation, not location. A parser handling hostile files is a distinct risk boundary even inside a private network. Authenticate its workload and authorize only export reads; subnet membership or a shared administrator credential would unnecessarily expand a compromise.
questions.tradeoff: Identity lifecycle requires management.
questions.followup: What if unrelated jobs share a host?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A report parser needs ledger-export reads but never ledger writes. It processes untrusted files.

questions.title: Mutual TLS limit
questions.prompt: A valid client certificate establishes identity. What still remains?

choices.why: Encryption does not decide allowed operations.
Identity is not universal permission.
The action must fit identity scope.
Sizes do not encode business rights.

questions.explanation: Transport identity and action authorization solve different questions. A certificate proves the peer controls an approved identity under the transport policy. The API must still map that identity to allowed ledger actions, and decide how certificate or permission revocation affects existing connections.
questions.tradeoff: Policy freshness must be explicit.
questions.followup: What is the revocation bound for an open connection?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A report parser needs ledger-export reads but never ledger writes. It processes untrusted files.

questions.title: Legacy migration
questions.prompt: Hundreds of internal clients lack distinct identities. Best approach?

choices.why: Unknown dependencies can fail unpredictably.

choices.text: Inventory calls, issue identities, then enforce progressively
choices.why: The migration narrows authority with compatibility evidence.

choices.text: Rename subnet trust as zero trust
choices.why: Labels do not change enforcement.
Callers remain indistinguishable.

questions.explanation: Migration requires both desired policy and evidence about use. Inventory actual call paths and issue identities that map to those uses before narrowing enforcement. Keep observation windows finite, since compatibility work should lead toward scoped authority rather than become a permanent reason to trust the whole subnet.
questions.tradeoff: Observation windows retain risk and need deadlines.
questions.followup: Which clients should migrate first?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A report parser needs ledger-export reads but never ledger writes. It processes untrusted files.

questions.title: Policy blast radius
questions.prompt: How can a central policy rollout be contained?

choices.why: A mistake spreads instantly.
Failure becomes an authorization bypass.
Effects become harder to detect.

choices.text: Version policies, stage cohorts and test rollback
choices.why: Errors can be discovered before broad exposure.

questions.explanation: Centralized policy also centralizes mistakes. A central policy service can distribute one mistake to every tenant unless rollout has containment. Use versions and representative cohorts, observe denied and unexpectedly allowed actions, and retain a compatible recovery version.
questions.tradeoff: Staging temporarily runs multiple versions.
questions.followup: How can a valid but overpermissive policy be detected?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A report parser needs ledger-export reads but never ledger writes. It processes untrusted files.

questions.title: Replay evidence
questions.prompt: What identifies reuse after successful rotation?

choices.why: Names do not establish lineage.

choices.text: A consumed token appears again in its family
choices.why: Durable state records prior consumption.
That does not show refresh reuse.
Size is not replay evidence.

questions.explanation: Rotation history provides evidence unavailable from an isolated token. The server can compare a presented token against durable family history and recognize that it has already been consumed. That is evidence of reuse, but distinguishing theft from a lost-response retry needs a documented policy and additional context.
questions.tradeoff: Legitimate lost-response retries need a policy.
questions.followup: How would replay differ from a safe retry?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A mobile service records refresh-token families and consumes each refresh token when issuing its replacement.

questions.title: Client refresh race
questions.prompt: Two features refresh simultaneously. Best client design?

choices.why: Chains can diverge.
Contention increases.

choices.text: Save tokens in analytics for recovery
choices.why: Credentials leak.

choices.text: One token manager sharing an in-flight refresh
choices.why: Concurrent callers coordinate one state transition.

questions.explanation: Client concurrency can create accidental consumed-token reuse. A shared token manager prevents two features from independently advancing the same credential chain. It should coordinate refresh results and failures, while server-side handling remains necessary for multiple devices, process restarts and uncertain responses.
questions.tradeoff: Multiple devices still require server-side policy.
questions.followup: How should a failed refresh reach waiting requests?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A mobile service records refresh-token families and consumes each refresh token when issuing its replacement.

questions.title: Confirmed theft
questions.prompt: What is targeted containment for one compromised family?

choices.text: Revoke the affected grant and require reauthentication
choices.why: The compromised lineage loses authority.
The scope exceeds the evidence.

choices.text: Ignore it because access tokens are short
choices.why: Refresh authority can mint new tokens.
Exposure lasts longer.

questions.explanation: Containment scope should follow evidence. Revoke the authority linked to the compromised family and require a fresh authenticated grant. Escalate to broader revocation only when evidence suggests wider exposure; global key rotation for one family would disrupt unrelated users.
questions.tradeoff: Legitimate users may be interrupted.
questions.followup: When is broader revocation justified?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A mobile service records refresh-token families and consumes each refresh token when issuing its replacement.

questions.title: Offline contradiction
questions.prompt: Product demands 90-day offline access with immediate remote revocation. What is true?

choices.text: Use encrypted tokens with a revocation timestamp embedded at issuance
choices.why: A timestamp written before revocation cannot communicate a later remote decision to an offline device.

choices.text: Maintain an authoritative server-side denylist while allowing all offline verification
choices.why: The denylist is not consulted while the verifier is disconnected.

choices.text: The requirements conflict without trusted contact
choices.why: A remote change cannot instantly reach an offline verifier.

choices.text: Rotate the server's signing key immediately on revocation, without requiring clients to reconnect
choices.why: An offline device retaining the old verification key cannot learn the rotation immediately.

questions.explanation: Identify the freshness conflict before choosing token format. A disconnected verifier cannot learn that a remote administrator has changed the user's permissions. The product must choose an offline validity bound, require contact for sensitive actions, or explicitly accept delayed revocation rather than promise incompatible guarantees.
questions.tradeoff: Relax offline duration or revocation delay explicitly.
questions.followup: Which operations can remain offline safely?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A mobile service records refresh-token families and consumes each refresh token when issuing its replacement.

questions.title: Promise boundary
questions.prompt: What must the workflow cover?

choices.why: Derived copies can still serve data.
Underlying data stays reachable.

choices.text: Identified serving copies and their completion states
choices.why: The promise spans actual retrieval paths.
Older content remains in scope.

questions.explanation: Deletion is a data-reachability promise, not one command. List every active serving copy and make completion depend on evidence from those stores. Removing the authoritative row does not stop a search index, export file or cache from returning content that it already holds.
questions.tradeoff: Copy inventories must evolve with architecture.
questions.followup: How does a new sink join the contract?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. The product promises deletion from active serving systems within 24 hours. Search, caches and analytics hold copies. Backup retention is separately disclosed; this is a product scenario, not legal advice.

questions.title: Late creation event
questions.prompt: What prevents old events resurrecting deleted content?

choices.text: A durable deletion or version fence
choices.why: Consumers can reject obsolete creation state.
That recreates content.
Late consumers lose their fence.
That guarantee was not given.

questions.explanation: Deletion intent must survive replay. A replayed creation event must be judged against current deletion intent, not just its original event type. Retain a version fence or tombstone long enough to cover replay and recovery windows so delayed work cannot recreate eligible content.

questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. The product promises deletion from active serving systems within 24 hours. Search, caches and analytics hold copies. Backup retention is separately disclosed; this is a product scenario, not legal advice.

questions.title: Completion evidence
questions.prompt: Which metric supports the 24-hour promise?

choices.why: Acceptance is not completion.

choices.text: Per-sink completion and oldest unresolved age
choices.why: This reveals both propagation and deadline risk.
It says nothing about derived copies.
Growth masks individual deletion state.

questions.explanation: Report pending and unknown separately from completed. A deletion request can be accepted while one sink remains pending or unreachable. Track that uncertainty explicitly and alert on the oldest unresolved deadline rather than reporting completion from the initial API response.
questions.tradeoff: Fine-grained evidence adds metadata cost.

questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. The product promises deletion from active serving systems within 24 hours. Search, caches and analytics hold copies. Backup retention is separately disclosed; this is a product scenario, not legal advice.

questions.title: Backup restore
questions.prompt: What must happen before restored data serves traffic?

choices.why: Deleted content may return.
Restore does not cancel user intent.
Names do not change content.

choices.text: Reapply deletion state and verify eligibility
choices.why: Historical restoration respects subsequent intent.

questions.explanation: Data recovery must not silently rewind deletion decisions. A backup represents historical data, but a later deletion remains a current obligation. Reapply the relevant deletion state before exposing restored records, and include this validation time in the recovery plan.
questions.tradeoff: Verification adds recovery time.
questions.followup: How would recovery and deletion deadlines be balanced?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. The product promises deletion from active serving systems within 24 hours. Search, caches and analytics hold copies. Backup retention is separately disclosed; this is a product scenario, not legal advice.

questions.title: Read versus act

choices.why: Direct callers bypass it.

choices.text: Distinct backend permissions for reads and actions
choices.why: Investigation sessions lack movement authority.
Callers approve themselves.
Secrecy is not permission.

questions.explanation: The API must distinguish investigation and execution authority. The backend needs an operation-level distinction between viewing an account and changing money state. questions.title: Evidence fields

choices.why: These connect permission to execution.
Secrets are not audit evidence.
Reviewers can compare approval with action.
Individual unauthorized actions cannot be traced.

questions.explanation: Capture authority context without reusable secrets. Link the executed action to who approved which target, amount and scope. This allows review to identify a mismatch between approval and effect without storing a password or another credential in the audit system.

questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Support can investigate accounts. Money movement requires separately approved scope, reason and a durable audit trail.

questions.title: Emergency workflow
questions.prompt: Which break-glass design fits?

choices.why: Emergency access becomes ordinary.
High-risk actions become untraceable.
Attribution and containment weaken.

choices.text: Scoped time-limited escalation with audit and review
choices.why: Emergency authority stays exceptional.

questions.explanation: Relax deliberate gates without erasing identity or accountability. Emergency access should have an explicit identity, purpose, scope and expiry even if normal approval steps must be relaxed. Durable evidence and later review preserve accountability while a rehearsed path keeps response time practical.
questions.tradeoff: Controls can slow response; rehearse them.
questions.followup: What if the normal approval service fails?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. Support can investigate accounts. Money movement requires separately approved scope, reason and a durable audit trail.

questions.title: Integration ownership
questions.prompt: A new internal tool calls the money API. Who verifies authorization compatibility?

choices.text: Both owners, with invariants enforced by the money API
choices.why: The authority boundary remains with the service.

choices.text: The tool team alone, because it owns the user experience
choices.why: The money API still needs to reject unauthorized direct calls even if the tool normally constructs safe requests.

choices.text: The network team alone, because the tool is on a private subnet
choices.why: Reachability controls do not establish which money operations a support identity may perform.

choices.text: The existing service contract can be reused without testing because the caller is internal
choices.why: A new caller may exercise assumptions about role, scope or request construction that older integrations never tested.

questions.explanation: Shared contracts need accountable enforcement and adversarial integration tests. Tool and service owners should agree on the contract and test malicious-but-authenticated requests, because internal origin does not make arguments trustworthy.
questions.tradeoff: Coordination adds release work.

questions.title: A durable commit with an old page
questions.prompt: The commit log is durable but its modified data page was not flushed before a crash. What enables recovery?

choices.why: That violates the acknowledgment contract.

choices.text: Replaying the durable log into the page
choices.why: Redo reconstructs the committed change.
Process memory is lost in the failure model.

choices.text: Waiting for the original client to resend
choices.why: Recovery must not depend on every client retrying.

questions.explanation: The commit's required log prefix survived, so recovery has authoritative evidence of the change even though the data page is older. Redo applies that evidence to reconstruct the committed state. This depends on the stated flush durability and correct replay rules; it does not assume process memory survived.
questions.tradeoff: Longer redo history can increase restart time.
questions.followup: What limits the amount of replay needed?

questions.context: Hypothetical transactional storage engine uses write-ahead logging and redo recovery. Acknowledged commits require the commit record and its preceding log records to be durably flushed. Data pages may be flushed later. The storage device honors successful flush requests.

questions.title: An unsafe flush order
questions.prompt: Why must a changed page not reach durable storage before its required log records?

choices.text: WAL requires all changed data pages to be written in transaction order
choices.why: The central requirement is that a page's recovery log becomes durable before the page change, not a global data-page write order.

choices.text: The database would lose all read concurrency
choices.why: That is not the ordering issue.

choices.text: Recovery could encounter a page change without the log needed to interpret or recover it
choices.why: The write-ahead invariant would be broken.

choices.text: Every page must be flushed on every commit
choices.why: WAL specifically permits deferred page flushing.

questions.explanation: If a changed page becomes durable before the log describing it, recovery can encounter an effect without the evidence needed to reconstruct a valid database state. WAL prevents that ordering. It does not require every changed page to be flushed at commit, which is a major source of its performance benefit.
questions.tradeoff: Enforcing durable ordering incurs I/O barriers.
questions.followup: How would a torn-page protection mechanism complement WAL?

questions.title: Group commit
questions.prompt: Why can several transactions share one log flush without weakening the stated guarantee?

choices.text: One flush can durably cover all of their complete commit records
choices.why: Each acknowledged transaction's required bytes are included.
Their atomicity boundaries need not merge.

choices.text: Only the first transaction needs durable state
choices.why: Every acknowledged transaction still needs coverage.

choices.text: One shared flush makes the transactions a single rollback unit
choices.why: Persistence batching need not merge the separate transactions' logical atomicity boundaries.

questions.explanation: One durable flush can cover several complete commit records and all log bytes they depend on. Each transaction is acknowledged only after its own record falls within that durable prefix, so individual transaction boundaries remain intact. The batching delay trades some latency for fewer persistence operations.
questions.tradeoff: Waiting briefly for a batch can add latency.

questions.title: A missing durable acknowledgment
questions.prompt: A response was sent before the flush completed, then power failed. What claim is invalid?

choices.text: Some unacknowledged work may be lost
choices.why: That can be allowed by the contract.

choices.text: Recovered pages can be older than committed log records
choices.why: Redo can repair that.

choices.text: Group commit can reduce flush operations
choices.why: That remains true.
The response preceded the required durability boundary.

questions.explanation: The response told the client its transaction was durable before the storage system established that fact. Power loss in this window can erase acknowledged work. An asynchronous durability mode may intentionally permit such loss, but then the API must advertise that weaker guarantee rather than claim the original contract.
questions.tradeoff: Asynchronous acknowledgment may be legitimate only with an explicit loss window.

questions.title: Recovery validation
questions.prompt: Which tests challenge crash durability? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Crash immediately before and after log flush completion
choices.why: This probes the acknowledgment boundary.

choices.text: Crash after log flush but before data-page flush
choices.why: This exercises redo.
A clean shutdown avoids important crash windows.

choices.text: Verify recovered business invariants, not just process startup
choices.why: Successful startup alone does not prove data correctness.

questions.explanation: Crash tests need to interrupt the exact persistence boundaries that normal shutdown avoids. Verify acknowledged business effects after restart, including the log-durable/page-stale case that requires redo. Process startup alone is insufficient, and a process kill may not reproduce loss of volatile device or operating-system buffers.
questions.tradeoff: Realistic power-loss tests are harder than process termination tests.
questions.followup: How would you simulate a device that lies about flush completion?

questions.title: Choose checkpoint cadence
questions.prompt: What is the staff-level trade-off in more frequent checkpoints?

choices.text: They remove the need for commit durability
choices.why: Commits still require the stated log boundary.

choices.text: They can reduce recovery work while increasing background I/O pressure
choices.why: Recovery objectives compete with steady-state resource cost.
Restart still performs work.

choices.text: They eliminate the need to retain any log needed by replicas or backups
choices.why: Checkpointing local pages does not automatically satisfy independent replication or recovery retention obligations.

questions.explanation: More frequent checkpoints can leave less work for crash recovery, but their page writes consume I/O while foreground traffic is running. Choose cadence using measured restart time and steady-state tail latency, not only log size. A recovery objective that passes under idle load may fail during peak ingestion.
questions.tradeoff: Aggressive flushing can harm foreground tail latency.
questions.followup: How would you demonstrate the recovery target under peak write load?

questions.title: Replication is a separate promise
questions.prompt: Local WAL is durable. What extra evidence is needed to survive complete loss of this node?

choices.text: A second database process reading the same local disk
choices.why: Both processes lose the same storage if the entire node is destroyed.
All local storage may be lost.

choices.text: A recoverable copy outside the failed node under the required acknowledgment policy
choices.why: Local durability is not remote durability.

choices.text: Only a successful TCP connection to a replica
choices.why: Connection establishment does not prove replicated commit state.

questions.explanation: Local WAL protects against failures for which that durable local storage remains recoverable. Complete loss of the node requires another copy outside the failed domain and an acknowledgment policy that establishes it in time. A connected replica or a later asynchronous transfer does not prove every acknowledged commit survived.
questions.tradeoff: Synchronous remote persistence increases commit latency.

questions.title: Interpret growing level zero
questions.prompt: What does a sustained increase in overlapping level-zero files suggest?

choices.why: New files can be driven by ongoing writes.

choices.text: Flush output is outrunning downstream compaction
choices.why: The background merge pipeline is falling behind.

choices.text: Every read is necessarily served from memory
choices.why: Disk files may still need checking.

choices.text: Compaction has removed every obsolete version
choices.why: Accumulating files suggest unfinished maintenance.

questions.explanation: Flushing memory buffers creates sorted files faster than compaction can merge them, so unfinished maintenance accumulates. Increasing buffers can absorb a short burst but cannot fix a sustained rate mismatch. Track pending bytes, file counts and stall thresholds to estimate how much time remains before ingestion is constrained.
questions.tradeoff: Larger buffers can absorb bursts but not an indefinite rate mismatch.
questions.followup: How would you estimate time until write stalls?

questions.title: Negative lookup optimization
questions.prompt: What can a correctly constructed Bloom filter safely establish?

choices.text: That a positive result guarantees the value exists
choices.why: False positives are allowed.
The filter does not store values.

choices.text: That a negative result excludes the key from that filtered set
choices.why: This can skip unnecessary file reads.

choices.text: That tombstones are no longer needed
choices.why: Deletion correctness depends on older versions and snapshots.

questions.explanation: A correctly built Bloom filter can rule out membership in its associated set, allowing the engine to skip a file that cannot contain the key. A positive result is only a candidate and still requires lookup. Its usefulness depends on absent-key frequency and the memory allocated to reduce false positives.
questions.tradeoff: More filter memory reduces false positives but consumes cache capacity.

questions.title: Why not drop every tombstone?
questions.prompt: Why can removing a deletion marker while an older value remains resurrect data?

choices.text: The older value can become visible again without its suppressing marker
choices.why: The marker encodes a newer deletion.

choices.text: Deletion markers are the only index entries
choices.why: Indexes can contain ordinary values too.

choices.text: A delete always removes all historical files instantly
choices.why: LSM deletion is often deferred.
Version metadata is essential to compaction decisions.

questions.explanation: A deletion marker is a newer logical fact that suppresses an older stored value. If compaction removes the marker while the older value remains reachable, a later lookup can treat that value as current again. Snapshot, replication and file-coverage rules determine when both historical states can safely be reclaimed.

questions.title: Recovery boundary
questions.prompt: What must a consistent checkpoint associate?
questions.explanation: Recovery needs a coherent cut of input progress and state. State from one point combined with offsets from another can either skip unapplied input or replay input already included in the restored state.
