questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A single register initially contains zero. Writes and reads record invocation and completion times. The contract is linearizability, not eventual consistency.

questions.title: Useful property
questions.prompt: Which property should hold after every accepted transition?

choices.text: The number of API calls equals the number of reservations
choices.why: Retries make that false legitimately.

choices.text: Available stock decreases on every request
choices.why: Release and duplicate operations differ.

choices.text: Stock conservation and at most one terminal outcome per reservation
choices.why: These express business invariants across sequences.
Conflicting or stale commands should fail.

questions.explanation: Properties describe legal state across many operation sequences. Checking only one response misses corruption that emerges after a later release or retry. Assert the invariant after retries and rejected commands as well as successful ones, because error handling can corrupt state even when the API returns failure.
questions.tradeoff: The model must encode legitimate adjustments such as restocking.
questions.followup: How would refunds or partial reservations extend the invariant?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An inventory API supports reserve, confirm, release and expire. Duplicate requests and reordered messages are allowed. A reference model tracks each reservation and available stock.

questions.title: Why generate sequences
questions.prompt: What can stateful generation find beyond isolated input tests?

choices.text: Interactions such as expire, late confirm and duplicate release
choices.why: Correctness depends on prior state and event order.

choices.text: An exhaustive proof over all possible production schedules
choices.why: Generated sequences remain bounded by the model, examples and execution budget.

choices.text: Only larger samples of isolated request payloads
choices.why: Stateful generation additionally explores the interactions between actions and prior state.

choices.text: Automatic validation of network and storage failure semantics without modeling them
choices.why: The test can explore only behavior represented by its model or exercised by its environment.

questions.explanation: An action can be correct alone and wrong after another action. Generated sequences explore those combinations and can shrink a failure to a small example. Generate identifiers that refer to earlier operations so later actions can interact with real model state, rather than sampling mostly unrelated requests that rarely collide.
questions.tradeoff: Longer sequences expand search cost.
questions.followup: Which actions should reuse previously generated reservation IDs?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An inventory API supports reserve, confirm, release and expire. Duplicate requests and reordered messages are allowed. A reference model tracks each reservation and available stock.

questions.title: Independent oracle
questions.prompt: Why avoid copying the production transition code into the reference model?

choices.why: Executable models can be useful.

choices.text: The same defect can appear in both implementations
choices.why: Agreement would then provide weak evidence.
Simplicity is usually more important.

choices.text: Models should always use random outputs
choices.why: That removes a meaningful oracle.

questions.explanation: A simpler independently expressed specification reduces correlated mistakes. Review the model's invariants separately from implementation details. Use a deliberately simpler representation, such as integer quantities and explicit states, and validate representative examples manually before trusting model agreement as meaningful evidence.
questions.tradeoff: Independent modeling takes thought and can still contain errors.
questions.followup: How would reviewers validate the oracle itself?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An inventory API supports reserve, confirm, release and expire. Duplicate requests and reordered messages are allowed. A reference model tracks each reservation and available stock.

questions.title: Shrunk counterexample
questions.prompt: The tool finds a three-action sequence causing extra stock. What is the best response?

choices.text: Discard it because it is synthetic
choices.why: Synthetic schedules can represent valid executions.

choices.text: Increase random seeds until the failure disappears
choices.why: That hides evidence.

choices.text: Fix only the test expectation to match production
choices.why: The invariant may still be broken.

choices.text: Turn it into a deterministic regression and repair the violated transition
choices.why: The minimal history becomes durable evidence.

questions.explanation: Preserve both the failing sequence and its invariant. After repair, retain broader generation because another schedule may reach the same flaw differently. Add the minimal failing sequence to routine tests and retain its original invariant, so future refactors cannot accidentally redefine success to match the broken behavior.
questions.tradeoff: Regression suites grow and need maintenance.
questions.followup: How would you verify the fix under concurrent rather than sequential execution?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. An inventory API supports reserve, confirm, release and expire. Duplicate requests and reordered messages are allowed. A reference model tracks each reservation and available stock.

questions.title: Experiment definition
questions.prompt: What should be written before injection?

choices.why: The result would be hard to interpret.

choices.text: Steady-state measure, expected outcome, scope and abort conditions
choices.why: The experiment has a falsifiable and bounded purpose.

choices.text: A promise that no error can happen
choices.why: Testing examines that assumption.

choices.text: A list of unrelated future features
choices.why: It does not define resilience evidence.

questions.explanation: A fault injection is useful when it tests a stated hypothesis. The measurement must reflect user behavior, not merely whether a process restarted. Confirm that the selected metric would reveal the failure you care about, and rehearse the stop mechanism before an experiment can affect real customer traffic.
questions.tradeoff: Tighter guardrails can stop experiments before long recovery behavior is observed.
questions.followup: Which user metric should trigger immediate abort?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A replicated read service claims it can lose one replica without breaching its user SLO. A team wants to test that claim on a small production cohort.

questions.title: Injection scope
questions.prompt: Which first experiment has the smallest justified blast radius?

choices.text: Lose one selected replica in a controlled cohort with recovery ready
choices.why: It matches the one-replica hypothesis.
That tests a different and much riskier claim.
That is not the read-replica hypothesis.
That introduces unrelated security risk.

questions.explanation: Match the fault to the claim under test. Start with an interpretable scope before increasing combination and duration complexity. Verify the target cohort and dependency reachability before injection, because a supposedly local replica may still host shared work whose impact exceeds the intended scope.
questions.tradeoff: Small cohorts may not expose fleet-wide correlated effects.
questions.followup: What evidence supports widening the next experiment?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A replicated read service claims it can lose one replica without breaching its user SLO. A team wants to test that claim on a small production cohort.

questions.title: Unexpected degradation
questions.prompt: The cohort breaches its abort threshold. What is the correct immediate action?

choices.text: Continue until the planned duration ends
choices.why: The agreed safety boundary has been crossed.

choices.text: Change the threshold during the run
choices.why: That invalidates the protection policy.

choices.text: Stop the injection and execute the recovery plan
choices.why: Contain harm while preserving observations.

choices.text: Delete experiment logs to reduce noise
choices.why: That loses diagnostic evidence.

questions.explanation: The abort condition is an operational commitment, not an optional suggestion. Recovery and data capture should be prepared before injection begins. Capture enough timing and state evidence during containment to explain the failure later, but do not prolong customer harm merely to obtain a cleaner experiment.
questions.tradeoff: Stopping early may leave the deeper failure mechanism unresolved.
questions.followup: How would you reproduce the failure safely outside the affected cohort?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A replicated read service claims it can lose one replica without breaching its user SLO. A team wants to test that claim on a small production cohort.

questions.title: Interpret the result
questions.prompt: A successful one-replica experiment proves what?

choices.text: The system survives every regional disaster
choices.why: The fault scope is much narrower.
Code and topology can change.

choices.text: The service has no hidden dependencies
choices.why: The experiment may not exercise them.

choices.text: The observed version and workload met the hypothesis for that fault scope
choices.why: The claim remains bounded by tested conditions.

questions.explanation: Record configuration, traffic and duration alongside the result. Re-run when changes invalidate the original assumptions. Repeat or revise the experiment when deployment topology, replica count or critical dependencies change, since those changes can invalidate the assumptions behind the earlier result.
questions.tradeoff: Repeated experiments have real cost and risk.
questions.followup: Which architecture changes should trigger a new resilience test?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A replicated read service claims it can lose one replica without breaching its user SLO. A team wants to test that claim on a small production cohort.

questions.title: Measurement blind spot
questions.prompt: What demand can the report omit?

choices.why: Those are still recorded.
Errors depend on instrumentation.

choices.text: Requests that would have arrived during the stall under an external arrival process
choices.why: The generator suppresses those arrivals.

choices.text: The size of the response body by definition
choices.why: Body measurement is separate.

questions.explanation: The observed distribution reflects the generator's feedback loop. It may underrepresent waiting experienced by a fixed-rate external population. Document which requests were never emitted and how that relates to the modeled user population, rather than correcting a histogram without understanding the intended arrival process.
questions.tradeoff: Closed-loop tests remain appropriate for some user models.
questions.followup: Which real workload naturally slows its own arrivals after latency rises?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A load generator submits the next request only after the previous response. During a two-second stall it sends no new requests, then reports latency only for requests it sent.

questions.title: Workload specification
questions.prompt: Which detail is essential for interpreting the result?

choices.text: Whether arrivals are open-loop, closed-loop or a stated mixture
choices.why: It defines the demand process behind latency.

choices.text: Only the load generator's hardware specification
choices.why: Hardware affects achieved load but does not define whether arrivals stop during slow responses.
It identifies code, not the arrival process behind the latency measurement.

choices.text: Only the maximum configured virtual-user count
choices.why: A user count does not reveal pacing, concurrency or whether offered load changes with latency.

questions.explanation: A latency number without its arrival model is incomplete. Describe how offered load changes when the system becomes slow. Describe payload and key distributions alongside arrival timing, because two generators at the same nominal rate can create very different contention and cache behavior.
questions.tradeoff: Real populations can mix feedback and independent arrivals.
questions.followup: How would retries modify the offered workload?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A load generator submits the next request only after the previous response. During a two-second stall it sends no new requests, then reports latency only for requests it sent.

questions.title: Safer stress test
questions.prompt: What should accompany an open-loop test beyond expected capacity?

choices.text: Unbounded generator queues with no stop condition
choices.why: The test can harm shared systems indefinitely.

choices.text: Rate limits, abort thresholds and complete error/backlog accounting
choices.why: The experiment remains bounded and interpretable.
Dropped and timed-out work would disappear.

choices.text: A rule to ignore downstream effects
choices.why: Shared dependencies may be the actual bottleneck.

questions.explanation: Fixed offered load can expose overload behavior but also cause real damage. Count rejected, queued and completed work so lower latency from rejection is not mistaken for improvement. Track server work that continues after caller timeout, since the generator can report failures while those abandoned requests still consume capacity and delay useful work.
questions.tradeoff: Safety limits bound what the experiment can demonstrate.
questions.followup: How would you isolate the test from customer-facing dependencies?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A load generator submits the next request only after the previous response. During a two-second stall it sends no new requests, then reports latency only for requests it sent.

questions.title: Capacity conclusion
questions.prompt: What qualifies a reported sustainable throughput?

choices.text: Maximum generated requests regardless of errors
choices.why: Generated demand is not successful capacity.
It may be a short transient.
Skew and payloads affect resource use.

choices.text: A sustained rate meeting stated latency, success and resource constraints
choices.why: The operating envelope is explicit.

questions.explanation: Capacity is conditional on workload and quality objectives. Include duration, headroom and failure assumptions so the number can guide deployment decisions. Measure sustained operation and recovery after a burst, not only the instant before queues begin growing, and state which resource limit ends the safe envelope.
questions.tradeoff: Conservative headroom leaves some resources unused.
questions.followup: How would losing one availability zone change the safe rate?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A load generator submits the next request only after the previous response. During a two-second stall it sends no new requests, then reports latency only for requests it sent.

questions.title: Relevant compatibility test
questions.prompt: Which test directly addresses the supported client contract?

choices.why: They may not encode old client expectations.

choices.text: Provider verification against the old client's actual contract
choices.why: It tests the promises that consumer relies on.

choices.text: Only a new client talking to a new server
choices.why: Mixed supported versions remain untested.
Equal size does not imply compatible meaning.

questions.explanation: Test the consumer's required interactions, not an imagined ideal API. Keep the contract tied to supported versions and meaningful semantics. Verify both ordinary and error responses that the supported client actually handles, including field meaning and missing-value behavior rather than just transport status or JSON syntax.
questions.tradeoff: Too-broad contracts can block harmless provider changes.
questions.followup: Which optional fields should an old client tolerate?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A mobile client expects an API field to contain a currency code and handles two documented error shapes. Backend unit tests pass, but an old mobile release remains supported.

questions.title: Contract test limit
questions.prompt: What does a passing contract test not establish by itself?

choices.text: That the tested response shape is accepted by the verifier
choices.why: That is within the test boundary.

choices.text: That the example interaction matches the contract
choices.why: That is the purpose of the check.

choices.text: Production capacity and multi-service recovery behavior
choices.why: Those require different tests.

choices.text: That the contract file can be parsed
choices.why: Parsing is part of normal verification.

questions.explanation: Compatibility tests protect an interface slice. They do not replace load, security or full workflow tests merely because they cross a service boundary. Pair the contract gate with focused workflow and operational tests, selecting each layer for the failure it can detect rather than duplicating the same happy-path assertion.
questions.tradeoff: Multiple test layers increase cost but address different risks.
questions.followup: Which end-to-end test complements this contract most efficiently?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A mobile client expects an API field to contain a currency code and handles two documented error shapes. Backend unit tests pass, but an old mobile release remains supported.

questions.title: Semantic change
questions.prompt: The field stays a string but now contains a localized currency name. What should catch this?

choices.text: A semantic contract assertion for the documented code format
choices.why: Type-only checks miss the meaning change.
Both representations are valid strings.
Transport success says nothing about field meaning.
Lifecycle testing does not validate this contract.

questions.explanation: Schema compatibility can be weaker than business compatibility. Encode the assumptions the client actually uses, such as standardized code values. Choose assertions broad enough to admit new valid standardized codes but narrow enough to reject localized names, preserving extensibility without discarding the field's documented meaning.
questions.tradeoff: Overfitting exact example text can make contracts brittle.
questions.followup: How would you permit new valid currency codes without listing all values?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A mobile client expects an API field to contain a currency code and handles two documented error shapes. Backend unit tests pass, but an old mobile release remains supported.

questions.title: Retiring an old contract
questions.prompt: What permits removing the old mobile contract from release gates?

choices.why: Users may not have upgraded.

choices.text: The backend team prefers a cleaner schema
choices.why: Consumer support obligations remain.
Rare users and offline devices can return.

choices.text: An explicit support policy and evidence that the version is no longer supported
choices.why: Retirement follows the external commitment.

questions.explanation: A contract's lifetime follows the client support window. Plan deprecation communication and fallback behavior before dropping compatibility. Make the support boundary visible to product and client teams, because removing a release gate is a user-compatibility decision rather than only a backend test cleanup.
questions.tradeoff: Long-lived clients increase testing and maintenance cost.
questions.followup: How would forced-upgrade policy affect critical offline functionality?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A mobile client expects an API field to contain a currency code and handles two documented error shapes. Backend unit tests pass, but an old mobile release remains supported.

questions.title: Count limitation
questions.prompt: What can equal counts fail to detect?

choices.text: Different values, one missing plus one extra row, or stale deletions
choices.why: Cardinality does not establish set equality.
Counts can reflect insertions.
That is not the relevant correctness property.
Content can differ substantially.

questions.explanation: Counts are a coarse progress signal. Compare identity and content under a defined snapshot or reconciliation boundary. Use identity and content comparison at a defined progress boundary, and inspect mismatched ranges rather than assuming one aggregate statistic certifies the entire migration.
questions.tradeoff: Full comparison can be expensive at large scale.
questions.followup: Which partitioned checksums can narrow mismatched ranges?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new store receives a backfill and change stream. Old and new stores have equal row counts, but some updates and deletions may have been missed.

questions.title: Moving target
questions.prompt: Why compare stores at a common logical boundary?

choices.text: To make both stores use the same hardware
choices.why: Logical state does not require identical machines.
Deletes remain important.

choices.text: To distinguish true divergence from different replication progress
choices.why: The same intended history can be compared.

choices.text: To eliminate all future races permanently
choices.why: Ongoing synchronization still needs correctness.

questions.explanation: A mismatch can be expected if one store has applied more events. Record replay positions and compare states representing the same history. Track deletes and updates as well as inserts, since two replicas can have matching row counts while representing different points in the source's accepted history.
questions.tradeoff: Coordinating snapshots may pause work or retain logs.
questions.followup: How would you compare if the target supports only eventual snapshots?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new store receives a backfill and change stream. Old and new stores have equal row counts, but some updates and deletions may have been missed.

questions.title: Release gate
questions.prompt: What should block cutover?

choices.text: Any difference in internal file layout
choices.why: Implementations can differ while semantics match.

choices.text: Unexplained invariant violations or incomplete required source ranges
choices.why: The target's authoritative readiness is unproven.
Physical efficiency can differ legitimately.

choices.text: A different database version string alone
choices.why: Version difference is not itself a failed invariant.

questions.explanation: A cutover gate should focus on the contract consumers require. Keep unexplained differences visible rather than masking them with aggregate agreement. Keep accepted differences explicit and versioned so later engineers can distinguish intentional semantic changes from discrepancies that were merely ignored to meet a deadline.
questions.tradeoff: Strict gates can delay migration while exceptions are investigated.
questions.followup: Which differences can be explicitly accepted and documented?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new store receives a backfill and change stream. Old and new stores have equal row counts, but some updates and deletions may have been missed.

questions.title: Repair validation
questions.prompt: A repair job rewrites mismatched rows. What evidence is still needed?

choices.why: It may have repaired incomplete or stale inputs.
Size is not correctness.

choices.text: The dashboard stopped showing errors after alerts were disabled
choices.why: That removes evidence rather than fixes state.

choices.text: Repeat reconciliation with concurrent-write protection and tracked coverage
choices.why: The corrected state is verified against the intended boundary.

questions.explanation: Repair execution is not repair correctness. Revalidation must ensure live updates were not overwritten during the fix. Verify repair checkpoints correspond to durable target effects, and rerun comparisons on changed ranges so a successful job exit cannot conceal partial or stale repair.
questions.tradeoff: Repeated comparison adds load and may need throttling.
questions.followup: How would a repair be made idempotent and safely resumable?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new store receives a backfill and change stream. Old and new stores have equal row counts, but some updates and deletions may have been missed.

questions.title: Deterministic clock
questions.prompt: What improves repeatability of lease-expiry tests?

choices.why: They remain slow and scheduler-dependent.

choices.text: Inject a controllable clock and explicit scheduler steps
choices.why: The test can place operations around the exact boundary.
Real code has timing transitions.

choices.text: Only run tests on faster laptops
choices.why: Speed does not control interleavings.

questions.explanation: Make time an input to the state machine where possible. Test just-before, at and just-after the defined expiry rule without waiting in real time. Keep a small number of real integration tests for scheduler and transport behavior, since a controllable clock validates state logic but can abstract away deployment-specific timing.
questions.tradeoff: A fake clock must not hide real network and scheduler behavior.
questions.followup: Which integration tests still need real-time execution?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A worker has a lease and an external write path. Production can pause a worker beyond lease expiry and later resume it. Unit tests currently use real sleeps.

questions.title: Stale worker schedule
questions.prompt: Which sequence most directly tests missing fencing?

choices.text: Pause owner A, expire its lease, let B acquire, then resume A's write
choices.why: It exposes authority that outlives ownership.

choices.text: Run A alone with no pause
choices.why: No competing ownership exists.

choices.text: Start ten workers and assert one log line
choices.why: Logs do not prove external write exclusion.

choices.text: Only test an expired credential string
choices.why: Lease authority may be separate from authentication.

questions.explanation: The dangerous schedule is not merely two workers starting together. It is a previously legitimate worker acting after replacement. Assert the actual external write result, not merely worker log messages, because both processes can believe their behavior is correct while the shared effect is duplicated.
questions.tradeoff: Controlled pauses require hooks or a test runtime.
questions.followup: How would the external store reject A's stale generation?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A worker has a lease and an external write path. Production can pause a worker beyond lease expiry and later resume it. Unit tests currently use real sleeps.

questions.title: Model checker scope
questions.prompt: What is a useful small model?

choices.text: Every production byte and packet at once
choices.why: The state space becomes impractical.
The risky interleaving is excluded.

choices.text: Two workers, lease generations, pauses and conditional writes
choices.why: It captures the invariant with manageable state.
It does not model ownership transitions.

questions.explanation: Abstract away irrelevant implementation detail while preserving competing authority. Check the safety invariant across all modeled interleavings. Document omitted mechanisms and map important assumptions back to code, because a correct abstract model does not establish that the implementation faithfully enforces its transitions.
questions.tradeoff: An abstraction can omit a real implementation bug.
questions.followup: How would model assumptions become executable integration tests?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A worker has a lease and an external write path. Production can pause a worker beyond lease expiry and later resume it. Unit tests currently use real sleeps.

questions.title: Classify the guarantee
questions.prompt: Match each claim to the property or evidence category it describes. Use each choice once.

items.text: No obsolete lease generation can commit an external write.
A valid pending job eventually completes if a worker is continuously available and scheduled.
Two hundred tested schedules showed no duplicate effect.
The model assumes messages are eventually delivered after the partition heals.

choices.why: It prohibits a bad state transition regardless of whether useful work progresses.

choices.text: Liveness property with explicit progress assumptions
choices.why: It promises eventual useful completion under stated availability and scheduling conditions.
Observed passing schedules increase confidence but are not an exhaustive proof.
The system's progress reasoning depends on a property supplied by the modeled environment.

questions.explanation: Separate the guarantee from the assumptions and the evidence supporting it. Fencing can establish a safety boundary while every worker remains stalled, so it does not alone prove liveness. A model's eventual-delivery assumption and a finite test campaign must remain visible when translating results into a production claim. Keep assumptions such as eventual delivery and worker scheduling visible in reports, since violating them can remove progress without contradicting the modeled safety invariant.
questions.tradeoff: Stronger progress guarantees require stronger environmental assumptions or additional mechanisms.
questions.followup: What happens to the liveness argument if message delivery can be delayed forever?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A worker has a lease and an external write path. Production can pause a worker beyond lease expiry and later resume it. Unit tests currently use real sleeps.

questions.title: Restore acceptance
questions.prompt: Which check is stronger than database startup?

choices.text: A successful process exit code from the restore command
choices.why: It does not prove application correctness.
Connectivity is only one prerequisite.

choices.text: Application-level invariants and representative read/write journeys
choices.why: They exercise usable restored state.

choices.text: The backup manifest reports a recent creation timestamp
choices.why: Recency is useful but does not prove that restored application invariants and required integrations work.

questions.explanation: Restore validation must cross the boundary the business needs. A healthy process can serve incomplete or internally inconsistent data. Include representative authorization and mutation checks after restoration, since readable rows alone do not prove that the recovered application can safely resume its normal responsibilities.
questions.tradeoff: Deep validation extends measured recovery time.
questions.followup: Which invariants are essential before admitting writes?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A database backup restores successfully in a clean region. The application starts, but there may be missing recent writes, invalid references or unavailable encryption keys.

questions.title: Data-loss boundary
questions.prompt: How should the drill measure recovery point?

choices.text: Compare known committed markers and recovered history against the failure boundary
choices.why: The gap is measured from evidence.

choices.text: Use backup job start time alone
choices.why: The captured consistency point may differ.
Replication state and acknowledgement policy matter.
Table presence does not measure recent history.

questions.explanation: Measure which acknowledged facts survived, not only when files were copied. Distinguish missing, pending and confirmed recovered operations. Represent timed-out or in-flight operations as uncertain where appropriate, and avoid counting their absence as confirmed data loss without knowing the original acknowledgement boundary.
questions.tradeoff: Fine-grained markers need durable correlation.
questions.followup: How would in-flight unknown writes be represented in the report?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A database backup restores successfully in a clean region. The application starts, but there may be missing recent writes, invalid references or unavailable encryption keys.

questions.title: Restore dependencies
questions.prompt: Which omission can invalidate a disaster-ready claim?

choices.text: Different hostnames in the recovery region with correctly updated routing
choices.why: Hostnames can legitimately change; the relevant issue is whether dependencies still resolve and authorize correctly.

choices.text: Untested access to required decryption keys and identities
choices.why: Restored bytes may be unusable.

choices.text: A changed dashboard layout with the same validated telemetry
choices.why: Presentation changes alone do not invalidate the service's recovery boundary.

choices.text: A different backup compression format that has been successfully decoded and validated
choices.why: An encoding change is not itself a recovery failure once data and application behavior are verified.

questions.explanation: Recovery includes authority and configuration as well as data. Ensure required control systems are not all in the failed region. Test access to keys and credentials under the intended disaster permissions, not an administrator's normal environment, because emergency identity restrictions can be the actual blocker.
questions.tradeoff: Duplicating key access needs careful security design.
questions.followup: How can key recovery preserve separation of duties?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A database backup restores successfully in a clean region. The application starts, but there may be missing recent writes, invalid references or unavailable encryption keys.

questions.title: Evidence statement
questions.prompt: What should the drill report say?

choices.text: Disaster recovery is guaranteed for all scenarios
choices.why: One drill cannot establish that.
That omits user-level outcome.
The full critical path matters.

choices.text: State tested scale, fault, recovered data boundary, validated journeys and remaining gaps
choices.why: The claim is bounded and actionable.

questions.explanation: A useful report enables another engineer to understand exactly what was exercised. Include failed assumptions and manual steps rather than hiding them behind a pass badge. Record manual decisions and untested dependencies as remaining gaps, so leadership can distinguish a rehearsed recovery envelope from a general promise the exercise did not establish.
questions.tradeoff: Honest reports may reveal unfinished readiness work.
questions.followup: Which gap should block a production launch?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A database backup restores successfully in a clean region. The application starts, but there may be missing recent writes, invalid references or unavailable encryption keys.

questions.title: Agreement limit
questions.prompt: What does agreement between engines prove?

choices.text: Both are correct for all inputs
choices.why: They may share a defect or omit cases.

choices.text: They agree on the tested input under the comparison rule
choices.why: Correctness still depends on a trustworthy specification.
Outputs do not measure speed.

choices.text: The old implementation is now bug-free
choices.why: Comparison does not repair it.

questions.explanation: Differential testing is a powerful discrepancy detector, not an automatic truth oracle. Known legacy bugs require independent expected behavior. Use known legacy defects as explicit exceptions backed by the desired semantics, rather than teaching the new engine to reproduce every behavior of an imperfect reference.
questions.tradeoff: Triangulating with a simple model adds effort.
questions.followup: Which query subset can be checked against a minimal reference implementation?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new query engine replaces a legacy implementation. The old engine has known bugs. Both can execute the same generated queries on synthetic datasets.

questions.title: Normalize carefully
questions.prompt: Which difference can be safely normalized only when the contract allows it?

choices.text: Row order for an explicitly unordered query
choices.why: Equivalent sets can appear in different orders.

choices.text: Missing rows in a complete-result query
choices.why: That changes meaning.
Arithmetic results are semantic.
That violates access policy.

questions.explanation: Comparison rules must follow the API contract. Over-normalization can hide real bugs while under-normalization creates noisy false alarms. State whether results use set, multiset or ordered-list semantics, because normalizing away duplicate rows or ordering can conceal real violations for the wrong query contract.
questions.tradeoff: Floating-point and approximate queries need explicit tolerances.
questions.followup: How would duplicate rows be compared under bag rather than set semantics?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new query engine replaces a legacy implementation. The old engine has known bugs. Both can execute the same generated queries on synthetic datasets.

questions.title: Discrepancy triage
questions.prompt: The engines disagree on a null-handling edge case. Best next step?

choices.text: Declare the new engine wrong automatically
choices.why: The legacy engine has known bugs.
They may affect correctness or security.

choices.text: Reduce the case and compare both against specified null semantics
choices.why: The expected result comes from the contract.

choices.text: Change the generator to avoid nulls
choices.why: That hides the uncovered boundary.

questions.explanation: A minimized case turns a vague discrepancy into a reviewable semantic decision. Record which behavior is intended before changing either implementation. Retain the reduced query and dataset as a regression case once the semantic decision is made, including why the intended result differs from any preserved legacy behavior.
questions.tradeoff: Clarifying undocumented behavior may require product decisions.
questions.followup: How would a deliberate bug fix be communicated as a compatibility change?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new query engine replaces a legacy implementation. The old engine has known bugs. Both can execute the same generated queries on synthetic datasets.

questions.title: Shadow execution safety
questions.prompt: What must shadow queries avoid?

choices.why: Comparisons need results.
Representative inputs can be useful with safeguards.
Performance evidence is valuable.

choices.text: Unintended writes, data exposure and overload of shared dependencies
choices.why: The shadow path must be non-authoritative and bounded.

questions.explanation: A shadow system is still real load and can have side effects. Constrain execution and sensitive-data access before treating it as a harmless observer. Budget shadow traffic separately and restrict sensitive data use, since a non-authoritative result can still overload storage or disclose data through debug traces and evaluation logs.
questions.tradeoff: Sanitization can reduce realism.
questions.followup: How would you sample expensive queries without biasing coverage toward easy ones?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A new query engine replaces a legacy implementation. The old engine has known bugs. Both can execute the same generated queries on synthetic datasets.

questions.title: Fuzz target boundary
questions.prompt: What is a useful target?

choices.text: A deterministic decode path accepting arbitrary bytes with bounded resources
choices.why: It exercises malformed input without unrelated network setup.

choices.text: Only a constructor called with one valid constant
choices.why: Most parsing paths remain untested.

choices.text: A full production deployment that sends real customer messages
choices.why: Side effects and nondeterminism hinder safe fuzzing.

choices.text: A target that silently skips every invalid input before decoding
choices.why: The risky parser is bypassed.

questions.explanation: Expose the smallest meaningful untrusted-input boundary. Preserve enough initialization to exercise real validation and error handling. Preserve parser state that matters for version negotiation while removing unrelated side effects, so the target remains reproducible without becoming an unrealistic simplified decoder.
questions.tradeoff: A narrow target can miss integration assumptions.
questions.followup: Which framing layer needs a separate target?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service decodes versioned binary messages from disk and the network. Malformed lengths, unknown fields and truncated records are possible. The parser must reject invalid input without unsafe resource use.

questions.title: Interesting assertions
questions.prompt: Which properties are useful? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Every byte string must decode successfully
choices.why: Malformed inputs should be rejected.

choices.text: No crashes or unbounded allocations on bounded input
choices.why: Resource safety is part of robust rejection.

choices.text: Decoded output must always be empty
choices.why: Valid messages carry data.

choices.text: Valid encode/decode round trips preserve defined semantics
choices.why: It checks behavior beyond process survival.

questions.explanation: Crash freedom alone is insufficient for a parser that can misinterpret data. Combine resource bounds with semantic properties and well-defined invalid-input behavior. Use independent valid-message fixtures and malformed-input cases alongside round trips, because an encoder and decoder can share the same mistaken interpretation and still agree.
questions.tradeoff: Round-trip agreement can still share encoder/decoder bugs.
questions.followup: What independent corpus covers compatibility with other implementations?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service decodes versioned binary messages from disk and the network. Malformed lengths, unknown fields and truncated records are possible. The parser must reject invalid input without unsafe resource use.

questions.title: Failure corpus
questions.prompt: What should happen to a minimized crashing input after repair?

choices.text: Remove the reproducer after the fix to keep the corpus small
choices.why: A minimized regression is useful evidence; deduplicate the corpus without discarding the only test of the repaired defect.

choices.text: Keep only the stack trace and a summary of the malformed message
choices.why: Exact bytes may be necessary to reproduce parser state and boundary conditions.

choices.text: Retain it as a regression case and continue broader fuzzing
choices.why: The known path stays covered while exploration continues.

choices.text: Run only the single regression input in future campaigns
choices.why: The known case remains covered, but broader input exploration would stop.

questions.explanation: A small reproducer is valuable operational evidence. Preserve the relevant parser version and expected rejection or decode result. Store the exact input and expected bounded behavior with appropriate confidentiality controls, then verify that the fix rejects or decodes it for the right semantic reason.
questions.tradeoff: Corpus growth needs deduplication and maintenance.
questions.followup: How would you prevent a sensitive production payload from entering a public corpus?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service decodes versioned binary messages from disk and the network. Malformed lengths, unknown fields and truncated records are possible. The parser must reject invalid input without unsafe resource use.

questions.title: Passing fuzz campaign
questions.prompt: What is an honest release conclusion?

choices.text: The parser accepts only safe inputs forever
choices.why: Finite coverage cannot establish that.

choices.text: No violation was found under the campaign's corpus, instrumentation and budget
choices.why: The evidence boundary is explicit.

choices.text: Schema compatibility is proven for every client
choices.why: Fuzzing may not cover supported semantic contracts.
Limits remain defense in depth.

questions.explanation: Fuzzing explores a large input space but is not an exhaustive proof. State sanitizer coverage, duration and known untested layers alongside the result. Report unsupported formats and integration layers explicitly, and rerun campaigns when framing, allocation or version-handling changes create paths outside the earlier coverage.
questions.tradeoff: Longer campaigns consume compute and still need triage.
questions.followup: Which changes should invalidate the previous campaign's confidence?
questions.context: Hypothetical scenario. A service decodes versioned binary messages from disk and the network. Malformed lengths, unknown fields and truncated records are possible. The parser must reject invalid input without unsafe resource use.

questions.title: Replace check-then-act
questions.prompt: Which statement protects one-row stock against concurrent decrements?

choices.text: Read quantity, then unconditionally write the computed value
choices.why: Concurrent clients can act on the same old value.

choices.text: UPDATE quantity = quantity - 1 WHERE quantity > 0, then check affected rows
choices.why: The predicate and modification share the row update boundary.

choices.text: Check a cached quantity before inserting an order
choices.why: The cache is not the reservation authority.

choices.text: Run the same unsafe code with a longer timeout
choices.why: Timing does not enforce the invariant.

questions.explanation: The stock predicate and decrement must be one authoritative atomic row operation. With the stated PostgreSQL behavior, a competing updater waits and reevaluates the condition against the updated row, so only available stock is consumed. Checking quantity earlier in application code leaves a race between observation and mutation.
questions.tradeoff: A popular SKU remains a contention point.
questions.followup: How would you reserve multiple units with the same approach?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 service stores one inventory row per SKU. Quantity must never be negative. Each order reserves one unit and records a unique order ID in the same database. Transactions run at Read Committed unless specified.

questions.title: Connect reservation and order creation
questions.prompt: Why should the decrement and order insert share a transaction?

choices.text: It makes every future refund automatic
choices.why: Refunds are separate business operations.
Transport failures remain possible.

choices.text: A failure should not leave stock consumed without its corresponding order, or vice versa
choices.why: The two records represent one local business transition.

choices.text: It removes the need for a unique order ID
choices.why: Retries can still duplicate intent without uniqueness.

questions.explanation: The stock decrement and order row describe one local business transition: the reservation must belong to an order, and a confirmed order must have its reservation. A shared transaction prevents a failure between those writes from exposing only one side. External payment or notification effects remain outside this database boundary.
questions.tradeoff: Larger transactions hold resources longer.
questions.followup: Which external effects cannot be included in this local transaction?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 service stores one inventory row per SKU. Quantity must never be negative. Each order reserves one unit and records a unique order ID in the same database. Transactions run at Read Committed unless specified.

questions.title: A zero-row update
questions.prompt: The conditional decrement affects no rows for an existing SKU. What should happen?

choices.text: Treat it as no reservation and do not create a confirmed order
choices.why: The stock predicate was not satisfied.

choices.text: Create the order because the SQL statement succeeded
choices.why: Statement execution success is not a successful reservation.
That can produce negative stock.

choices.text: Assume the database lost the SKU
choices.why: The SKU is stated to exist.

questions.explanation: A successfully executed SQL statement can legitimately affect zero rows when its predicate is false. For the existing SKU, that means no unit was reserved, so order confirmation must not proceed. Distinguish this business outcome from database failure and from a missing SKU when defining the API response.
questions.tradeoff: Clients need a clear out-of-stock response.
questions.followup: How would you distinguish missing SKU from insufficient quantity?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 service stores one inventory row per SKU. Quantity must never be negative. Each order reserves one unit and records a unique order ID in the same database. Transactions run at Read Committed unless specified.

questions.title: A lost commit response
questions.prompt: The transaction may have committed before the connection failed. What enables safe retry?

choices.text: A fresh order ID each time
choices.why: That creates another business intent.

choices.text: Reading stock and guessing whether this order caused the change
choices.why: Other orders can change the same row.

choices.text: Assuming connection failure rolled back everything
choices.why: The commit outcome is uncertain.

choices.text: A stable order ID with transactional duplicate handling
choices.why: The retry can discover or reuse the original order outcome.

questions.explanation: A connection can fail after the database committed but before the client learned the result. A stable unique order ID lets a retry find or reuse that original intent rather than decrement inventory again. Guessing from current stock cannot identify the first attempt because other orders also change quantity.
questions.tradeoff: Replay records and conflict semantics need retention policy.
questions.followup: How would you return the original result after a retry?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 service stores one inventory row per SKU. Quantity must never be negative. Each order reserves one unit and records a unique order ID in the same database. Transactions run at Read Committed unless specified.

questions.title: Relevant concurrency tests
questions.prompt: Which tests directly challenge the invariant? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Many buyers compete for one remaining unit
choices.why: This probes overselling.

choices.text: Failure between decrement and order insert
choices.why: This probes local atomicity.

choices.text: Only sequential orders with plentiful stock
choices.why: That avoids the critical race.

choices.text: Retry the same order ID after ambiguous commit
choices.why: This probes duplicate business effects.

questions.explanation: The one-unit race tests exclusion between different buyers, the mid-transaction failure tests atomicity between stock and order, and the ambiguous-commit retry tests duplicate intent. These are independent properties. Assert durable order counts and remaining stock after recovery rather than only checking which requests returned success.
questions.tradeoff: Fault injection must assert durable state after recovery.
questions.followup: Which counts should agree after every test run?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 service stores one inventory row per SKU. Quantity must never be negative. Each order reserves one unit and records a unique order ID in the same database. Transactions run at Read Committed unless specified.

questions.title: Address a hot SKU
questions.prompt: One row limits a flash sale. Which staff-level response preserves the invariant?

choices.text: Remove the stock predicate under peak load
choices.why: That abandons correctness.

choices.text: Compare admission queues or allocated inventory partitions with explicit conservation rules
choices.why: Throughput changes must preserve total available stock.

choices.text: Read stock from an async replica before decrementing blindly
choices.why: Stale reads can oversell.

choices.text: Shard reservation rows by order ID without allocating a conserved stock budget to each shard
choices.why: Independent shards could each admit orders against the same original stock unless rights or coordination preserve the total.

questions.explanation: A hot SKU is one logical scarce resource, so adding API workers does not remove its conservation constraint. Admission queues or allocated inventory rights can change where contention occurs, but must preserve the total number of sellable units. Rebalancing rights and returning unused allocations require their own safe protocol.
questions.tradeoff: Escrowed partitions can strand units and complicate rebalancing.
questions.followup: How would you return unused allocated stock safely?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 service stores one inventory row per SKU. Quantity must never be negative. Each order reserves one unit and records a unique order ID in the same database. Transactions run at Read Committed unless specified.

questions.title: Lock only what the invariant needs
questions.prompt: Why prefer a row-scoped atomic operation over locking the entire inventory table?

choices.text: Table locks never block readers or writers
choices.why: Their conflict scope can be broad.

choices.text: Row locks remove every deadlock possibility
choices.why: Multi-row operations can still deadlock.

choices.text: Unrelated SKUs need not serialize with this SKU
choices.why: The invariant here is per row.

choices.text: Row locks make local data globally replicated
choices.why: Lock scope and replication are different concerns.

questions.explanation: Unrelated SKU rows do not participate in this SKU's nonnegative-quantity invariant. Row-scoped atomic updates preserve their concurrency, while a table lock unnecessarily serializes independent sales. A bundle reservation changes the invariant's scope and may need multiple locks in a consistent order or another transaction strategy.
questions.tradeoff: A later cross-SKU bundle requires a wider protocol.
questions.followup: What lock ordering would a multi-SKU reservation use?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 service stores one inventory row per SKU. Quantity must never be negative. Each order reserves one unit and records a unique order ID in the same database. Transactions run at Read Committed unless specified.

questions.title: Define failure before scaling
questions.prompt: An architecture proposal splits orders and stock across services. What must be reevaluated?

choices.text: The former local atomic transition and its failure recovery contract
choices.why: Separate databases no longer share the same transaction automatically.

choices.text: Assume two local ACID transactions automatically preserve the old combined atomicity
choices.why: Each database can commit independently, leaving partial cross-service outcomes.

choices.text: Keep the original isolation level and omit cross-service recovery states
choices.why: Local isolation does not resolve a failure between independent service commits.

choices.text: Treat an exactly-once broker feature as proof that stock and order effects are atomic
choices.why: A transport or broker guarantee does not automatically include both services' business-state transitions.

questions.explanation: Splitting stock and orders across independent databases removes the local all-or-nothing boundary that made their transition simple. Revisit pending states, compensation, retries and reconciliation before calling the split equivalent. The new design may be acceptable, but temporary reservation leakage or overselling must be an explicit business decision.
questions.tradeoff: A saga may expose pending states or require compensation.
questions.followup: Would overselling or temporary reservation leakage be acceptable?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 service stores one inventory row per SKU. Quantity must never be negative. Each order reserves one unit and records a unique order ID in the same database. Transactions run at Read Committed unless specified.

questions.title: Identify the anomaly
questions.prompt: Why can both transactions commit and leave no one on call?

choices.text: Both necessarily update the same row
choices.why: They update different rows.

choices.text: Each snapshot supports its decision, but the decisions violate a cross-row invariant together
choices.why: This is a write-skew pattern.
PostgreSQL Repeatable Read does not allow dirty reads.

choices.text: The database must choose one transaction as a deadlock victim
choices.why: Different-row updates need not deadlock.

questions.explanation: Both transactions read the initial two-person roster and update different rows, so they can each see a valid reason to leave without a direct write-write conflict. Together their decisions violate the cross-row rule. A stable snapshot prevents some anomalies, but does not make every read-dependent decision serializable.
questions.tradeoff: Higher isolation or explicit coordination adds contention or retries.
questions.followup: How would this differ if both transactions updated one shared guard row?
questions.caseTitle: A snapshot permits the wrong pair of decisions
questions.context: Hypothetical on-call roster has two rows, A and B, initially on_call=true. At least one must stay on call. Under PostgreSQL 18 Repeatable Read, each transaction reads both rows and turns only its own row off if it sees the other on call. They execute concurrently.

questions.title: Serializable resolution
questions.prompt: What should an application expect if both use PostgreSQL Serializable correctly?

choices.text: Both invalid decisions must still commit
choices.why: That would violate serializable execution.

choices.text: The database silently edits their business logic
choices.why: It does not invent a valid roster assignment.

choices.text: A conflicting execution can abort a transaction, which must be retried from the start
choices.why: Serializable isolation preserves valid serial outcomes through conflict handling.

choices.text: No transaction can ever fail once begun
choices.why: Serialization failures are an expected possibility.

questions.explanation: Serializable execution must correspond to some valid one-at-a-time order, and in either such order the second departure should observe that nobody else remains. The database can therefore abort a conflicting transaction. The application must retry the whole decision on a fresh transaction rather than treat aborts as exceptional corruption.
questions.tradeoff: Retries can be frequent under heavy contention.
questions.followup: What backoff and retry limit would protect the database?
questions.caseTitle: A snapshot permits the wrong pair of decisions
questions.context: Hypothetical on-call roster has two rows, A and B, initially on_call=true. At least one must stay on call. Under PostgreSQL 18 Repeatable Read, each transaction reads both rows and turns only its own row off if it sees the other on call. They execute concurrently.

questions.title: An explicit guard
questions.prompt: Now use PostgreSQL Read Committed. Every writer first acquires the same per-roster guard lock in one statement, then reads the roster in a new statement in that transaction and holds the guard through commit. What does this accomplish?

choices.text: It serializes the read-decide-write critical section for that roster
choices.why: The second writer reads after the first releases the guard.

choices.text: It makes all unrelated rosters wait if guards are per roster
choices.why: Different guard rows need not conflict.

choices.text: It proves no writer can bypass the protocol
choices.why: All writers must actually follow it.

choices.text: It makes cached roster reads authoritative
choices.why: The guarded transaction must still read appropriate state.

questions.explanation: The guard serializes participating writers. Under Read Committed, the separate roster-read statement takes a fresh snapshot after guard acquisition, so a waiting writer observes the prior holder's committed change. Combining the lock and roster read into one statement could retain a snapshot taken before the wait. Every write path must hold the guard through its decision and commit.
questions.tradeoff: The guard can become a bottleneck and requires universal participation.
questions.followup: How would administrative tools be forced to obey the guard protocol?
questions.caseTitle: A snapshot permits the wrong pair of decisions
questions.context: Hypothetical on-call roster has two rows, A and B, initially on_call=true. At least one must stay on call. Under PostgreSQL 18 Repeatable Read, each transaction reads both rows and turns only its own row off if it sees the other on call. They execute concurrently.

questions.title: Retry scope matters
questions.prompt: A serializable transaction aborts. What is unsafe?

choices.text: Starting a new transaction and rereading the roster
choices.why: That is the intended retry shape.

choices.text: Keeping the same logical request ID
choices.why: This can preserve business identity.
That protects capacity.

choices.text: Retrying only the final UPDATE using the old decision
choices.why: The decision depended on a snapshot that no longer supports it.

questions.explanation: The rejected transaction's decision was computed from a snapshot involved in a serialization conflict. Retrying only its final write preserves that stale decision and discards the protection. Restart the complete read-decide-write operation, keeping irreversible external effects outside the retried region or making them replay safe.
questions.tradeoff: Whole-transaction retries repeat computation.
questions.followup: How would you keep irreversible external actions out of the retried region?
questions.caseTitle: A snapshot permits the wrong pair of decisions
questions.context: Hypothetical on-call roster has two rows, A and B, initially on_call=true. At least one must stay on call. Under PostgreSQL 18 Repeatable Read, each transaction reads both rows and turns only its own row off if it sees the other on call. They execute concurrently.

questions.title: Separate isolation properties
questions.prompt: Which statements hold for PostgreSQL 18 Repeatable Read? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Repeated ordinary reads use a stable transaction snapshot
choices.why: Later committed changes do not refresh the snapshot.

choices.text: Cross-row write skew can still occur
choices.why: Stable snapshots do not guarantee serializability.
They are not allowed.

choices.text: Concurrent updates of the same row can cause a serialization failure
choices.why: The implementation can reject such an update.

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL 18 Repeatable Read uses a stable snapshot and rejects some concurrent same-row updates, but different-row write skew can still violate a cross-row invariant. Its behavior is not identical to every database product using the same isolation label. Review the engine's actual semantics and test the business invariant.
questions.tradeoff: Portability requires reviewing each engine's semantics.
questions.followup: Which tests would you rerun when changing database engines?
questions.caseTitle: A snapshot permits the wrong pair of decisions
questions.context: Hypothetical on-call roster has two rows, A and B, initially on_call=true. At least one must stay on call. Under PostgreSQL 18 Repeatable Read, each transaction reads both rows and turns only its own row off if it sees the other on call. They execute concurrently.

questions.title: Choose a system-wide policy
questions.prompt: Several services modify the roster using different isolation levels. What should a staff engineer establish?

choices.text: Let every service choose independently without an invariant contract
choices.why: One unsafe writer can break the shared rule.

choices.text: A shared invariant protocol covering every write path and operational tool
choices.why: Correctness depends on participation, not one endpoint's setting.

choices.text: Require all reports to use cached data
choices.why: Read caching does not coordinate writers.

choices.text: Only add an alert when everyone is off call
choices.why: Detection is useful but does not enforce the rule.

questions.explanation: One correctly configured endpoint cannot protect a shared invariant if another service or maintenance script writes through a weaker path. Establish a common protocol covering every participant, with migration and enforcement ownership. An alert can detect violations, but does not replace the mechanism preventing invalid commits.
questions.tradeoff: A common protocol can restrict autonomous service evolution.
questions.followup: How would you migrate legacy writers without an unsafe overlap period?
questions.caseTitle: A snapshot permits the wrong pair of decisions
questions.context: Hypothetical on-call roster has two rows, A and B, initially on_call=true. At least one must stay on call. Under PostgreSQL 18 Repeatable Read, each transaction reads both rows and turns only its own row off if it sees the other on call. They execute concurrently.

questions.title: Construct the exposing schedule
questions.prompt: Which test setup reliably targets write skew?

choices.text: Commit A completely before B starts reading
choices.why: That allows B to observe A off call.
There is no competing decision.

choices.text: Synchronize both reads before allowing either different-row write
choices.why: Both decide from the initial roster.

choices.text: Use two transactions updating an unrelated table
choices.why: That does not exercise the roster invariant.

questions.explanation: The anomaly requires both decisions to be made before either change is visible to the other transaction. Synchronizing both reads before releasing the different-row writes creates that schedule deliberately. A sequential test allows the second reader to see the first departure and therefore misses the write-skew behavior.
questions.tradeoff: Deterministic tests are narrower than randomized stress tests.
questions.followup: What invariant checker would you run after random concurrent schedules?
questions.caseTitle: A snapshot permits the wrong pair of decisions
questions.context: Hypothetical on-call roster has two rows, A and B, initially on_call=true. At least one must stay on call. Under PostgreSQL 18 Repeatable Read, each transaction reads both rows and turns only its own row off if it sees the other on call. They execute concurrently.

questions.title: Redesign the invariant boundary
questions.prompt: A single roster now contains thousands of participants and changes constantly. What should be evaluated?

choices.text: Narrower independent rosters or a guarded count with equivalent business semantics
choices.why: Changing the model may reduce coordination while preserving the rule.

choices.text: Dropping the last-person constraint because contention is high
choices.why: That changes the product's safety requirement.
More contenders may increase conflicts.

choices.text: Assuming snapshots become serializable at larger scale
choices.why: Scale does not strengthen isolation.

questions.explanation: Coordination cost follows the invariant's data boundary. If the business can define independent rosters or a correctly maintained shared count, the design may reduce the expensive read set or contention pattern. That is a semantic redesign requiring proof of equivalent rules, not permission to remove the last-person constraint.
questions.tradeoff: A count must remain consistent with membership and may itself be hot.
questions.followup: What failure cases arise when maintaining a materialized on-call count?
questions.caseTitle: A snapshot permits the wrong pair of decisions
questions.context: Hypothetical on-call roster has two rows, A and B, initially on_call=true. At least one must stay on call. Under PostgreSQL 18 Repeatable Read, each transaction reads both rows and turns only its own row off if it sees the other on call. They execute concurrently.

questions.title: Read the wait graph
questions.prompt: What condition exists after both second lock requests?

choices.text: Only a slow query with no dependency cycle
choices.why: Each transaction waits for the other.
Neither can proceed while holding its first lock.
The scenario describes locks, not uncommitted reads.
Both are blocked before completion.

questions.explanation: T1 holds account 10 while waiting for 20, and T2 holds 20 while waiting for 10. These dependencies form a cycle, so neither can finish without intervention. A long wait alone is not necessarily a deadlock; the cycle is the distinguishing evidence in this schedule.
questions.tradeoff: Detection resolves a victim but does not remove the underlying pattern.
questions.followup: How would lock-wait telemetry identify the participating statements?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 ledger updates two account rows in one transaction. Transfer T1 locks account 10 then requests 20. Transfer T2 locks 20 then requests 10. Account identifiers are immutable. Transfers can be retried with a stable business operation ID.

questions.title: Prevent this cycle
questions.prompt: Which rule prevents the stated account-row cycle if all transfers follow it?

choices.why: Opposite-direction transfers still acquire opposite orders.

choices.text: Sleep before taking the second lock
choices.why: Timing cannot exclude the cycle.

choices.text: Acquire account locks in ascending account-ID order
choices.why: Every transfer uses the same total order.
That prolongs waiting without removing the cycle.

questions.explanation: If every transfer acquires its account locks in ascending immutable-ID order, no transfer can hold 20 while waiting for 10. That removes the circular-wait pattern for these account locks. Other tables, advisory locks or external resources can still create cycles unless their acquisition order is also addressed.
questions.tradeoff: Other resources can still introduce different deadlock cycles.
questions.followup: How would the rule extend to account and transfer-metadata locks together?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 ledger updates two account rows in one transaction. Transfer T1 locks account 10 then requests 20. Transfer T2 locks 20 then requests 10. Account identifiers are immutable. Transfers can be retried with a stable business operation ID.

questions.title: Recover the victim
questions.prompt: The database aborts T2 as a deadlock victim. What should the application retry?

choices.text: The entire transfer transaction with its stable intent ID
choices.why: Its previous transaction has failed and all dependent decisions must be redone.
The transfer would no longer preserve debit-credit atomicity.
No response can complete an aborted transfer.
That may duplicate intent if outcome handling is ambiguous.

questions.explanation: After deadlock victim selection, the transfer transaction has failed; its debit, credit and read-derived decisions must be retried together. Preserve the logical transfer identity so recovery does not create a new intent. Retrying only one statement can break the two-sided balance invariant even if the statement itself succeeds.
questions.tradeoff: Repeated contention requires bounded backoff and visibility.
questions.followup: Which errors should not be retried automatically?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 ledger updates two account rows in one transaction. Transfer T1 locks account 10 then requests 20. Transfer T2 locks 20 then requests 10. Account identifiers are immutable. Transfers can be retried with a stable business operation ID.

questions.title: Keep transactions short
questions.prompt: Why avoid waiting for an external fraud API while holding both account locks?

choices.text: The external fraud decision automatically rolls back when the SQL transaction aborts
choices.why: An unrelated external service does not participate in the local database rollback unless an explicit protocol says so.

choices.text: Holding the account locks guarantees the external API cannot time out
choices.why: Database locks do not control network or external-service availability.

choices.text: An external call does not count toward lock-holding time because no SQL is executing
choices.why: The transaction still retains its locks while application code waits.

choices.text: The wait extends lock occupancy and contention for unrelated transfers involving those accounts
choices.why: Remote latency expands the critical section.

questions.explanation: A remote fraud call can take unpredictable time or never respond while the transaction retains both account locks. That extends the critical section and blocks other transfers involving those accounts. Moving work earlier helps only if the final transaction revalidates any assumptions that could change during the remote wait.
questions.tradeoff: Moving validation outside requires revalidating assumptions before commit.
questions.followup: Which fraud decision inputs could change while the call is in flight?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 ledger updates two account rows in one transaction. Transfer T1 locks account 10 then requests 20. Transfer T2 locks 20 then requests 10. Account identifiers are immutable. Transfers can be retried with a stable business operation ID.

questions.title: Read the right operational evidence
questions.prompt: Which measurements help investigate transfer contention? Select all that apply.

choices.why: They expose the dependency chain.
Long transactions retain locks longer.
It conceals waiting and aborted work.

choices.text: Deadlock rate grouped by statement and account-access pattern
choices.why: It links failures to acquisition patterns.

questions.explanation: Blocker identity and lock-wait duration reveal who is waiting for whom, while transaction duration shows how long locks remain held. Deadlock grouping connects those observations to acquisition patterns. Successful transfer counts alone can look acceptable while customers experience long queues, repeated aborts and retry amplification.
questions.tradeoff: Detailed lock telemetry can be expensive at high volume.
questions.followup: How would you sample without missing rare but severe incidents?

questions.title: A misleading scaling response
questions.prompt: Why can doubling the connection pool worsen this incident?

choices.text: More connections always halve database CPU
choices.why: Capacity is not guaranteed to scale that way.

choices.text: More simultaneous contenders can lengthen queues around the same hot accounts
choices.why: The serialized resource has not become faster.

choices.text: Row locks are disabled with larger pools
choices.why: Pool size does not change lock semantics.

choices.text: The pool determines transaction isolation automatically
choices.why: Isolation is configured separately.

questions.explanation: The hot accounts still serialize conflicting transfers, regardless of how many connections submit them. A larger pool can add contenders and lengthen queues without increasing useful throughput. Increase concurrency only when evidence shows independent work was unnecessarily limited, not as a reflexive response to lock waits.
questions.tradeoff: A larger pool can help when independent work was unnecessarily limited.
questions.followup: Which evidence would justify increasing versus reducing admitted concurrency?
questions.context: Hypothetical PostgreSQL 18 ledger updates two account rows in one transaction. Transfer T1 locks account 10 then requests 20. Transfer T2 locks 20 then requests 10. Account identifiers are immutable. Transfers can be retried with a stable business operation ID.

questions.title: Do not use SKIP LOCKED blindly
questions.prompt: Why is skipping a locked account unsuitable for an exact two-account transfer?

choices.text: SKIP LOCKED is invalid for any queue workload
choices.why: It can be useful for work claiming.
Skipping does not corrupt IDs.

choices.text: Omitting one required account changes the business operation
choices.why: Both sides are necessary for this transfer.

choices.text: It guarantees the other transaction has failed
choices.why: A held lock does not imply failure.

questions.explanation: An exact transfer requires both specified account rows; skipping one because it is locked changes the operation rather than making it safely concurrent. SKIP LOCKED is useful when a worker may choose any available task from a set. Its semantics do not fit a mandatory two-account update.
questions.tradeoff: Queue consumers may intentionally accept incomplete candidate sets.
questions.followup: What query is an appropriate use of skipping locked rows?

questions.title: Order a documented lock protocol
questions.prompt: For a transfer between accounts 10 and 20, the protocol requires ascending locks, both mutations, then commit. Order these steps.

The order prevents the stated account-lock cycle and keeps debit and credit atomic. questions.title: The dual-write gap
questions.prompt: Why is 'commit order, then publish event' insufficient on its own?

choices.text: Database crash recovery automatically reruns the application's later broker call
choices.why: Database recovery restores database state; it does not reconstruct an unrecorded application obligation to publish.

choices.text: A crash after commit but before publish can leave a durable order without its event
choices.why: The two writes do not share atomicity.

choices.text: Every database commit is eventually rolled back
choices.why: Committed state normally persists.

choices.text: A broker acknowledgment automatically includes the earlier database commit in one distributed transaction
choices.why: The scenario defines independent systems without such a shared commit protocol.

questions.explanation: The order can commit durably and then the process can crash before sending its event. Reversing the writes creates the opposite risk: an event for an order that never commits. Persisting both business state and publication intent in one local transaction closes that local dual-write gap.
questions.tradeoff: Cross-system transactions may be possible but impose their own constraints.
questions.followup: What changes if publication occurs before the database commit?
