questions.context: Hypothetical order service uses one transactional database and an external message broker. Each committed order must eventually produce an OrderCreated event. Broker delivery is at least once. Consumers perform their own durable business effects.

questions.title: Persist the intent atomically
questions.prompt: What should the local transaction include?

choices.text: Only a flag in process memory
choices.why: Memory does not survive the relevant crash.

choices.text: A broker acknowledgment stored before creating the order
choices.why: That reverses rather than closes the atomicity gap.

choices.text: The order row and an outbox event record
choices.why: Both either commit or fail together locally.
Operational logs are not the defined delivery queue.

questions.explanation: The outbox row records a durable obligation to publish exactly when the order becomes durable. Either both records commit or neither does, so recovery can find unfinished publication work. This does not atomically include the broker; a relay still needs retry, monitoring and cleanup semantics.
questions.tradeoff: The outbox needs a relay, retention and monitoring.
questions.followup: Which fields are needed to identify and order events?

questions.context: Hypothetical order service uses one transactional database and an external message broker. Each committed order must eventually produce an OrderCreated event. Broker delivery is at least once. Consumers perform their own durable business effects.

questions.title: The relay crash window
questions.prompt: The relay publishes, then crashes before marking the outbox row delivered. What should be expected?

choices.text: The event may be published again after restart
choices.why: The durable row still appears pending.

choices.text: The broker automatically removes the order
choices.why: Broker delivery does not undo the database.

choices.text: No duplicate is possible because the order transaction was atomic
choices.why: The relay crosses another boundary.

choices.text: The outbox must be discarded entirely
choices.why: Pending records remain useful recovery state.

questions.explanation: After publishing successfully, the relay can crash before its database records that success. Recovery sees the same pending row and may publish it again. This is expected at-least-once behavior, not evidence that the local order transaction failed; consumers must handle repeated event identity safely.
questions.tradeoff: Consumers need replay-safe handling.
questions.followup: How would a consumer atomically deduplicate and update its own database?

questions.title: Consumer atomicity
questions.prompt: A consumer inserts event ID into a dedup table, then separately updates its business state. What is unsafe?

choices.why: Stable identity is useful.
Redelivery is expected.

choices.text: The dedup table has a unique key
choices.why: Uniqueness helps but is not sufficient alone.

choices.text: A crash between the two commits can suppress an effect that never happened
choices.why: Deduplication and effect must share an atomic or recoverable boundary.

questions.explanation: Marking an event processed in one commit and applying its business effect in another creates a loss window. A crash after the first commit makes retries skip an effect that never happened. questions.title: Measure eventual delivery
questions.prompt: Which signals help establish the relay's health? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Age of the oldest unpublished event
choices.why: It reveals delayed obligations.
They reveal growing work and failures.
Orders can commit while publication stalls.

choices.text: Consumer lag and reconciliation of expected versus observed event IDs
choices.why: Publishing alone is not downstream processing.

questions.explanation: Order latency can remain healthy while the relay accumulates unpublished obligations or a downstream consumer stops progressing. questions.tradeoff: Cross-system reconciliation requires stable IDs and retention.

questions.title: Event order contract
questions.prompt: Two updates to the same order must be consumed in order. What is needed beyond an outbox table?

choices.why: Timestamps can tie or reflect skew.

choices.text: A per-order sequence and a relay/consumer protocol that preserves or verifies it
choices.why: Ordering must survive publication and processing.

choices.text: Only sorting the dashboard by order ID
choices.why: Display order is unrelated to event application.

choices.text: Assuming all brokers guarantee one global order
choices.why: Ordering guarantees are product- and partition-specific.

questions.explanation: The outbox table alone does not define how multiple events for one order reach and execute at a consumer. A per-order sequence supplies ordering evidence, while partitioning, relay behavior and consumer gap handling must preserve or verify it. Do not infer global order from timestamps or a broker's existence.
questions.tradeoff: Per-entity ordering can constrain parallelism for hot entities.
questions.followup: What should a consumer do when it receives sequence 8 before 7?

questions.title: Backfill during migration
questions.prompt: A new consumer needs historical orders and live events. What risk must the migration address?

choices.text: Order IDs cannot appear in snapshots
choices.why: They can and should identify records.

choices.text: Live events always wait for backfill automatically
choices.why: Coordination is not automatic.

choices.text: A gap or overlap at the snapshot-to-stream boundary
choices.why: A consistent frontier and deduplication are needed.

choices.text: A larger broker message size proves completeness
choices.why: Capacity does not establish coverage.

questions.explanation: Historical backfill and the live stream must meet at a defined frontier. Otherwise a record can fall between the snapshot and subscription, or be processed twice in their overlap. Use stable identities, a consistent coverage boundary and validation before claiming the new consumer has complete history.
questions.tradeoff: Dual processing and validation cost resources.
questions.followup: How would you prove every pre-cutover order was represented?

questions.title: Delete delivery evidence carefully
questions.prompt: When can outbox records be purged safely?

choices.text: After the defined delivery, replay and audit obligations no longer require them
choices.why: Retention follows the recovery contract.
The relay may not have published yet.

choices.text: Whenever the table becomes inconveniently large
choices.why: Space pressure does not prove delivery.

choices.text: As soon as one consumer polls the broker
choices.why: Other consumers and replay requirements may remain.

questions.explanation: An outbox record can be removed only after the system's delivery, replay and audit obligations no longer depend on it. Table size alone is not evidence of that condition. Define the recovery horizon and, if needed, move older evidence to a separate archive before reclaiming operational storage.
questions.tradeoff: Long retention raises storage and indexing costs.
questions.followup: Would a separate archive preserve audit needs more cheaply?

questions.caseTitle: Translate a benchmark into fleet size
questions.context: Peak demand is 7000 requests per second. In a hypothetical representative benchmark, one worker sustains 300 requests per second at full usable capacity. Planning allows only 55 percent of that capacity. Assume even distribution and linear scaling.
questions.title: Translate a benchmark into fleet size · exercise 1
questions.prompt: What is the minimum whole number of workers needed before adding any separate failure reserve?
questions.explanation: The utilization target reduces usable capacity per worker. Divide demand by that reduced capacity and round up, because a fractional worker cannot serve the remaining demand. This is not a claim that real fleets scale linearly.
questions.tradeoff: More reserve costs money; a lower reserve can amplify queues during pauses, hot partitions or deployment churn.
questions.followup: Which benchmark distributions would make this average per-worker number unsafe?

numeric.rounding: Use an integer, applying the stated ceiling or floor.
numeric.formula: ceiling(peak ÷ (per-worker capacity × allowed fraction))

questions.prompt: What is the minimum whole number of workers needed before adding any separate failure reserve?
questions.explanation: The utilization target reduces usable capacity per worker. Divide demand by that reduced capacity and round up, because a fractional worker cannot serve the remaining demand. This is not a claim that real fleets scale linearly.
questions.tradeoff: More reserve costs money; a lower reserve can amplify queues during pauses, hot partitions or deployment churn.
questions.followup: Which benchmark distributions would make this average per-worker number unsafe?

numeric.rounding: Use an integer, applying the stated ceiling or floor.
numeric.formula: ceiling(peak ÷ (per-worker capacity × allowed fraction))

questions.caseTitle: Survive the loss of one availability zone
questions.context: A service runs the same integer number of nodes in each of 3 zones. A node has a tested safe capacity of 500 requests per second after headroom. questions.title: Survive the loss of one availability zone · exercise 1
questions.prompt: What minimum total node count satisfies both equal placement and the single-zone-loss requirement?
questions.explanation: First size the nodes per surviving zone. A failed zone contributes zero capacity. Round the per-zone requirement up and then multiply by the original zone count. Rounding a fractional total without enforcing equal placement can under-provision a survivor.
questions.tradeoff: The reserve is only useful if routing, quotas and downstream stores can also tolerate the zone loss.
questions.followup: What shared dependencies could make a mathematically sufficient multi-zone fleet fail anyway?

numeric.rounding: Use an integer, applying the stated ceiling or floor.
numeric.formula: zones × ceiling(peak ÷ ((zones − 1) × safe node capacity))

questions.caseTitle: Separate logical data from retained physical bytes
questions.context: Ingest 2000 records per second, each 300 uncompressed bytes. Retain 7 days. Compression leaves 35 percent of the original bytes. Keep 3 full copies of the compressed records. Ignore indexes, metadata and compaction workspace. One TB is 10^12 bytes.
questions.title: Separate logical data from retained physical bytes · exercise 1
questions.prompt: How many decimal TB are required for the retained record copies?
questions.explanation: Count logical bytes over the full retention period, then apply compression and replication. A retention figure in days must be converted to seconds before multiplying by a per-second ingest rate.
questions.tradeoff: This excludes several real storage costs. Deletes, indexes, repair traffic and compaction may need substantial additional capacity.
questions.followup: How would you measure the worst temporary disk footprint while backfilling and compacting simultaneously?

numeric.rounding: Round to four decimal places, or enter a more precise value.
numeric.formula: rate × bytes × seconds/day × days × compression fraction × copies ÷ 10^12

questions.caseTitle: Convert payload bytes into link demand
questions.context: A service emits 1000 responses per second, each 12000 application bytes. For this estimate, total on-wire bytes equal 1.1 times application bytes. Use decimal gigabits.
questions.title: Convert payload bytes into link demand · exercise 1
questions.prompt: What outbound bandwidth is required in gigabits per second?
questions.explanation: Multiply rate by response size to get bytes per second, include the stated overhead, then convert bytes to bits. A gigabit is not a gigabyte.
questions.tradeoff: A bandwidth budget does not establish latency; loss, connection setup and congestion can still dominate.
questions.followup: When would compression reduce total cost but worsen the latency objective?

numeric.rounding: Round to four decimal places, or enter a more precise value.
numeric.formula: responses/second × bytes/response × overhead × 8 ÷ 10^9

questions.caseTitle: Estimate concurrent requests with Little’s law
questions.context: A stable system completes 1000 requests per second. Mean time inside the measured boundary, including waiting, is 40 milliseconds. Assume the measurement window is long enough for the averages to be representative.
questions.title: Estimate concurrent requests with Little’s law · exercise 1
questions.prompt: What is the mean number of requests inside that same boundary?
questions.explanation: The rate and duration must refer to the same system boundary and compatible units. Convert milliseconds to seconds. Little’s law relates averages; substituting p99 latency does not give a valid p99 concurrency estimate.
questions.tradeoff: This is a mean, not a safe admission limit. Bursts and correlated latency require additional measurements.
questions.followup: How would you distinguish time waiting for a connection from time executing at the database?

numeric.rounding: Round to four decimal places, or enter a more precise value.
numeric.formula: L = arrival rate × mean time in system

questions.caseTitle: Drain a queue while new work keeps arriving
questions.context: A queue contains 100000 jobs. New jobs arrive at 800 per second. Workers complete 1500 per second. Rates remain constant and no jobs fail or retry.
questions.title: Drain a queue while new work keeps arriving · exercise 1
questions.prompt: How long until the initial backlog is cleared while continuing to serve new arrivals?
questions.explanation: Only capacity above ongoing arrivals reduces the backlog. Dividing by total completion capacity assumes arrivals stop, which is not this scenario. If completion did not exceed arrivals, the queue would not drain under these assumptions.
questions.tradeoff: More consumers may overload the sink or leave a hot partition unchanged; capacity must exist at the bottleneck.
questions.followup: What is the safest way to accelerate a replay when customer traffic shares the same downstream store?

numeric.rounding: Round to four decimal places, or enter a more precise value.
numeric.formula: backlog ÷ (completion rate − arrival rate)

questions.caseTitle: Size the database behind a cache
questions.context: The application receives 10000 reads per second. A request-level cache hit avoids all database reads and occurs for 60 percent of requests. Each miss issues 1 database reads. Ignore retries and refresh traffic.
questions.title: Size the database behind a cache · exercise 1
questions.prompt: What database read rate does this model predict?
questions.explanation: Apply the hit rate at the request boundary where it is defined. Only misses fan out. This is different from independently caching each database lookup.
questions.tradeoff: A high steady-state hit rate hides cold-cache risk; invalidation storms can expose the full read demand.
questions.followup: What admission controls would protect the database after a fleet-wide cache restart?

numeric.rounding: Round to four decimal places, or enter a more precise value.
numeric.formula: request rate × miss fraction × reads per miss

questions.title: Size the database behind a cache · exercise 20
questions.prompt: What database read rate does this model predict?
questions.explanation: Apply the hit rate at the request boundary where it is defined. Only misses fan out. This is different from independently caching each database lookup.
questions.tradeoff: A high steady-state hit rate hides cold-cache risk; invalidation storms can expose the full read demand.
questions.followup: What admission controls would protect the database after a fleet-wide cache restart?

numeric.rounding: Round to four decimal places, or enter a more precise value.
numeric.formula: request rate × miss fraction × reads per miss

questions.context: A request succeeds only when three required components are available. Their modeled availabilities are 98, 99, and 99.5 percent. Assume availability events are statistically independent and there are no other failure causes.
questions.title: Combine required dependencies · exercise 1
questions.prompt: What is the modeled end-to-end availability percentage?
questions.explanation: All three required events must occur, so multiply their probabilities under the explicit independence assumption. Adding availability percentages or averaging them does not model a required serial dependency chain.
questions.tradeoff: Real outages are often correlated. Shared regions, identities or networking can make this simple estimate optimistic.
questions.followup: Which dependency could become optional without violating the core user journey?

numeric.rounding: Round to four decimal places, or enter a more precise value.
numeric.formula: A = A1 × A2 × A3, using fractions, then × 100

questions.context: There are 2 identical replicas, each available 90 percent of the time. One healthy replica can serve the entire workload. Failures are independent; routing and detection are perfect. No shared dependency can fail.
questions.title: Model independent active redundancy · exercise 1
questions.prompt: Under this deliberately idealized model, what is the service availability percentage?
questions.explanation: The service fails only when every replica is unavailable. Multiply the failure probabilities and take their complement. Requiring a majority instead of one replica would produce a different answer.
questions.tradeoff: Independence and perfect failover are strong assumptions. This is an upper-level model, not an achievable SLO promise.
questions.followup: How would you test the correlated-failure assumptions before presenting this number to leadership?

numeric.rounding: Round to four decimal places, or enter a more precise value.
numeric.formula: 1 − (1 − per-replica availability)^replicas, then × 100

questions.caseTitle: Translate an availability objective into time
questions.context: A time-based availability objective is 99 percent over exactly 28 days. Every minute has equal weight, with no excluded maintenance periods.
questions.title: Translate an availability objective into time · exercise 1
questions.prompt: How many unavailable minutes does the full-window error budget allow?
questions.explanation: The error budget is the permitted unavailable fraction of the specified window. Use the exact number of days, rather than silently assuming every month is 30 days.
questions.tradeoff: Time-based and request-based objectives answer different questions when traffic is uneven.
questions.followup: Would a ten-minute outage at peak business hours deserve the same product response as one overnight?

numeric.rounding: Round to four decimal places, or enter a more precise value.
numeric.formula: window minutes × (1 − objective fraction)

questions.followup: Which customer and incident signals would justify freezing a rollout before the projected budget exhaustion?

questions.caseTitle: Find the minimum intersecting read quorum
questions.context: A fixed replica set has N = 5 members. Each acknowledged write stores its value on any W = 2 members. A read contacts any R members. Consider only the combinatorial guarantee that each read set intersects each acknowledged write set. Ignore sloppy quorums and membership changes.
questions.title: Find the minimum intersecting read quorum · exercise 1
questions.prompt: What is the smallest R that guarantees this intersection?
questions.explanation: Two subsets can be disjoint when their combined size is at most the full set size. Requiring their sum to exceed N forces overlap. Overlap alone does not solve concurrent writes, version selection or linearizability.
questions.tradeoff: Larger read quorums reduce available reads during failures and may add latency.
questions.followup: What additional protocol rules are needed before claiming that an overlapping quorum read returns the latest completed write?

numeric.rounding: Use an integer, applying the stated ceiling or floor.
numeric.formula: R + W > N, so minimum integer R = N − W + 1

questions.caseTitle: Satisfy both storage and write-rate limits
questions.context: The dataset occupies 8 TB and receives 18000 writes per second. Each shard safely stores 1.2 TB and sustains 2500 writes per second. These capacities already include local headroom. Assume perfectly even data and write distribution.
questions.title: Satisfy both storage and write-rate limits · exercise 1
questions.prompt: What minimum shard count satisfies both constraints?
questions.explanation: Storage and throughput are independent lower bounds on the same shard count. Choose the larger bound, not their sum. Even distribution is explicit and often the least reliable assumption.
questions.tradeoff: More shards add routing and operational overhead, and do not automatically split a single hot key.
questions.followup: How would a tenant occupying 30 percent of total write traffic change the placement plan?

numeric.rounding: Use an integer, applying the stated ceiling or floor.
numeric.formula: max(ceiling(total bytes ÷ bytes/shard), ceiling(total writes ÷ writes/shard))

questions.caseTitle: Stay within a shared connection limit

questions.prompt: What is the largest whole-number pool limit per application instance?
questions.explanation: This is an upper-bound allocation, so round down. Rounding up lets aggregate pools exceed the database limit. A larger connection pool does not by itself increase database throughput.
questions.tradeoff: Small pools introduce local queueing; large pools can worsen contention and overload. Autoscaling changes the aggregate demand.
questions.followup: How should the application pool budget change while both old and new instances coexist during a rollout?

numeric.rounding: Use an integer, applying the stated ceiling or floor.
numeric.formula: floor((database limit − reserved connections) ÷ instance count)

questions.explanation: This is an upper-bound allocation, so round down. Rounding up lets aggregate pools exceed the database limit. A larger connection pool does not by itself increase database throughput.
questions.tradeoff: Small pools introduce local queueing; large pools can worsen contention and overload. Autoscaling changes the aggregate demand.
questions.followup: How should the application pool budget change while both old and new instances coexist during a rollout?

numeric.rounding: Use an integer, applying the stated ceiling or floor.
numeric.formula: floor((database limit − reserved connections) ÷ instance count)

questions.context: A process can use 4 CPU cores. Target utilization is 50 percent. Profiling a hypothetical workload shows 1.5 CPU milliseconds per request, summed across all its threads. Ignore every non-CPU bottleneck and assume parallel efficiency.
questions.title: Estimate CPU-bound sustainable throughput · exercise 1
questions.prompt: What request rate consumes exactly the target CPU budget?
questions.explanation: A core contributes 1000 CPU milliseconds per second. Divide the usable aggregate CPU time by per-request CPU cost. Wall-clock request latency is not interchangeable with CPU service demand.
questions.tradeoff: Memory bandwidth, locks, garbage collection and downstream waits can invalidate a CPU-only sizing model.
questions.followup: How would you prove that adding cores, rather than reducing lock contention, is the right next optimization?

numeric.formula: cores × target fraction × 1000 CPU ms/second ÷ CPU ms/request

questions.context: 5 percent of a fixed workload remains serial. The rest parallelizes perfectly over 2 workers. Ignore communication, scheduling and synchronization overhead. Compare with one worker on that same fixed workload.
questions.title: Bound the payoff of parallelization · exercise 1
questions.prompt: What ideal speedup does Amdahl’s model predict?
questions.explanation: Normalize the original runtime to one. The serial portion stays unchanged while only the parallel portion shrinks. Speedup is original time divided by new time, not the number of workers.
questions.tradeoff: This already optimistic bound excludes overhead. Reducing the serial fraction can outperform buying more parallel capacity.
questions.followup: Which profiling evidence would distinguish a fundamentally serial stage from accidental implementation contention?

numeric.rounding: Round to four decimal places, or enter a more precise value.
numeric.formula: 1 ÷ (serial fraction + parallel fraction ÷ workers)

questions.explanation: Normalize the original runtime to one. The serial portion stays unchanged while only the parallel portion shrinks. Speedup is original time divided by new time, not the number of workers.
questions.tradeoff: This already optimistic bound excludes overhead. Reducing the serial fraction can outperform buying more parallel capacity.
questions.followup: Which profiling evidence would distinguish a fundamentally serial stage from accidental implementation contention?

numeric.rounding: Round to four decimal places, or enter a more precise value.
numeric.formula: 1 ÷ (serial fraction + parallel fraction ÷ workers)

questions.caseTitle: Estimate the cost of outbound data

questions.title: Estimate the cost of outbound data · exercise 1
questions.prompt: What is the modeled egress charge for this period?
questions.explanation: Count billed bytes, convert to the explicitly decimal billing unit and multiply by the stated unit price. Request charges and compute costs are separate dimensions, deliberately excluded.
questions.tradeoff: A CDN or compression changes both traffic and price structure; do not compare just one isolated bill line.
questions.followup: How would you compare total cost of ownership for caching when hit rate varies sharply by region?

numeric.rounding: Round to four decimal places, or enter a more precise value.
numeric.formula: response count × bytes/response ÷ 10^9 × price/GB

questions.context: A cache has 2 GiB of RAM, where one GiB is 2^30 bytes. Only 65 percent is allocated to entries. Each entry uses 1000 payload bytes and 128 overhead bytes. Assume fixed-size entries and that the reserve covers every other memory cost.
questions.title: Budget cache entries including overhead · exercise 1
questions.prompt: What maximum whole number of entries fits the allocated entry budget?
questions.explanation: Add overhead to payload before dividing the memory budget. Use binary GiB rather than decimal GB. Round down because the final partial entry cannot be stored.
questions.tradeoff: Real allocators, variable sizes and fragmentation complicate the estimate; validate resident memory under realistic churn.
questions.followup: Why could a cache with enough bytes still have poor value if its eviction policy does not match the workload?

numeric.rounding: Use an integer, applying the stated ceiling or floor.
numeric.formula: floor(GiB × 2^30 × usable fraction ÷ (payload + overhead))

questions.title: An interleaving of read-modify-write operations · trace 1
questions.context: The counter starts at 11. Every displayed event executes atomically in this exact order, under a sequentially consistent toy model. A thread computes from its saved read, not the current counter. There is no lock or atomic increment.
questions.trace:
T3: read counter -> 11
T2: read counter -> 11
T1: read counter -> 11
T2: write saved_read + 5 -> 16
T1: write saved_read + 1 -> 12
T4: read counter -> 12
T4: write saved_read + 5 -> 17
T3: write saved_read + 2 -> 13
questions.prompt: What value remains in the counter after the final displayed event?

choices.why: This is the result obtained by applying the stated transition rules to every event in order.
This adds every intended increment as though each read-modify-write operation were atomic; the shown schedule must be checked for stale saved reads.
This ignores completed writes. The final displayed write overwrites the shared counter.
This is an earlier value, not necessarily the last completed write.

questions.explanation: The write values in order are 16, 12, 17, 13. The final write wins, leaving 13. The fully serialized total would be 24; equality in a particular schedule does not make this implementation safe for all schedules.
questions.tradeoff: An atomic increment or one lock covering the entire read-modify-write protects this single counter. Separate synchronization for the read and write is insufficient.
questions.followup: Give a different legal schedule that exposes a lost update, and specify the invariant a concurrency test should check.

questions.title: Reject stale writers at the protected resource · trace 1
questions.context: The storage resource durably remembers the greatest accepted token, initially zero. It atomically accepts a write if token is at least that greatest value, then updates the greatest value. Equal-token writes are allowed. Smaller-token writes are rejected. Do not infer acceptance from the writer’s belief about a lease.

This ignores rejection of older fencing tokens after a newer token is accepted.
The largest token is an authority epoch, not a count of accepted writes.
Multiple writes may be accepted, including repeated writes with the same current token.

questions.explanation: Acceptance by write number: 1: accept; 2: accept; 3: reject; 4: accept; 5: reject; 6: reject; 7: reject; 8: reject. The resource finishes with greatest token 5. It accepted 3 writes; a repeated current token does not represent an older owner in this specified rule.
questions.tradeoff: Fencing requires enforcement at the resource doing the mutation. A lease check only in the client cannot stop a paused old process after it resumes.

questions.caseTitle: Recover from the durable prefix of a log
questions.title: Recover from the durable prefix of a log · trace 1
questions.context: A toy redo-only engine starts at a durable snapshot balance of 100. Transactions run sequentially, with absolute SET records. On recovery, replay only transactions whose BEGIN, SET and COMMIT are all in the durable log prefix. Ignore volatile memory and all records beyond the stated flush boundary.
questions.trace:
1. BEGIN T1
2. SET T1 balance=172
3. COMMIT T1
4. BEGIN T2
5. SET T2 balance=254
6. COMMIT T2
7. BEGIN T3
8. SET T3 balance=356   <-- durable prefix ends here
9. COMMIT T3
10. BEGIN T4
11. SET T4 balance=462
12. COMMIT T4
CRASH
questions.prompt: What balance does recovery produce?

choices.why: This is the value written by the last fully committed transaction in the durable prefix, or the snapshot if none committed.
This value belongs to the snapshot or another transaction. A visible SET without its durable COMMIT is not replayed by the stated recovery rule.
This value belongs to the snapshot or another transaction. A visible SET without its durable COMMIT is not replayed by the stated recovery rule.
This value belongs to the snapshot or another transaction. A visible SET without its durable COMMIT is not replayed by the stated recovery rule.

questions.explanation: There are 8 durable log records, containing 2 complete three-record transactions. T2 is the last replayed transaction and sets 254. A record shown in the trace is not necessarily on stable storage.
questions.tradeoff: Flushing every commit minimizes acknowledged loss but costs latency. Group commit can amortize a flush while retaining a clearly defined acknowledgement boundary.
questions.followup: What changes if pages can contain uncommitted updates or the storage device lies about flush completion?
